blocks.p: The stories of Magic take place in the Multiverse: a vast number of separate worlds, which are called planes. One plane, Dominaria, lies at the centre of most of the story, and the history of the whole Multiverse is dated by Dominaria's calendar. That calendar counts years before and after the birth of a man named Urza, who comes into the story much later. A date written "AR" is a year in that calendar, and a date with a minus sign is a year before Urza's birth. Almost everything in the history happened within the last twenty-five thousand of those years. One entry stands far outside that span. About a hundred thousand years before Urza, on a plane called Equilor, a people began to seek enlightenment. Nothing older is recorded anywhere.

Everything known of Equilor comes from a single visit, made by Urza himself and his companion Xantcha, about a hundred thousand years after the Equilorans began their search. The story of that visit belongs to its own time. What they saw there is set down here, because it is all there is to say about the age before the dragons.

parts.h: A plane at the edge of time

blocks.p: Urza called Equilor the most ancient of all planes, a world from the edge of time. Equilor is also one of the most remote planes. Urza and Xantcha spent well over a thousand years looking for it. The people of Equilor told Urza afterwards that he had found them only because they had allowed him to. The Equilorans' magic, it is said, can hide their whole plane from the rest of existence.

Equilor did not look like a place of power. Nearly everything on the plane seemed used up and lying fallow. Its mountains were low and flat, as if nothing but the passing of ages had worn them down, and a mist hung over the land that never lifted: the Eon Fog. Stars were few. The nights, though, were crowded with life, with bats in great chittering carpets, birds whose songs were both sweet and sad, and things that howled. Travellers found it secretive, but not unfriendly.

There was one road, of grey stone cut in chevrons and fitted so closely that no grass grew between the blocks, lit by globes like spun cobweb that hung in the air. The road led to one town, without walls, of graceful houses that were pure white inside from the floors to the furniture.

The people of that town looked human. They wore knee-length robes over trousers, woven from a light silvery thread that rippled and caught the light when they moved. They were not immortal, but their lives ran to thousands of years; a child Urza and Xantcha met, still toddling, was past eighty. Their minds could not be read. No one can say whether they were planeswalkers or simply a civilisation that had taken magic further than any other.

What struck Urza most was how much the Equilorans knew, and how little they did with their knowledge. Over the ages of their search the Equilorans had gathered an immense store of knowledge, reaching far beyond their own world to distant matters in the wider Multiverse. And they left almost all of it unused. They seemed to have outgrown the wish to be great, and even boredom.
In caves in the flattened mountains lived the elders, who are described as mysterious spirits. It was the elders who spoke with Urza, for weeks at a time.
One other place on the plane is known by name, though not explained: Bloodhill Bastion, a city on a hill that seems to be grown from living flesh, with sphinx-like creatures standing guard over it.

parts.h: What it means for the rest of the story

blocks.p: Two things follow from Equilor. The first is that Dominaria, for all that the chronicle is counted from it and so much of the Multiverse's fate turns on it, was not always the centre of things. There was at least one world far older. The second is a judgment that the elders gave Urza. Urza had come to Equilor in fear of a dark power called Phyrexia, whose story begins a few chapters from here. The elders told Urza that the Multiverse is full of such dark powers, and that in the end those powers fall.
The Equilorans had been at their search for eighty thousand years when a shadow crossed the sky of a much younger world and the first dragons fell out of it.

chapters.title: The Birth of the Elder Dragons
sources: Kate Elliott, "Chronicle of Bolas: The Twins" (Wizards of the Coast, 13 June 2018)
Kate Elliott, "Chronicle of Bolas: The First Lesson" (Wizards of the Coast, 20 June 2018)
Kate Elliott, "Chronicle of Bolas: Things Unseen" (Wizards of the Coast, 27 June 2018)
Kate Elliott, "Chronicle of Bolas: Perspectives" (Wizards of the Coast, 8 August 2018)

blocks.p: Nobody wrote down the first days of the dragons. Writing did not exist yet, and the people who lived through what followed told it their own way. What survives is one witness's account: Ugin, the Spirit Dragon, told it long afterwards to the first shamans of the Jeskai on Tarkir, and they passed it on, master to student, learned by heart. Twenty thousand years later a young monk recited it to a Temur chief in the wilderness, and that is the telling followed here. It is Ugin's version. His brother tells it differently, and that comes later.

Before the dragons there was the Ur-Dragon: the first essence of all dragonkind, a thing older than the worlds it flies between. Those who glimpsed it in visions describe a shadow vast enough to darken a sky, terrible and blind, a creature of the place between places. Where its wings beat, storms follow, and out of the storms fall stones of many colours. Each stone is a dragon curled tight upon itself. Some never wake, and strike the ground as dead rock. The ones that wake uncurl in the air, open their wings and fly.

One beat of those wings passed over Dominaria about twenty thousand years before Urza was born, and seven egg-stones fell from it towards a lone volcano standing in a forested plateau. These were the first dragons the plane had known, and they came to be called the Elder Dragons.
A dragon names itself. It wakes knowing who it is, and no dragon suffers another to name it.

The first to uncurl was the brightest, pale-winged and shining. It named itself Arcades Sabboth, and its eye went at once to a cluster of buildings beside a river, orderly and interesting. The second had scales with the sheen of metal and a voice full of pleased surprise: Chromium Rhuell, who wanted to know what all of it meant, and who settled on the rim of the volcano to dry his soft scales in the heat rising from it. The third burst out reddish-green and howling, with spiralling horns: Palladia-Mors, whose name was hers and no one else's.

Two of the largest stones never opened. They ploughed into the mountainside and left craters with broken bodies in them. Palladia-Mors looked them over, judged them too weak to wake, and was glad to be rid of them. Then two last, small stones came tumbling down behind the rest, like an afterthought. She called those useless too, and left to hunt the herds on the grassland. Arcades flew off towards his buildings. Chromium, the only one who wondered what had become of the late stones, circled the peak, saw nothing, noticed another fall of egg-stones far away over a distant range, decided those must be cousins, and went to look.
So none of them saw what happened at the foot of the mountain.

The sixth stone opened late. A green dragon unfurled just above the trees, landed hard in a clearing, rolled, and came up with one wing dragging. The clearing was not empty. A party of human hunters stood there with nets, iron-tipped spears and lean dogs over a great beast they had just brought down, its blood still steaming. The dragon was newborn and ravenous. She roared her name at them, Merrevia Sal, and demanded the meat on pain of death.

The hunters gave way, and Merrevia Sal ate. But the hunters had seen the injured wing. While her head was down they spread out around her, drawing back when she coughed smoke at them and creeping in again when she returned to the carcass. Then they threw a net over her head. She heaved upward to fly, lifting the men who clung to the net's edges clean off their feet, but the net fouled her wings above the treetops and she came down thrashing. She crushed one man in the fall, burned two, tore a fourth open. That gave the hunters' leader an opening on her other side, and the leader drove his spear deep into the soft scales of her belly. Two more put spears in her eye. The dogs went for the wound.
She dragged herself into the trees and went on fighting, because she was a dragon. She killed five hunters and three dogs before the shouting in the forest turned to cheering.

The seventh stone had held two dragons. They fell twenty paces from that clearing, through the branches and into the ferns, and one of them was pinned under a broken trunk. The smaller dragon was free. He looked at the trapped one and knew his name at once: Nicol. Nicol knew the smaller dragon's name just as surely: Ugin. Nicol told Ugin to be quiet and look at what was happening in the clearing.

The twins watched their sister Merrevia Sal die through the leaves. Nicol, trapped, was in a frenzy to reach her: that small, weak creatures should lay hands on one of his own was not to be borne. Ugin worked the branches off Nicol piece by piece, quietly, and clamped his claws round his brother's muzzle when Nicol opened his mouth to roar, because a roar would have brought the hunters down on a dragon who could not move. By the time Nicol was loose it was over. The death of a dragon smells of honey, and the smell came to them on the wind.

Nicol wanted to burn every one of the hunters. Ugin held Nicol back by the leg. There were many hunters and only two small dragons, Ugin pointed out, and not one of those men could have killed Merrevia Sal alone. First the twins should find the other dragons who had fallen with them, Ugin said, since numbers were what had made the hunters strong. Nicol called that running away. Ugin answered that being careful and being afraid are different things. When the hunters' dogs found the twins' scent, Nicol bit the head off the first dog, liked the taste, and learned something he never forgot: the dogs' teeth could not hurt him. The men were the danger, with their weapons and their way of doing together what none of them could do alone.

On the summit the twins found one of the craters and the dead dragon in it, far bigger than either of them. Nicol asked which was worse, never to wake, or to wake and spend your few moments in fear and fighting. Then he watched Palladia-Mors take a running beast out of a scattering herd, and decided that the fault had been Merrevia Sal's for failing to survive, and that the thing to be in this world was the hunter. Ugin was looking the other way, up, asking where they had come from and what lay beyond the sky.
That is the whole difference between them, and it was there on the first day.

Nicol Bolas remembers that day differently, and said so himself many ages later. In his version he fell alone. He woke first, breathed first and was already flying when he noticed a smaller creature still curled up and dropping beside him; he woke it with a slap of his wingtip and taught it what wings were for. He does not call Ugin his twin. That, he says, is a story Ugin spread to claim a share of his glory. He counts six dragons from that wingbeat where Ugin counts eight, leaving out the two who never woke. He says nothing of being pinned under a tree while his sister died. And he adds two things Ugin never mentions: that after a long childhood spent entirely on the wing it was he alone who first dared to land, and that he gave the world its name, Dominaria, because in setting his claws on it he had taken dominion over it.
Nobody else was there to say which of them is right. The rest of this chapter is Ugin's account.

The twins went looking for their kin. Ugin could not stop thinking about how short their sister's life had been. Nicol could not stop asking how they might have prevented it, and Ugin understood, though his brother would have denied it to the end of time, that Nicol was angry because he had been afraid.

The twins found their brother Chromium Rhuell stretched on a rock above a dark mountain lake, studying the things that lived in the water. Chromium was not glad of the interruption. He told the twins they were small, and that it took both of them to make one dragon his size. Dragons can read each other's names, and when Chromium read theirs he noticed something odd: each twin had only one name, where every other dragon had two. Chromium concluded that two names had been shared out between the pair. Chromium believed there was an order under the world, hard to see and worth a lifetime's looking. When Nicol only asked about hunting, Chromium sent the twins to their sister Palladia-Mors, who had no higher ambition than hunting.

Palladia-Mors was on the plains, burning down the hindmost animal of a herd, and she let the twins know that everything in sight was hers. She called the twins runts, flung the charred carcass of an old ibex at them, and went after something tastier. Ugin ate the ibex. Watching the flies and the small scavengers gather around it, Ugin had the first of his great thoughts: that nothing in the web of living and dying is wasted, and that death is a turn in a cycle and not an end. Nicol would not touch another dragon's leavings.

Learning to hunt was humiliating. The herds were better at escaping than the twins were at catching, and once Palladia-Mors glided in and lifted a gazelle from under their very claws. It was Nicol who saw the answer, and he took it from the men who had killed his sister: hunt together. The twins spent years at it, until no herd could keep its best animal from them.

The twins also learned to stay clear of the cousins from the other egg-fall. Vaevictis Asmadi, big and ugly, held a wide territory with his siblings and drove the twins out of it more than once, though it had game enough for many.

Far from the birth mountain the twins came on the largest human town they had ever seen, ringed by a wall of timber, stone and packed earth. Their eldest brother, Arcades Sabboth, was living in the middle of it. Arcades lay at his ease in a courtyard of river stones before a high-roofed hall, between bronze shields polished like mirrors, with a tree of carved ivory and golden leaves set before him. Scribes sat on mats painting letters on barkcloth. Petitioners knelt and waited for Arcades's judgment. The people called Arcades their Dragonlord.

The twins flew in openly, since the humans plainly did not fear dragons. Horns sounded, the walls filled with archers, and arrows rattled off the twins' bellies. Ugin felt his sister's death rise in his throat. Nicol did not hesitate: he rose against the sun, dived, and burned a tower and the soldiers on it. Then Arcades struck Nicol out of the air. It was Ugin who flew between his two brothers and talked.

Arcades explained. His people had taken the twins for raiders, because there were raiders: Vaevictis and his gang, and others. Arcades protected his humans from other dragons, and he was teaching them a better way to live than their own violence, under law. When Nicol reminded Arcades that humans had killed their sister, Arcades said that struggle was the way of life and death, and that humans had as much right to live as dragons. Arcades found humans interesting. Unlike dragons, he said, humans work together.

It was on that hill, to that brother, that Nicol first gave a second name: he introduced himself as Nicol Bolas. Ugin had never heard it before and asked when that had happened. Every proper dragon has two names, his twin said. Ugin was content with one.

The twins stayed for years as Arcades's guests while the walls widened and the fields spread and ships that had crossed the ocean came into Arcades's two ports. The twins spent the years differently. Nicol made himself useful at Arcades's side and pushed his snout into every corner of human life: its greed, its rivalries, its worries, what people wanted and what they resented. Ugin found the noise of all that wearying, and attached himself to an old ascetic called Te Ju Ki, who lived in a roofless stone tower older than the town and spent her days thinking about things that cannot be seen.

Te Ju Ki taught Ugin that nothing ends; things only change form. She taught him to sit in silence. And she showed him a meditation in which she spun globes of light in the air, each tied to the others by threads of magic, turning about one another without touching. She called each globe a plane. This world, she said, was one layer among many, though no living body could ever pass from one to the next. Ugin did not know what a plane was. He only knew he could watch the globes for ever. After long practice he could make one small globe of his own.

One afternoon, while Ugin was admiring that single globe, screaming broke out in the storehouse yard. Ugin went to look, and found a man on his knees in the blood of the man's own brother. The two human brothers had run their parents' carting business together for years in perfect peace, their old quarrel over the inheritance long settled. Now, witnesses said, one brother had suddenly shouted that the other was stealing his birthright, and had put a knife in the other's chest. The killer stared at his own hands and asked who had stabbed his brother.
On the ridge of a roof above the yard lay Nicol, watching the scene the way one watches something one has made.

Ugin asked Nicol what he had done. Nothing, said Nicol; he had not moved from that spot. Then Nicol added that he had discovered a better way to get revenge. Was Ugin coming, or would Ugin stay with his tiresome old sage? Nicol was going to avenge their sister, as the twins should have done long ago. Nicol left without a word to Arcades, and was out of sight before Ugin understood that he meant it.

Arcades was not troubled by the killing. A magistrate would hear the case, Arcades said; humans keep their feelings weighted down for years and then a spark sets them off. It had happened before. Ugin could not rest. Te Ju Ki told Ugin that he could not study in that state, and that his journey was his own path to walk. Ugin did not want to leave. He went after his twin anyway, with the feeling of standing in a dry riverbed while rain darkens the far hills.

chapters.title: The Dragon-killers' War
sources: Kate Elliott, "Chronicle of Bolas: Things Unseen" (Wizards of the Coast, 27 June 2018)
Kate Elliott, "Chronicle of Bolas: Whispers of Treachery" (Wizards of the Coast, 11 July 2018)
Kate Elliott, "Chronicle of Bolas: Perspectives" (Wizards of the Coast, 8 August 2018)
Kate Elliott, "Chronicle of Bolas: Blood and Fire" (Wizards of the Coast, 18 July 2018)

blocks.p: The last chapter ended with the twin dragons parting for the first time. Nicol Bolas had flown off to take revenge on the humans who killed the twins' sister, Merrevia Sal, and Ugin had set out after him. This chapter is still Ugin's account.

Ugin had never flown anywhere without his twin. The road back to the birth mountain was long, because the years of wandering that had taken the twins to Arcades's realm had wound all over the continent. For the first time in his life Ugin slept with no other breathing beside his own.

Being alone frightened Ugin, and then it taught him something. Lying awake, he began to hear that everything breathes, plants too, and that no life is ever truly alone: each creature is one knot in a web too large to see. Some nights that comforted him. Other nights the sheer crowd of living things pressed on him like thunder that would not stop, and he understood how easily a single life is rubbed out and forgotten. He did not yet believe that could happen to a dragon's name.

Ugin found Nicol by accident, and found him in trouble. In a range of poor hill farms, where people in furs cleared ground with digging sticks behind log palisades, Vaevictis Asmadi and his red-crested siblings were burning longhouses and granaries for the pleasure of it. The burning was a sideshow. Vaevictis and his siblings were chasing another dragon, who ducked and twisted through every valley trying to lose them. Ugin knew the hunted dragon's shape at once. It was Nicol.
Ugin shouted his brother's name. Nicol vanished over a hill. Vaevictis turned, and came for Ugin with wings that covered half the sky and claws wet from slaughtered cattle.

Ugin could not outfly Vaevictis. For a moment Ugin simply froze, ashamed to discover that after all Te Ju Ki's teaching he was afraid to die. Then he thought that Nicol needed him. Ugin reached for the only magic he had. He spun two of Te Ju Ki's weightless globes of light and blew them at the huge dragon. Vaevictis had never seen anything like them. Vaevictis tumbled over himself trying to stop, and bellowed for his siblings. When the globes drifted against Vaevictis's scales and popped, harmless as soap bubbles, his roar of fright shook the air.

Nicol was suddenly at Ugin's side, laughing. Nicol had seen it all. Had Ugin really thought that Nicol would leave his twin to be torn apart by cousins who had not one brain between the four of them? After a while Ugin laughed too.

That night Nicol asked what the globes were, and lost interest as soon as he heard that the answer involved the old human teacher. No human, however old, could be as wise as the youngest dragon, Nicol said. Nicol had learned something special himself: there were lands beyond the ocean, with their own creatures and their own dragons. He was put out to find that Ugin already knew this. Nicol was sure those foreign dragons could not be the equals of the dragons of his own birth, since his own family had been the first and were therefore the strongest. Ugin asked how Nicol knew they had been first. Nicol would not hear the question.

parts.h: What had become of the birth mountain

blocks.p: Boulders scored with a double curve of claw marks told the twins when they had reached the hunting ground of their sister Palladia-Mors. She arrived in time to take all four of the animals the twins had just killed. The whole plain was hers now, Palladia-Mors informed them. She also warned the twins not to go on to the birth mountain. The humans there had got above themselves and fancied they were dragon hunters. Palladia-Mors would kill the humans' leaders when she felt like it, she said. Not today.

Nicol wanted to fight Palladia-Mors for the meat. Ugin talked him out of it. As the twins argued, Ugin noticed Nicol's eyes turning in slow circles, and Ugin suddenly found himself thinking that perhaps it was time to fight one of their siblings after all. Ugin shook the thought off as an irritation. He did not yet realise that it was not his own thought. Nicol had put it there.

The mountain itself had not changed. Everything around it had. Where there had been unbroken forest, roads now ran between walled settlements. Outside each palisade crowded the huts of people who worked stony fields with stone tools under overseers' whips; inside stood the fine longhouses of those who carried iron. The gates were carved with men spearing a dragon. And over the gate of the greatest hall, on its mound in the middle of the chief settlement, hung a dragon's skull, with the ribs set up as arches along the path to the door. The skull and the ribs were Merrevia Sal's. The humans had made the twins' sister into an ornament.

Horns sounded as the twins passed overhead, and crews ran to machines like giant grounded crossbows. One iron bolt grazed Ugin's hind claw. It was barely a scratch, but the point had been smeared with something, and the venom burned and then numbed. Five drops of Ugin's blood fell, each the size of a man's fist, and the people below fought one another to stand under the falling drops. One woman who was struck sank down as if in prayer; a man howled in triumph; others crammed the bloodied dirt into their mouths.

Flying on, sick with the poison, Ugin still counted. Four more settlements, set far out around the first like the points of a star, each displayed a true dragon's skull on its chief's house. Five dragons had died here.

Ugin spent a wretched night on the rim of the birth mountain's crater with his poisoned foot in a snowbank. He wanted to leave. Nicol, perched on the highest rock, refused. Greed is not frail, Nicol said, and nor is ambition. These humans could kill dragons because they were clever and because they worked together, and they would come for the twins next. The twins had come to avenge their sister, and they would do it. Ugin said he would not slaughter innocent people the way Vaevictis did. Nicol promised that Ugin would not have to kill anyone. Nicol had taught himself to do something that no one else could do.

At dawn a single small figure came climbing the mountain, waving cheerfully. It looked like a pregnant human woman, except that its eyes shone like sapphires. It was the twins' brother Chromium Rhuell. Chromium had taught himself to wear a human body so that he could walk among humans unnoticed. Nicol, sniffing, admitted that Chromium even smelled like a human.

Chromium had been living among the humans below the mountain, and he told the twins what he had learned. The humans' chief was the very hunter who had killed Merrevia Sal in his youth. The chief was an old man now, and he sat on a chair made of her bones. The chief had decreed that anyone who killed a dragon would join the ranks of his heirs. He also claimed the favour of heaven. Anyone who was touched by dragon's blood, or who ate or drank it, was counted holy and lived in ease, and everyone else served the holy ones as slaves. Chromium had come to investigate because three dragons had gone missing, and he had watched the chief's hunters trap and kill a newly hatched dragon. The chief's sorcerers had worked spells into a venom until it could poison dragon flesh. If that knowledge spread to other peoples, Chromium said, every dragon alive would be in danger.
Chromium's remedy was to fetch Arcades, gather siblings and cousins, kill the chief, his heirs and his priests, burn the temples, salt the fields and drive the survivors from the mountain.

Nicol took the plan apart in a soft, reasonable voice. Would that not kill the helpless and spare the armed? Was Chromium saying humans might torment each other freely so long as they left dragons alone? One law for them and another for us? Chromium's temper broke. In a blaze of blue light Chromium stood over the twins in his true dragon shape, vast and mirror-bright. He told Nicol that he could hear exactly what Nicol was doing with words. He told Nicol that Nicol was the least of the siblings, the last to fall, and not even a whole dragon but only half of one. Then Chromium flew off into the sky.

Ugin had been stung by the insult too, since it covered both twins. He asked why Nicol had provoked their brother. Nicol was staring at the sun, which only dragons can look at without harm. Temples, heirs and blood, Nicol said quietly, and scraped his mark into the rock with his horns.

The twins watched the chief come out in procession to his temple at the mountain's foot, carried in a curtained chair behind scale-armoured riders, while the well-fed threw flowers from scaffolds and the thin knelt by the road with their hands over their eyes. The compound had three courts. The gate of the first was a dying dragon; the second, a man clothed in blood with a spear in one hand and a dragon's claw in the other; the third gate was Merrevia Sal's spine, wired together. Before a square temple with three stacked roofs painted with eyes and suns, a priestess whose own eyes had been burned out brought the old man dragon's blood in a cup of dragon bone, and he drank it.

Two of the chief's heirs attended him, each in a helmet crested with dragon's teeth. One heir was a proud man in middle age, and the other was a young woman with a scarred face. The chief shouted abuse at both heirs, and ordered them to bring him the head of the dragon that his machine had wounded, which was Ugin. The two heirs took the abuse without blinking. They exchanged one look, like two tigers after the same deer.

Ugin's bones began to hum. Words slid through his head that were not his own. The words were meant for the two heirs, and Ugin was only overhearing them. To the proud man the voice whispered that the scarred woman was younger, that the chief preferred her, and that she meant to have him strangled on the day the old chief died. To the scarred woman the voice whispered that the chief had never trusted her and would have her knifed. A cloud crossed the sun and the voice stopped. It was a while before Ugin understood that the voice had been Nicol's.

Nicol went first to the farthest settlement, a fishing town on a lake. On the way Nicol snatched one of the chief's messengers off the road, bit off the boy's head and dropped the body in the forest. When Ugin protested, Nicol asked how Ugin's poisoned claw was feeling.

The fishing town belonged to the third heir, who was the chief's own firstborn son. The son was a tall, handsome man loaded with twisted gold. For years he had been mocked as inadequate, until at last he killed a dragon, and his warriors now wore that dragon's green scales as armour. His reward had been a posting at the far edge of the chiefdom, ruling over fishermen. Nicol circled the town slowly. The humming came again, and this time Ugin could follow what the voice was saying to the son. The old chief was past his prime, the voice said, and favoured upstarts over his own flesh and blood. And what was a dragon's skull on a gatepost, compared with a living dragon at a man's command? A dragon could respect a man who marched against the other heirs and killed his own father.

The son made a speech to his warriors about the good omen of two dragons who had flown over the town and not burned it. Then he marched. Nicol raked his claws along the roof-beam of the son's hall as a sign of blessing. The son captured the chief settlement, whose soldiers had all gone up the mountain to hunt the dragons. He killed his father's supporters and sat down on the throne of bones.

Nicol dealt with the first two heirs, the proud man and the scarred woman, by simply sitting on top of the mountain. Each of the two came after him with a band of warriors. Nicol drew both bands higher and higher and round and round the slopes, until the two bands met each other on a field of old lava. There the two heirs fought each other among the sharp stones. While they fought, Nicol flew down to the temple. He burned it, together with everyone who served in it, and lifted the old chief out of the ashes, almost gently.

Nicol set the old chief down, alone and unguarded, in the courtyard of the fourth heir. The fourth heir was the chief's second wife. She was a mage, with braided hair wound with pearls, and it was she who had first put sorcery into the dragon-killing venom. The old chief, filthy and shaking, started barking orders at his wife for a bath. Nicol's whisper told the wife that her husband had taken her secret and handed it to others, that the other heirs had only ever profited from her brilliance, and that she alone was fit to rule. At her signal, the wife's guards turned their weapons inward to point at the chief. The chief raged that he had raised her up from a hut of swamp grass. The wife pressed the tip of her dragon-claw staff to his face until he knelt. She told him that she had raised herself. Then she stabbed him three times and had his body thrown into a latrine. After that the wife marched to war as well.

The war among the heirs was fought to exhaustion. By the end of it the proud man and the scarred woman were both dead, and their surviving followers had joined either the son or the wife. The son and the wife sat behind high walls and glared at each other across a country where nobody had planted any crops. People starved. Ugin watched all this from the mountain and could not think what to do. His thoughts went round in circles, and he did not ask himself why they did.
Then one night Ugin woke to find Nicol gone. A voice in Ugin's head invited him to come and see the end, and the beginning.

Torches burned in the great courtyard before the chief's hall, and Nicol lay along the roof-beam of the hall with his eyes shining. Below Nicol the son and the second wife stood face to face, unarmed and splendidly dressed, as if at a wedding. A voice announced that it was a wedding: the marriage of the dragon-killer's two last heirs. The son and the wife clasped hands on their oath. The voice said that the oath must be sealed in blood. The two let go of each other's hands. Each took up the dragon claw that was the sign of his or her rule, which for the wife was her staff and for the son was a long knife. Each drove the claw into the other, and the two fell dead together.

Nicol rose off the roof. The heirs had made the proper sacrifice, Nicol told the crowd, and now the people understood the truth about dragon's blood. Nicol ruled them now. They would bow to him. A long frightened sigh went through the courtyard, and the people knelt and covered their faces, as they had been taught to do for their chiefs.
So the dragon-killers were destroyed without one dragon lifting a claw in battle, and Nicol Bolas had his first kingdom.

In Bolas's own telling there is no web of whispers. The hunters, Bolas says, had only stumbled on a dragon who was already wounded and dying, and had puffed themselves up as her killers. The chief and his heirs were cruel to the weak, and the sight moved Bolas to act. Bolas was outnumbered and had no answer to the humans' sorcery, so he outwitted them, setting the heirs against each other until every one of them had lost. Bolas risked himself against the poisoned weapons while Ugin hung back out of range, made excuses, and tried to talk Bolas out of acting at all. Afterwards the grateful people offered Bolas the throne, and Bolas ruled as his brother would have wished.
On one point the two accounts agree: no dragon fought. They differ on whose idea the killing was, and on what it was for.

In the torchlit courtyard, with the people kneeling, Ugin cried out that this was not what Nicol had learned from Arcades. Nicol answered that it was exactly what he had learned from Arcades. In Nicol's glittering eyes Ugin saw again the two human brothers in the storehouse yard, and understood that Nicol had reached into one brother's mind and woken the buried grudge that made him kill.

Then the whispering voice turned on Ugin himself, warm and persuasive. Now that the twins had this magic, the voice said, nothing could stop them. They would build a greater realm, pay back Vaevictis and his brutes, and put their elder siblings in their place. Chromium had called the twins the least of the fallen, and Chromium and the others would learn better. This was what Ugin wanted, the voice told him. The power would belong to both twins.

It was not what Ugin wanted. In that moment Ugin understood several things at once. His twin did not know him and had no wish to know him. Nicol had been inside Ugin's mind before, on the plain and on the mountain. And Nicol meant to use Ugin exactly as he had used the heirs. The one bond Ugin had never questioned was empty.

Something burst inside Ugin like a hot spark. A wind out of nowhere dragged him into a darkness where he could not breathe, and wrung him like a cloth. When Ugin came to himself he was hanging over a flat, still sea that showed him his own reflection. He had left Dominaria. He was in a place that lay between the worlds, the place his teacher Te Ju Ki had seen in her visions and had believed no living thing could ever reach.

What had happened to Ugin has a name. Dominaria is one world among a great many, and these worlds are called planes. Almost every creature lives and dies on the plane where it was born. A very few are born carrying something called a planeswalker's spark. The spark can lie asleep for a whole lifetime. If it wakes, usually at a moment of terrible shock, its owner becomes a planeswalker: a being who can step from one plane to another. Ugin was the first planeswalker that the histories know of.

Ugin fell out of the place between the worlds like a shooting star. He woke under an unfamiliar sky, and the land seemed to rise to meet him as though he had come home. The plane he had landed on was Tarkir.

Bolas saw none of that. Bolas saw his brother in front of him, then a ripple in the air, and then nothing. In one of Bolas's tellings, Ugin simply ran away in fright. In another, Ugin was struck down by a last burst of human sorcery, the dragon-killers' revenge. Bolas says that he howled with grief.
On Dominaria one war was finished. A far larger one was coming, and Ugin would not be there for it.

chapters.title: The Elder Dragon War
sources: Kate Elliott, "Chronicle of Bolas: Blood and Fire" (Wizards of the Coast, 18 July 2018)

Kate Elliott, "Chronicle of Bolas: Perspectives" (Wizards of the Coast, 8 August 2018)

blocks.p: The last chapter ended with Ugin torn away from Dominaria to another world, and with his twin, Nicol Bolas, ruling the country of the dead dragon-killers. This chapter tells what Bolas did with that country over the following ages.

Ugin was absent from Dominaria for the whole of the war described here, so Ugin's account, the one the Jeskai monks preserved, says nothing about how the war began. What is known of its beginning comes from Bolas. Bolas told the story himself, twenty thousand years later, speaking through the mouth of a young monk on Tarkir whose tongue he had taken over by magic. Bolas told it the way he tells everything: as the story of a wise and patient king who was forced into each thing he did. The events below come from Bolas. The flattering colour he gave them has been left out.

There is a second difficulty, over dates. The chronicles place the war between about -19,000 and -17,000 AR. Ugin, in his own memories, says that four or five thousand years passed between the day he left Dominaria and the day he came back to find the war ending. That would put the war's last battle nearer -15,000 AR. The sources do not settle it.

After the dragon-killers died, Nicol Bolas kept their country. In Bolas's telling, the people acclaimed him as their saviour, and he ruled the country with justice for generations, held a yearly festival in memory of the tyrants' fall, and governed by the principles he and his lost brother had once talked over together. His people called him the second sun.

Bolas had settled on a story about his brother's disappearance. Ugin had vanished before Bolas's eyes in a ripple of air, and Bolas decided that some last sorcerer of the dragon-killers must have destroyed Ugin in revenge. Bolas needed to believe this. The only other explanation was that Ugin had run away at the very moment his twin needed him, and Bolas refused to think that. So Bolas rounded up every human sorcerer in the region and forced them to give up what they knew. He killed the sorcerers who refused, and later he killed the ones who had helped him as well. Then he founded academies of his own, where humans gifted with magic could be trained under his eye. For generations those academies had one standing task: find the spell that made a dragon disappear. They never found it. They did learn to make large rocks fly apart.

What the kingdom actually was, Ugin saw later from the air. Those who wore the badge of the curved horns prospered and feasted. Beneath them were the chained and the starving. It was the old chiefdom, grown.

Many human lifetimes passed. Then one day a pack of dragons came burning through the villages along the river that marked the kingdom's edge, on the side of the plains where Palladia-Mors hunted. Bolas flew out over a line of scorched farms and found seven large young dragons eating their way through a stockyard. The seven raiders barely looked up at him. Bolas ringed them with fire to get their attention, and asked what they thought they were doing. The raiders answered that they were descendants of Vaevictis Asmadi and raided wherever they pleased. They had already driven Palladia-Mors off her own plains, they said. Next they would drive Bolas out, and take his rich lands and his tame herds for themselves.

Bolas could not beat seven dragons alone. He did not need to. He had a human army that sang his praises, columns of sorcerers in gold and black, and, kept in good repair all these generations, the weapons of the people he had destroyed: the great crossbows on wheels, and the venom their mages had taught to bite through dragon scale.

As Bolas gave the order to attack, a thought spoke up in his head in a voice that sounded like Ugin's. If it was wrong for humans to kill dragons, the thought said, then it was also wrong for dragons to kill their own kin. Had their sister Merrevia Sal died for nothing? Had Bolas's revenge ever been about her, or only about his shame at failing to save her? Bolas answered the thought. This was different, he told himself. These seven were bullies. And Ugin was not here.

At the river the poisoned bolts flew true. Six of the seven young dragons fell out of the sky with their wings going numb, and died under the spears of Bolas's soldiers. Bolas found the sight intoxicating. The seventh dragon got away.

Bolas chased the dragon that had escaped. His army marched out beyond its own border for the first time, north over the plains, living off the towns it passed, until the grass gave out and a wall of badlands rose ahead, all gullies and stone pinnacles, with the mountains where Vaevictis laired behind. Supplies ran short and some of the soldiers complained. Bolas ate the soldiers who complained, and the rest marched on.

Four dragons met Bolas's army at sunrise. Three of them were the brothers Lividus, Ravus and Rubra, who shouted the old insults at Bolas: runt, least-born. In front of them flew their eldest brother, Vaevictis Asmadi, who was simply bigger than anything else alive. In his claws Vaevictis carried the dead body of the young dragon that had escaped from the river. Vaevictis let the body fall on Bolas's army. It flattened a whole company of slingers and set the dry grass alight. Then Vaevictis told little Nicol to run away while he still could.

Bolas did not lose his temper at Vaevictis. He spent it on his own generals instead, and beheaded several of them on the spot. Then Bolas made use of what Vaevictis had dropped. He lined up his giant crossbows behind the dead dragon's neck and tail, using the corpse as a rampart. The crossbow crews knew that men who missed their shots were made slaves, and they shot well. A bolt hit Rubra in the eye. The venom reached Rubra's brain. Rubra blundered away toward the stone pinnacles and crashed to the ground behind Bolas's baggage train. The soldiers of Bolas's rearguard swarmed over the fallen dragon with swords, killed him, and bathed in his blood.

That was the end of the good news for Bolas. Iron bolts would not pierce Vaevictis's hide at all. Vaevictis was hit five times and laughed, and he burned the line of crossbows from end to end. Lividus and Ravus picked soldiers up and threw them through the air. The supply wagons burned with their drivers in them. Vaevictis promised to pin Bolas to the ground and strip the flesh off him while he was still alive. With Bolas's army in pieces, the threat was a real one.

Strength had failed, so Bolas fell back on being cleverer. Bolas's sorcerers threw a pall of sooty haze over the battlefield. Hidden by the haze, Bolas led what was left of his army into a deep canyon between cliffs. He still had a third of his soldiers, two giant crossbows and seven bolts. One general ventured that the canyon looked like a death trap. On the way Bolas noticed something worth remembering. The soldiers of the rearguard, still wet with Rubra's blood, had passed through dragon fire without being burned.

Round a bend in the canyon Bolas made his army wait. Lividus came first, walking, and he filled the canyon from wall to wall. Both crossbows fired, and both bolts glanced off Lividus. Lividus looked up and laughed, because his brother Ravus was dropping on Bolas's army from above.

This was the moment Bolas had saved his sorcerers for. Together the sorcerers threw their rock-breaking spell at the dragon overhead, and Ravus burst apart like a stone left too long in a fire. The falling pieces of Ravus killed half the sorcerers who had cast the spell.

Lividus, howling with grief for Ravus, burned the last two crossbows. Bolas now had only one weapon left: the whispering magic with which he turned minds. For ages he had believed that this magic did not work on dragons, because it had not worked on Ugin. He caught Lividus's eye and tried it anyway. Had Lividus never noticed, Bolas asked, that Vaevictis always sent his brothers into danger first? That Vaevictis flew in front only when it was safe? That it was Vaevictis's fault that Ravus and Rubra were dead? Lividus was the only dragon as big as Vaevictis, Bolas said, and Vaevictis had always feared him and kept him down because of it. Bolas and Lividus could be rid of Vaevictis together.

The whisper worked on Lividus as easily as it had ever worked on humans. When Vaevictis came round the bend in the canyon, Lividus rose and tore Vaevictis's shoulder open to the bone. Bolas's surviving sorcerers cast their spell once more. Spread across two such huge bodies, the spell only staggered the two dragons, but each dragon felt the blow and blamed the other for it. Vaevictis screamed that Lividus was a traitor and attacked him, and the canyon shook with their fight.

Bolas did not stay to see which of the two won. The winner would still be bigger than Bolas was. He had every soldier of his own rearguard killed, so that no one would carry home the secret that an Elder Dragon's blood protects human skin from dragon fire. He kept his sorcerers alive just long enough for them to hide his retreat, and then he killed them too, so that no one at home would hear that there were greater dragons in the world to worship. What Bolas took away from the canyon was a discovery: greed and envy are handles, and dragons have them like everyone else.

Bolas did not go home to his kingdom. Ruling suddenly looked dull beside what he had just done. He flew up into the mountains to find the children of Lividus, Ravus and Rubra, and brought them terrible news. Vaevictis had turned on his own brothers, Bolas told them, and would surely come for his brothers' children next, so as to leave no witnesses. Then Bolas found his sister Palladia-Mors. She greeted him with a blow to the head, and then listened with great interest as he explained how weak Vaevictis now was. After that Bolas went on to the next dragon's lair, and the next.

What followed was told afterwards at ten thousand refugee fires. Clan fell on cousin clan among the peaks, and burned meat rained on the valleys. The hungriest ate the fallen of their own kind. When the mountains were no longer enough for them, the dragons looked down at the human farms. Some dragons wanted to hunt humans as game. Some wanted to keep humans as herds, to be culled when needed. A few dragons wanted to teach humans, and were thanked with fear. Chromium Rhuell took to living in disguise among the people he said he loved, hidden from the humans who would have dreaded him and the dragons who despised his kindness.

Then the dragons and their war crossed the seas. On every shore dragons raised warbands under their own standards from the peoples who worshipped or feared them, and sorcerers came crawling to serve the only creatures whose power they envied. In the end even Arcades Sabboth marched. Arcades was the lawgiver who had once lectured his younger brothers about order. Now Arcades heard a voice in his mind telling him that the other dragons would never respect his peace, and would attack him unless he attacked them first. It was the same whispering voice that had spoken to the dragon-killers' heirs. Arcades led his people against the fortresses of distant relatives, and threw his relatives' bones into the sea.
Bolas watched most of it from a safe distance, and took half the world.

It ended on the plains of Jamuraa. Two human armies met there with dragons over them: one under the crown of Arcades Sabboth, already beaten and falling back, the other under the curved horns. The soldiers on both sides had been at war for generations and went in screaming. Lesser dragons died in the first charge. Arcades commanded brilliantly that day, and everywhere Arcades turned, Bolas was already there to counter him.
Into the middle of the battle dropped a dragon whom neither Arcades nor Bolas had seen for thousands of years.

It was Ugin. He had spent those thousands of years walking from world to world, and over that time he had talked himself into forgiving his twin. Nicol had been very young, Ugin told himself. Perhaps Ugin had judged him too quickly. So Ugin came home to mend things between them, and arrived above a field of the dead. Shielded by magic that he had learned on other planes, Ugin hung in the air between the two armies with his wings spread, and roared at both his brothers to stop. Arcades shouted back that he was fighting only to protect his people. Then Arcades saw that Bolas had forgotten all about him, and used the moment to lead his beaten army away.

Bolas at first took the dragon in the sky for an illusion made by Arcades, and tried to burn it. The fire ran harmlessly off Ugin's shield. When Bolas understood that this truly was his twin, his manner changed in an instant. Bolas said that he had seen Ugin destroyed by human sorcery, that he had avenged Ugin, and that he had spent all the ages since then making the world worthy of Ugin's own dream of peace. He invited Ugin to come and see it. Bolas left his victorious army standing in the field and flew off with his brother. Long afterwards Arcades said that he had taken those abandoned soldiers into his own service.

The twins crossed Jamuraa and the ocean together. Dominaria was as beautiful as Ugin remembered, and everywhere Ugin looked the land was wounded: blighted fields, burned villages, bones, rivers dammed to drown towns, canyons torn across plains by magic nobody had thought twice about using. Nicol flew over all of this damage smiling. Nicol said that he ruled half the world now, and that the other half would soon kneel to him. Nobody called him the least of the dragons any more.

On the birth mountain a pair of horns carved from marble stood on the crater's rim, so that the mountain itself seemed to wear them. Humans had once built a temple on that summit, but Bolas had come to feel that human feet did not belong on ground meant for dragons. He meant ground meant for himself. And for Ugin too, he added, of course. The country below the mountain had turned cold. The great city of Bolas's first kingdom was now a ruin with trees growing through it, and around the mountain stood rings of forts, then horned temples, then towns, every one of them built facing inward.

Bolas asked how Ugin liked his domain. Ugin said nothing for a long time, and then everything he felt came out at once. First Ugin accused Bolas of the mind-trick. Using it on strangers had been bad enough, but Bolas had tried to use it on his own twin. Bolas laughed the accusation off. He had been young then, Bolas said, and only testing his strength. Then Bolas called himself the emperor of everything, and this time it was Ugin who laughed. Ugin told Bolas what "everything" really was. Dominaria was one splinter among countless worlds, Ugin said, and to boast of ruling Dominaria was like claiming that one mountain was the whole earth. Ugin told Bolas that he himself had become a being who could walk between worlds. Ugin had seen a hundred worlds. He knew of no one else who could do it. Compared with that, Ugin said, Bolas's wars were no better than the squabbling of the old dragon-killer chief and his heirs. And Bolas, unlike those humans, should have known better.

Bolas went very quiet. He asked how long Ugin had been able to walk between worlds. Ugin answered that he had been able to do it since the day he vanished. That day, Bolas said, was four or five thousand years ago. In all that time, had it never occurred to Ugin to come back and share this power with his twin? Then Bolas asked Ugin to show him how it was done, and to take him along.

Ugin eagerly began to explain, and stopped in the middle of a sentence. There was nothing he could explain. Ugin could walk between worlds because of a spark that he had been born with. A being without that spark could never do it, however well it was taught.

Bolas saw Ugin falter and drew his own conclusion: the whole story was a lie. Bolas said that Ugin had hidden somewhere like a coward for five thousand years, and had crept back now that the hard work was done, to steal a share of Bolas's glory. Ugin answered that Bolas saw only himself in everything. Perhaps, Ugin said, the real lie was the one Ugin had told himself, in believing that his brother was better than this. Ugin said he should never have come back. Let Bolas enjoy Dominaria, Ugin said. Dominaria was all that Bolas would ever have, while worlds beyond counting stayed out of his reach for ever.
Then Ugin vanished in a shimmer of heatless fire, and Nicol Bolas was alone on the mountain in the snow.

That is the quarrel as Ugin remembered it. Bolas tells the same scene with the parts exchanged. In Bolas's version, Ugin was a timid brother who had never strayed far from the birth mountain, and Bolas kindly showed him the whole wide world for the first time. Ugin, in this version, sat beside Bolas sick with envy. It was Ugin who sneered at Bolas's achievements, who said he wanted none of his brother's leftovers, and who boasted of secrets learned from his old human teacher. Bolas answered that the old woman's wisdom was dust. Then, in Bolas's version, Ugin screamed that one day he would find the way between worlds, as his teacher had promised him, and that Bolas would be sorry. And Ugin disappeared into a blizzard. In this telling Ugin could not walk the planes at all yet. He only wished he could.

Bolas stood in the snow where his brother had been, and went over what had just happened. Ugin had abandoned him once before, at the moment Bolas needed him most. Now Ugin had come back only to announce that he possessed something Bolas could never have, and had left again, laughing. When Bolas told this story later, he put all the envy on Ugin's side. But even Bolas did not hide what he himself felt on the mountain. For the first time in his life Bolas felt cold. Under the cold was rage, and the rage was about one thing above all: Ugin had something that Bolas did not have.
Something white-hot caught fire in Bolas's chest and blinded him. He fell through blackness, tumbling and wrenched about. When he righted himself he was flying over water.

It was a sea without a ripple, stretching flat and silver to every horizon, broken here and there by craggy islets. There was no sun. Bubbles drifted in the still air. Where a bubble touched Bolas's scales it burst, and for a heartbeat it showed him another land under another sky. Bolas understood at once what had happened. A spark had awakened in him too. He had become a planeswalker, the very thing his brother had boasted of being.

Ugin had visited this same sea of still water many times. But Bolas noticed one thing about it that Ugin seems never to have noticed. Bolas felt a faint hum in his bones, and the hum told him that this place was no natural world. Someone had built it. That someone had possessed enormous power, and had then gone away and left no trace of who they were. Bolas did not let the mystery trouble him for long. He claimed the place for himself and named it his Meditation Realm.

After that first crossing, the later ones were easy. Bolas walked through a hundred worlds and then a hundred more. He met no one else who could do the same, and he concluded that he was the first being in all existence to travel between the planes. In his own account of things, Bolas has always been the first.

The war itself guttered out. Of all the Elder Dragons and their broods, the chronicles count few survivors: Arcades Sabboth, Chromium Rhuell, Palladia-Mors and Vaevictis Asmadi, with Bolas and the absent Ugin, and their cousin Piru. An old tradition holds that the dragons who lost were stripped of their rank and their wings and crawl the earth still as the elder land wurms.

Nicol Bolas was not there for the peace. He stayed away from Dominaria for a very long time, and the next chapter tells what happened on the plane without him. The chapter after that tells what Bolas did when he finally went looking for his brother.

The Elder Dragon War has burned itself out. Nicol Bolas, newly able to walk between worlds, has left Dominaria behind, and by the chronicle's reckoning he stays away for about two thousand years. This chapter covers what happened on the plane while he was gone: the rule of the dragons' children, and how humans took the world from them. It rests on later chronicles and on what is reported of two old books, the novel Legions and the story collection The Dragons of Magic, and it is told far more briefly than the war was. No eyewitness account of these events survives.

When the war ended, dragons ruled Dominaria, and five dragons ruled all the others. These five belonged to the second generation: they were children of the Elder Dragons who had survived the war. Crosis was the offspring of Chromium Rhuell and Piru. Rith and Rhammidarigaaz, who is more often called Darigaaz, were brother and sister, both born of Palladia-Mors. With Treva and Dromar they are known as the Primevals.

The Primevals had begun as ordinary dragons. What made them more than that was each other. When all five were awake together, their combined magic unlocked a greater power in each of them, and the five declared themselves gods. Each Primeval carried one aspect of the Ur-Dragon, the ancient spirit from which all dragons come. Their names, in the old language of dragons, were the stages of a dragon's life, in the order in which the five arose.

Darigaaz, the Igniter, was first, and his name meant conception. He was red, and breathed a white fire that left nothing of what it touched. Rith, the Awakener, was childhood: a green dragon whose breath made vines erupt and lash over whatever it fell on. Treva, the Renewer, was youth, gleaming white with scales like feathers, and her breath was a shaft of light that cut steel. Dromar, the Banisher, was adulthood, a huge blue dragon who breathed a wave of disruption that flung people away and shook solid things to pieces. And Crosis, the Purger, jet black, was death. Crosis killed with a single word: anyone who heard Crosis scream that word died.

Under the five Primevals, lesser dragons lorded it over humankind. One glimpse of what that was like has survived. Somewhere on Dominaria, its place now forgotten, a mountain had been hollowed into a city of dragons called the Obsidian Well: one vast cavern, open to the sky at the top so that its masters could fly in and out. Five dragon chiefs shared the Obsidian Well. One chief was the red dragon Heptane, who kept hundreds of slaves to feed and groom her, and whose agents drew a steady supply of sacrifices from the villages round about. The others were Varuna, Macumba, Pizoondertanx and Siliq.

Every slave in the Well wore a band of supple metal about the belly. Any of the five chiefs could pour mana, the energy of magic, into those metal rings to cause the wearer pain, and the chiefs did so. One of the people so ringed was a man called Rokin, from the village of Mitrokin, who had been handed over to the dragon lords as an offering.

The answer to the Primevals came from five human wizards, one for each colour of magic, remembered as the Numena. Three of their names are known. Lowallyn, of blue, was called the Lord of Hidden Waters. Kuberr, of black, was the Wealthy One. Averru, of red, was the mightiest. The white and the green Numena are not named.
The five Numena plotted the downfall of the five dragon gods, and carried it out almost by themselves, one wizard against one dragon. Each wizard took for himself the power of the dragon he overcame.

Averru shut Darigaaz under a caldera in the volcanic land of Shiv. Kuberr sealed Crosis in a catacomb of tar pits in Urborg. The green wizard caught Rith and put her inside a living thing: Nemata, one of the colossal magnigoth treefolk of Yavimaya. The white wizard lured Treva down into the lowest levels of an ancient library, in a city of the country later called Argive, and crucified her there.

Lowallyn's method was the subtlest. Lowallyn did not fight the dragon Dromar at all. In a cavern far beneath the sea, Lowallyn piled up a hoard of treasure so immense that it satisfied every desire Dromar had. With nothing left in the world to want, Dromar had no reason left to move. Dromar lay down on the hoard and did not get up.

It was said afterwards that humankind stole something from each of the Primevals: the mastery of fire from Darigaaz, farming from Rith, writing from Treva, and desire itself from Dromar. The five Primevals were not killed. They stayed in their prisons for almost twenty thousand years.

The power of the lesser dragon lords had flowed from the five Primevals. As the Primevals were imprisoned one after another, that power drained away. In the Obsidian Well, the slaves noticed that the rings about their bodies had become nothing but harmless bands of soft metal. The slave Rokin led a revolt. Heptane and the other four dragon chiefs had been beyond anyone's reach the day before. Now they were pulled down and killed by a mob of hundreds of the people they had tormented. What became of the Well after that is not recorded.

The five Numena then ruled Dominaria themselves, for about a thousand years. They did not stay partners for long. Averru, Kuberr and Lowallyn were unwilling to divide the world five ways. These three conspired together and killed the white wizard and the green wizard, to be rid of the competition. The three also brought down a king named Themeus. After that only three Numena remained.

When Averru at last grew feeble with age, he prepared a great spell that would one day bring him back to life, and so make him in effect immortal. The spell needed an enormous amount of power. To feed it, Averru started a war against Kuberr and Lowallyn. Kuberr and Lowallyn attacked Averru in return, and each of those two hoped to seize the resurrection spell for himself.

The magic of the three wizards collided as they fought, and by accident it created something that none of the three had intended: a living being who was magic itself, given a body. The Numena called this being Mother. She called herself Karona.

Karona was magnificent and immensely strong, and she did not yet know what she was or how much she could do. The three wizards understood that once Karona discovered her full power, nothing on Dominaria would be able to stand against her. The three stopped their war at once and joined forces to destroy Karona before that could happen. Karona lived thirteen months. Bringing her down took all the power the Numena had, and their lives with it.
So ended the first human masters of Dominaria. They died about sixteen thousand years before the birth of Urza, and a thousand years after they had caged the dragon gods.

Almost nothing in this chapter stayed finished. The five Primevals lay in their prisons, alive. Averru's spell was still running. Kuberr would be worshipped again, as a god of wealth, by a guild of killers who had never heard how he died. Lowallyn would be born a second time as a maker of illusions, and Karona would walk Dominaria once more. All of that lies more than twenty thousand years ahead, in the age of the Phyrexian Invasion and the troubles of Otaria that followed it.
About a thousand years after the Numena fell, Nicol Bolas came back to the plane of his birth. How he came back, and what he had just done, is the next chapter.

blocks.p: Two chapters ago, the Elder Dragon War ended with a quarrel between the twin dragons Ugin and Nicol Bolas on their birth mountain. Ugin revealed that he was a planeswalker, a being who can walk between worlds, and left. Bolas, alone in the snow, became a planeswalker himself. Bolas then left Dominaria and spent a long age exploring other worlds, believing he was the first being ever to do so. The last chapter told what happened on Dominaria while Bolas was away.

This chapter begins when Bolas at last thinks of his brother again. It tells what Bolas then did to Ugin. Both brothers left an account of these events. In Bolas's account, he defended himself against an envious attacker. Ugin's account is the one preserved in Ugin's own memories. Where the two accounts disagree, this chapter follows Ugin's, and says so.
After hundreds of worlds, Bolas thought of Ugin again. By Bolas's own telling, he wanted to share his triumph with his twin, and even to forgive him. Bolas went home to Dominaria to look for Ugin.

Dominaria had aged while Bolas was away. Rivers ran in new beds, islands had broken apart, and seas had risen over coasts where people once lived. The dragon wars were long over, and a fragile peace lay on the land. Bolas's brother Chromium Rhuell wandered the world in borrowed shapes as a kindly observer, praised by everyone and refused by nobody. Bolas's cousin Vaevictis Asmadi still burned and stole wherever he liked, sometimes in the company of Palladia-Mors. Bolas found no sign of Ugin anywhere.
So Bolas went to his eldest brother, Arcades Sabboth. Arcades now ruled from a palace on a cliff, above a city laid out as neatly as a diagram.

Arcades had not seen Ugin since the twins left his realm long ago to deal with the dragon-killers. Afterwards Arcades had been told that Ugin was dead. Bolas insisted that Ugin had flown between their two armies at the last battle of the war. Arcades answered with an elder brother's pity. Nobody else had seen any such thing, Arcades said. Bolas had not been himself that day. Bolas had fled the battlefield and left his own soldiers behind, and Arcades had taken those soldiers in.

Arcades added that he had always wondered about Ugin's death. Had Bolas failed to protect his twin? Or had Bolas stood aside and let Ugin die? Arcades said he had always suspected that Bolas envied Ugin, because Ugin was the cleverer and the wiser of the two.

Bolas did not lose his temper. He reminded himself that he was a planeswalker, and that Arcades was only the ruler of one corner of one world. Before he left, Bolas looked over the tidy streets of his brother's city and planted a thought in Arcades's mind. Perhaps Arcades's subjects only pretended to love his laws. Perhaps they whispered that Arcades was a tyrant. Arcades could send spies into every corner of his realm. He could pay people to inform on their own families. And if that did not uncover the plotters, he could burn the districts where they lived.
Then Bolas left Dominaria again. He did not much care whether the thought took root in Arcades or not.

Ugin, meanwhile, had gone to the realm of still water. This was the same strange, silent sea that Bolas had named his Meditation Realm. Ugin had discovered it long before Bolas did, and used it as a place to think.

This time Ugin could not make his thoughts lie quiet. He had been so sure that his twin would be glad to see him. Now he asked himself whether the quarrel was his own fault. Ugin had not chosen to leave Dominaria. His spark had thrown him out of the world like a fish hauled out of water on a hook. But after that, the plane of Tarkir had held Ugin's attention for far too long. Would things have gone the same way if he had stayed with his brother? Ugin grieved for what the dragon wars had done to the world of his birth.
Ugin allowed himself one cold comfort. His brother could not walk between worlds. Whatever Bolas did to Dominaria, all the other worlds were safe from him.
Then gold light burst over the water like a second sunrise. Ugin's comfort had been false. Bolas had arrived.

Bolas came down out of the light with fire and claws. Ugin was so far from expecting an attack that for an instant he mistook his brother's dive for a greeting. Then the flames seared Ugin's eyes. Ugin rolled away, cut the water with one wingtip, and fled toward the rocky islets that rose from the sea. Ugin knew those islets rock by rock, and for a while he was able to lose Bolas among them. Then Bolas simply climbed above the rocks and hunted Ugin from high in the air.

Ugin shouted to ask why Bolas was attacking him. Bolas told him. Ugin, Bolas said, had hoarded the knowledge of the other worlds, had lied about it, had dangled it in front of his twin, and had then gone away to let his twin suffer for eternity over a prize he could never touch. Ugin answered that he had come back for Bolas, and that he had not known how the power worked. Bolas said that of course Ugin had known. Ugin asked how Bolas had come by a spark of his own. Bolas answered only that the spark was his now, and that he would not share the worlds with an enemy.

In all his ages of wandering, Ugin had studied the magic of discovery and understanding, and the magic of shielding himself. He had never troubled to learn how to attack. Ugin raised a fog off the water to hide in, and saw that the fog would not save him.

So Ugin ran, and did not care what his brother would call it. He stepped out of the realm of still water into the storms of a plane called Zendikar, meaning only to catch his breath and think of something to say. Bolas burst out of the darkness behind him in a flash of gold. Ugin stepped to another plane, bustling Kephalai. Then to another, Ravnica, whose cities were still spreading across its surface. Ugin fled on and on through world after world, and each time the gold light followed him.

Ugin's burned eyes were blistering shut. The sorcery that Bolas had thrown at him was creeping up Ugin's limbs and numbing them, like the venom of the old dragon-killers. A dragon heals with time, but Bolas gave Ugin no time. Ugin could not rest and could not eat. He could only run, and he could feel his strength wearing away.

There was one world where Ugin could have gone to be healed, because that world itself loved him. That world was Tarkir. Ugin would not lead his brother there. Bolas would destroy Tarkir for no better reason than that Ugin loved it.

That thought brought the still water back before Ugin's eyes, and with it the memory of Te Ju Ki, the old human woman who had taught him in a roofless tower when he was young. Ugin had once asked Te Ju Ki whether dying frightened her. She had answered that what she was would go on in other forms. All things end, she had said, but ending is sometimes a different thing from dying.
Ugin understood then that there was only one way this hunt would ever stop. Bolas had to believe that Ugin was dead.
Ugin returned to the Meditation Realm and waited above the water. He was exhausted, and he felt strangely light.

The gold light flared overhead, and Bolas dropped toward him for the last time. Ugin looked properly at the dragon who was coming. Ugin saw malice worked all through his brother's being. Perhaps the malice had once been only a small seed. Perhaps Ugin's own long absence had given the seed room to grow. The dragon Ugin had fallen out of the sky beside, and had learned to hunt with, had been called Nicol. That dragon no longer existed. He had been swallowed by "Bolas", the second name that Nicol had given himself, because Nicol could only ever measure his own worth against someone else's. Ugin was sorry it had come to this. He did not believe, in the end, that he could have changed it.
Ugin stopped resisting.
Bolas roared in triumph. His magic closed around Ugin. His claws tore into Ugin's hearts, and his teeth into Ugin's throat. Ugin fell, and struck the water with a sound like thunder.

What followed was more than a death. Huge waves spread out from the place where Ugin's body fell. The waves broke the ancient islets apart and kept going. They passed the edge of the Meditation Realm and poured out into the darkness that lies between all worlds. The whole sea drained away after them, until the seabed lay bare like bones in the sun. It was as though a heavy weight had been dropped into a bowl and had cracked the bowl.
The same shock seized Bolas. It hurled him out of the Meditation Realm and through world after world like a thrown spear, until he crashed down on Dominaria, the plane where he had been born.
Bolas believed that he had killed his brother. He said, long afterwards, that believing it was his mistake.

Bolas's version of these events runs as follows. Bolas stepped into his Meditation Realm and was overjoyed to find his lost brother floating there, admiring his own reflection in the water. Bolas greeted Ugin warmly. Ugin said not a word and attacked. According to Bolas, Ugin attacked out of envy, because Bolas had reached the other worlds first, and out of fear of what Bolas might tell others about him. The brothers fought with claws and sorcery across the still sea and then from world to world, for days, for years, for generations. Ugin refused every offer of peace. At last the fight returned to the place where it had begun. There Bolas, having no other choice, killed his brother in self-defence.

So each brother says that the other struck first. Each brother also says that he himself was the first being to walk between worlds. On that second point Ugin has the stronger case. Ugin's memories of Tarkir and of a hundred other worlds were formed thousands of years before Bolas gained his spark.
The Meditation Realm lay empty and dry. It may have stayed that way for a moment or for a thousand years. Nothing was left in the realm that could have told the difference.

Then a film of silver began to seep up out of nowhere. The water was returning from the darkness it had drained into. It rose without a sound until the sea was full and still again. In the surface of the water hung the reflection of a dragon.

The dragon breathed in. The water flowed toward him and ran into every scale and hollow of his body, until his horns shone and his eyes burned with magic. It was Ugin. He could not tell whether the body that rose from that sea was made of flesh or of spirit, and he found that it did not matter. From this time on he is called Ugin, the Spirit Dragon.

Ugin looked over the wreckage of the realm: the broken islets, the scoured rock. This ruin, he thought, was what Bolas promised to everything that refused to bow to him. Somebody would have to stand in Bolas's way. It would have to be somebody who knew Bolas well enough to defeat him, and only one such person existed. Ugin also knew that his brother was not the only danger loose among the worlds. Ugin had a great deal of work to do.

Ugin left the realm in a ripple of invisible flame. After he had gone, bubbles began to rise from the seabed. One by one the bubbles burst, and the realm slowly filled with memories. These are the memories that a young woman on Tarkir would one day wander through in her sleep, and that is how this part of the story came to be known.

Bolas fell to earth on Madara, an island country off the coast of the continent of Jamuraa. By then the wars of the Elder Dragons were already half legend on Dominaria. Bolas was bruised and stunned by his fall, and he recovered.

What happened next comes from other sources than Ugin's memories. Some time after Bolas's return, another planeswalker crossed his path on Dominaria. This planeswalker was a demonic leviathan, an enormous sea monster. Bolas and the leviathan fought. It was the first duel between planeswalkers that Dominaria had ever seen, and it lasted a month.

When the duel was over, Madara had been reduced to a third of its former size. The violence of the fight had also torn a rift in time itself. This was the first of the time rifts that would trouble Dominaria far into its future.

Bolas won the duel in the end by using the touch of his mind on the leviathan. Then Bolas ate what he had killed. He fed on the leviathan's carcass for more than a year, and took its power into himself. When Bolas had finished, nothing remained of the leviathan except some blubber and two long spurs of bone standing up out of the sea. In later ages, people who sailed between the two spurs took them for rocks, and named them the Talon Gates.

Bolas made Madara the seat of an empire. In time he also returned to the Meditation Realm. The cataclysm of Ugin's fall had thrown down an old temple there, and Bolas sat among the temple's ruins and counted the whole realm as a monument to his greatest victory. Bolas could no longer say exactly where in that sea his brother's body had gone under. To give his thoughts a centre, Bolas raised two colossal curved horns out of the open water. They looked like the horns of a dragon the size of a mountain range, sleeping just beneath the surface.

The victory did not content Bolas. Not all of Dominaria obeyed him yet. Beyond Dominaria lay worlds without number that had never heard his name. Bolas had once been called the least of the dragons who fell. He intended to show every one of those worlds how wrong that had been.

chapters.title: Ravnica and the Guildpact
sources: MTG Wiki, "Ferrous Rokiric" and "Titans of Ravnica"

blocks.p: So far the story has stayed on the plane of Dominaria, because that is where the chronicle is kept. This chapter leaves Dominaria for another world. In the long gap between the dragons' wars and the fall of the Thran, the record notes a handful of dates on another world entirely, and they matter, because that world is Ravnica, where a great deal of the later story will be decided. The Thran chapters that follow take place a few centuries after the main event here, far away, and neither world knew of the other.

The sources for Ravnica's beginnings are thin. What follows is drawn from the chronicles and from what they report of the novels of the Ravnica cycle; it has dates and names, and little of the detail that the dragon chapters had.
In -12,208 AR, a few thousand years after Ugin's first death, a dragon hatched on Ravnica. Ravnica's own calendar calls that year 6691 AC. The dragon was named Niv-Mizzet.

Ravnica's ancient dragons were not like the beasts of later ages. They could speak from the moment they left the egg, they were born already knowing things, and they would not share ground with one another. Niv-Mizzet's first hunting grounds are said to have taken in part of a region called Utvara, where his earliest lair is supposed to lie. Other dragons hatched in the same age as Niv-Mizzet. One by one Niv-Mizzet defeated every one of these rivals. When he had finished, he was the only one of his kind left: the last great dragon of Ravnica, and before long its most brilliant mind.
Niv-Mizzet will take part in the one great event of this chapter, and he will be at the centre of events ten thousand years after it.

parts.h: A world at war with itself
