blocks.p: Ravnica in those ages was already a plane of cities, though they had not yet run together into the single city that would one day cover its whole face. Ravnica was not a peaceful plane. Its many factions made war on each other without end, in campaigns that lasted centuries. By the time the record picks the story up, the fighting had resolved itself into two great camps under two champions.

One champion was Razia. Razia was an angel, though she had not been born: she was an ageless being made of red and white mana, the energy of magic. To the soldiers who marched behind her she was more a demigod than a general. It is said that every angel of her host was made in her image.

The other champion was Cisarzim, called the Lord of Chaos, who carried an axe named Skullhammer. Alongside Cisarzim, in the name of chaos, fought Svogthir, a necromancer who had gathered an army of elves and outcasts and filled out its ranks with legions of the dead he had raised himself.
The cyclops Borborygmos, who led the wild clans of Ravnica ten thousand years later, is said to be Cisarzim's descendant.

Into this war came a visitor from beyond the world. His name was Azor. Azor was a sphinx, born about -6740 AR on a plane that nobody now remembers, and he was a planeswalker: one of the rare beings who can walk from one world to another. Azor was also a lawmage, a master of the kind of magic that binds people by rules and oaths, and he thought of himself as the Arbiter of Law. Azor travelled widely. Many old civilisations on many planes have a legend of a winged, half-divine figure who came and gave them their laws, and sphinxes on many different planes behave in ways that suggest Azor once visited their worlds.
Azor arrived on Ravnica in -5564 AR. Ravnicans remember him as Supreme Judge Azor the First.

The war had fought itself to a standstill. The leaders on both sides had come to see that if the war went on, nothing would be left for anyone to rule. The heads of ten factions came together. At an event remembered as the Clash of Two Champions, Azor put a proposal before these ten leaders: that all ten factions bind themselves by a single enchantment. Not a treaty on parchment that the next generation could tear up, but a living spell, which would keep the peace by its own power and keep every one of them alive.

The factions that loved order least did not like Azor's proposal. They were talked into it all the same. The leader who did most of the persuading was Svogthir, the necromancer, who had fought on the side of chaos and now convinced the forces of chaos to sign.

The Guildpact was made in -5517 AR. Azor wrote most of its text. Each founder signed in blood and magic, and the order of the first names is remembered: Azor, then Razia, then Svogthir. Among the rest were Cisarzim; Niv-Mizzet; Mat'Selesnya, an elemental born of the joining of several dryads, who is the very soul of the world; and Szadek, the last of an ancient race of vampires who feed on minds.

The founders are called the paruns, and what they founded became the ten guilds. Azor's followers became the Azorius Senate, keepers of the law. Razia's host became the Boros Legion. Svogthir's swarm of the living and the dead became the Golgari. Cisarzim's followers became the Gruul Clans. Niv-Mizzet founded the Izzet League, and gave it the building and upkeep of the city's great works. Mat'Selesnya's guild was the Selesnya Conclave, and Szadek's guild was House Dimir. The Orzhov Syndicate, the Cult of Rakdos and the Simic Combine made up the ten.

The Guildpact gave each guild its own part in the running of the world, and forbade each guild to meddle in the business of the others. The chronicle speaks of duties shared out among nine guilds, not ten. That may be because of the part given to Szadek's guild, which was a strange one: by the terms of the pact itself, House Dimir existed to oppose the pact.

The Guildpact did not work by soldiers or courts. Its power was quiet. When a guild reached into another guild's business, or tried to upset the balance among the ten, luck and circumstance simply turned against that guild until its attempt came to nothing. The guilds learned to live within the Guildpact, and to hunt for loopholes in it.

Ravnicans count their years from that day. The year of the Signing is the year 0 of the Ravnican calendar, called the Zal Concordant. The anniversary of the Signing was kept ever after as a festival on which the whole plane put down its weapons. Azor's first draft still exists, pressed under three inches of enchanted glass in the Old Laws Library of the Azorius. From the Signing, too, the chronicle dates the long growing-together of Ravnica's cities into one.

Azor stayed about a century and a half in all. At some point he left one more thing behind him, hidden in the lines of power that run beneath the city's districts: a provision for the day the Guildpact might fail. Nobody would find it for ten thousand years. In -5419 AR, which is the year 98 of the new Ravnican calendar, Azor left Ravnica to bring order to other worlds. Ravnica's histories record that year as the year the First Judge died.
Azor did not come back to see how his law turned out. Much later, somebody would tell him.

The peace was real, and it was not complete. Four hundred years after the Signing the city was close to coming apart. The Golgari and the Rakdos had risen in rebellions more destructive each time, and the Wojek League, the arm of the Boros that kept order in the streets, was stretched to breaking.

The Wojek League's Commander-General, Ferrous Rokiric, found the answer in stone. In -5117 AR Rokiric brought to the city ten colossal statues that could be brought to life to fight. Each statue was worth a hundred soldiers. These statues, the Titans, put down the rebellions. When the streets were quiet again, nine of the Titans were set to stand at the city's borders. The tenth, named Zobor, was placed over the Tenth District, at the heart of things, where Zobor stood for the next ninety-six centuries as a reminder of what the Boros Legion could do.
On Dominaria, in almost the same years, a floating city called Halcyon was making itself the capital of an empire.

chapters.title: The Thran and the Healer
sources: MTG Wiki, "The Thran" (summary of the novel by J. Robert King, 1999)

blocks.p: Ten thousand years have gone by since the dragons' wars. On the continent of Terisiare, on Dominaria, humans have in that time built the greatest civilisation the plane has yet seen: the Thran Empire. This chapter and the next tell how the Empire ended, and what it gave birth to as it died. Both rest on one book, the novel The Thran, as the chronicles report it.

The story has four people at its centre, and it helps to know them before it starts. Glacian is the Empire's greatest inventor. Rebbec, his wife, is its greatest architect. Yawgmoth is a healer whom the Empire has thrown out. Gix is a rebel from the caves beneath the capital. All four lived in the Empire's last fifty years.

No one remembers how the Thran began. They came into Terisiare out of the east, and by the time their story can be picked up they held two thirds of the continent, with colonies as far off as Shiv and Caliman. The Empire was a league of eight city-states strung along a single desert highway, the Pilgrim Way. Phoenon, in the mountains, was the oldest. Nyoron lay on the southern shore, and Losanon on a tropical river delta. The others were Seaton, Orleason, Chignon and Wington, and Halcyon, which in the Empire's last age became the capital.

Everything the Thran made ran on powerstones. A powerstone is a crystal charged with mana, the raw energy of magic, and the Thran grew them in vast machines called mana rigs. Powerstones drove the Empire's artifact creatures, which were machines built to walk, work and fight. They armed its weapons. They lifted its ships, the caravels, which sailed through the air. Later ages dug up Thran devices for thousands of years and never learned to match them.

The capital was the proof of what powerstones could do, because Halcyon floated. The city hung in the air above the crater of a dead volcano. It rose in eight terraces of white brick and limestone toward a high western plateau. On the lower terraces stood townhouses roofed in blue tile. On the highest stood minarets with onion domes, flying arches, a stadium, an amphitheatre, the Council Hall and the high court. A white wall ran round the whole city, and archways in the wall opened on five ports where merchant caravels rode at anchor in the sky.

Under the city, in the caves of the old volcano, lived the people the Thran had cast out. The Thran called those caves the Caves of the Damned, and the people in them the Untouchables. The mana rig that made Halcyon's powerstones stood directly on top of the caves. That fact matters to everything that follows.

The Empire was governed by council, in three stages. A question was put first to the full assembly and settled by which side shouted louder. If the shout was unclear, the eldest delegate of each of the eight city-states voted. If those eight elders tied, the question went to the leaders: twenty-eight people who had each done the Empire some great service, healers and artificers and heroes.

Halcyon became the capital about a hundred and fifteen years before the Empire fell. Almost at once the Thran fell out among themselves, and they stayed that way for a century. At bottom the Thran Civil War was a fight about how much the other city-states owed the new capital. It came to be fought under two banners that had little to do with that question.

One banner was the artificers'. An artificer is a maker of magical machines. The artificers' party held that the Thran should be perfected by their machines and their magic, healing included. The imperial elite stood behind this party.

The other banner was the eugenicists'. They held that the body was itself a machine, and a marvellous one, which ought to be opened and understood. They cut up the dead to see how the living worked, practised surgery, and argued that sickness was carried by things too small to see. The republican commoners took up the eugenicists' cause.
The real artificers and the real eugenicists never fought each other. The politicians fought in their names.

Two of the people in this story were children of that war. Glacian was born in the later part of it, forty-nine years before the Empire's end. Yawgmoth was born six years after Glacian. Yawgmoth grew up fascinated by the machinery of flesh, and as a young man he became the eugenicists' champion.

The war ended fourteen years before the fall, when the elite finally crushed the republicans. Somebody had to carry the blame, and the Elder Council chose the eugenicists, whose ideas the best people found degrading. Yawgmoth was thirty years old. The Council banished him and two hundred of his followers to the deserts of the continent of Jamuraa, and the Thran congratulated themselves on a century of trouble ended.

Glacian, on the winning side, was by then the chief artificer of Halcyon. The city and its powerstones were older than Glacian was, and he did not invent them. But the sources credit him with the designs on which the Empire's technology rested in its final age, and with its greatest machines. He built the mana rig that fed the capital. He was the Empire's most famous mind.

Glacian's other great work was the Null Sphere, which stood in a crater not far from Halcyon. The Null Sphere was a hollow ball of metal larger than the whole capital. It was not solid: it was a shell of walkways and lattice around an enormous empty space, so light and so strong that it was counted a wonder in a nation of wonders. The Sphere was an antenna. It drank mana from the mountain beneath it and from the sky above it, and with that power its crew could watch and command every artifact creature in the Empire from one place.

Glacian's wife, Rebbec, was Halcyon's chief architect. Rebbec had built the city's infirmary, and she was now raising her masterpiece above the rooftops: the Thran Temple, a temple made of crystal that would float by itself on a single powerstone the size of a man. Glacian and Rebbec both sat among the twenty-eight leaders.
Yawgmoth did not sit still in the desert. He travelled the world for the five years of his exile in pursuit of knowledge, and he treated every people he met as material for experiments.

Among the dwarves of Oryn Deeps, Yawgmoth let loose a sickness called the Black Cough. The workers' revolt that came of it nearly killed the dwarven king and ended a thousand years of dwarven rule. On the island of Argoth he bred the local creeping mould into a plague that ate away the elves. He then kidnapped the elves' priestess, Elyssendril Lademmdrith, together with her healers, and demanded a ransom for the priestess and for the cure she had discovered. The elves paid. Yawgmoth sent them sweetened water and the bodies of twelve healers.

He gave the minotaurs of Talruum a disease called the White Death only to see what it did. He infected the rulers of the cat-people's nations with rabies, and those rulers tore one another apart. He poisoned the human tribes of Gulatto Meisha. And he seized the Bey, the ruler of the lizard-like viashino of Shiv, destroyed the Bey's brain, and cut him open while he was still alive.
Nobody in Halcyon knew any of this.

Nine years before the Empire's end there was a riot of Untouchables in the mana rig. In the confusion one of the rioters, a rebel named Gix, reached Glacian and stabbed him with a shard of powerstone.

Gix struck out of the outcasts' long anger at the city above them, and Glacian was the man who had made that city what it was. Gix and nearly everyone he knew in the caves were rotting from a sickness that had no name.
Glacian did not die of the wound. He caught the same sickness. The healers of the Thran worked their magic on him, and the magic made him worse.

Rebbec used every bit of her standing to do the one thing left. She persuaded the Council to recall Yawgmoth, the exile whose kind of medicine the Empire had outlawed five years earlier. Rebbec met Yawgmoth herself at the gates of the city. He was now thirty-five, a tall man, hard-muscled from five rough years, with thick black hair that shadowed his eyes.
Yawgmoth was as good a physician as Rebbec had hoped. He studied Glacian. He also had Gix captured and brought up to his laboratory, and studied him. And he found what the healers had missed.

The sickness came from the powerstones. The stones gave off an invisible radiation, and long exposure to it broke the body down in spreading sores and broke the mind down too. Yawgmoth named the disease phthisis, from a Thran word meaning continual decay. Nearly all the Untouchables had it because they lived under the mana rig. And the citizens of the floating city, who had been surrounded by powerstones since birth, were beginning to show it as well.
Gix overheard this in the laboratory. He understood that his people had been slowly poisoned for the city's convenience, and he escaped to tell them.

The elite did not want to believe it. Many of the leading families seemed untouched by the disease, and Glacian, from his sickbed, distrusted his doctor from the first day to the last. But the Council gave Yawgmoth money and apprentices. A healer named Xod gave Yawgmoth an idea, and from that idea Yawgmoth made a serum of four metals ground to powder: copper, silver, gold and iron. Each metal turned aside one colour of mana. When a patient took the mixture, the sores shrank and closed before the watchers' eyes, and they stayed closed for about a week.

There were things about the cure that Yawgmoth told no one. The serum stopped four colours of mana out of five. He had left out lead, which would have stopped the fifth, so black mana still reached the people who took the serum and went on working in them slowly. The disease was not catching, and Yawgmoth said that it was. The long list of symptoms he published was padded, so that when he wished he could find phthisis in a healthy enemy. In time he learned how to give the disease to anyone he chose.

Two years after the stabbing, Gix led the Untouchables up out of the caves and into the city in arms. One of the rebels' chief targets was the half-built Thran Temple, because Rebbec, the wife of the hated Glacian, was building it.

Yawgmoth ended the revolt without a battle. He offered the Untouchables the serum for nothing. The grateful city rewarded Yawgmoth with a seat among the twenty-eight leaders, and with the authority to make law in matters of public health.

Yawgmoth used that authority at once. By his law the infected were sent down to the Caves of the Damned, and healthy Untouchables were brought up into the city to take their places. It was Yawgmoth who decided who was infected. His opponents began to disappear from Halcyon by the downward road.

Glacian was the one patient the serum did nothing for. He grew worse year by year. His mind split into several personalities, he lost his memory, and he saw traitors everywhere. Since his own physician was fast becoming the most powerful man in the Empire, Glacian's suspicion was not entirely madness.

While Glacian lay in a coma, Yawgmoth took Rebbec on a tour of the great city-states, founding health corps in each of them. Rebbec was the most admired woman in the Empire, and Yawgmoth was its saviour. Somewhere on that journey Rebbec and Yawgmoth fell in love with each other, and neither of them acted on it. Rebbec went on loving her husband as well, and was torn between the two men.

Four years before the end, a stranger appeared in Glacian's sickroom. She looked like a young woman, slender and strong, with skin like polished ebony and eyes that gleamed like crystal. She wore beads braided into her cropped hair and black leggings embroidered with coiling snakes, and her smile had some mockery in it. Her name was Dyfed.

Dyfed was a planeswalker: one of the very few beings able to step from one world to another. Dominaria is only one world, or plane, among a great many, and almost nobody born on any of them can ever leave. Nobody in Halcyon had imagined such a person could exist.

Dyfed had come to meet a mind. Glacian had proved, by mathematics alone, that worlds beyond Dominaria must exist, and he had even worked out how an entire world might be mapped inside a powerstone. Dyfed could also see something in Glacian that he did not know about himself. He carried a planeswalker's spark, the inborn seed of her own power, and in him it had never awakened.
Glacian took his visitor for a trick arranged by his doctor to torment him, and would have nothing to do with her.

Then the doctor himself walked in. Yawgmoth grasped what Dyfed was faster than Glacian had. He talked to her as he talked to everyone, about healing, and about a clean new world where the Thran could be made whole. Dyfed was charmed. She agreed to search for an empty plane where Yawgmoth could build his paradise. As a foretaste she showed him a world called Pyrulea, and she gave him an amulet with which he could call her.

In the meantime Yawgmoth had been watering down the serum he sent to the caves, and telling the Untouchables that supplies were short. Gix grew restless, as Yawgmoth intended. Gix began sending his people up into the city, the sick and the healthy together. Each new alarm brought Yawgmoth more money from the Council, and in the end it brought him full command of the Halcyte Guard, the soldiers of the capital.

A year after Dyfed's visit, Gix rose in revolt a second time. Yawgmoth had been waiting for exactly that. Using designs that Glacian had drawn, Yawgmoth had built a device that gave him control of every powerstone machine in Halcyon at once.

With the device and the Guard, Yawgmoth crushed the rising. He took emergency authority over the whole defence of the city. Then he had Gix brought before him and offered the rebel a bargain: the true cure, and his life. In return Gix swore to serve Yawgmoth faithfully for ever.
It took months to repair the damage to the city. When the work was done, Halcyon declared a festival in honour of the man who had now saved it twice.
On the day of the festival, visitors arrived whom nobody had invited.

This is a short chapter about a third world. The chronicle gives it one line, placed some time before the Thran fell, and no year. It comes from the oldest layer of the lore, the tales of the desert plane of Rabiah, and it is told here because it is the story of how one more person became a planeswalker, a being who can walk between worlds. Her reason was very different from the rage that made planeswalkers of the dragons Ugin and Nicol Bolas.

Fatima was a princess of Rabiah and one of the most powerful women of that plane, rich in camels and silks and richer in magic. What she valued above all of it was that she belonged to no one. On Rabiah a woman was commonly ruled by her father or her husband. Fatima's father was dead, and her lover, al-Abin, had promised that he would never ask her to marry him.
One night al-Abin changed his mind, and asked Fatima to marry him.

Fatima's fury at al-Abin, and at the whole country that had made him think he could ask, lasted for days. When her fury cooled, Fatima put all of it into her magic. She meant to build a place where nobody would ever dare trouble her again.

What Fatima built was a city made entirely of stone and brass, and it burned with the heat of her anger. The City of Brass stands twenty degrees hotter than the desert around it. Its walls throw back the sun all day and glow on for hours after dark. Even the mountains nearby are sheathed in brass, and the snow that gathers on their peaks at night is gone just after sunrise.

As Fatima worked, her power grew, until it was great enough that she could step from one plane to another and leave her people behind. She moved the city to the farthest edge of Rabiah and laboured there alone.

The place is thick with mana, and that has always drawn wizards to it. But the mana burns like molten brass, and nobody draws on it without pain. Hardly anything can live there: efreets and djinn, and little else.

In the end even Fatima felt a touch of loneliness. Fatima answered her loneliness the way she answered everything, by making something. The first Brass Man was a clumsy, slow figure of metal and magic, with not much of a mind. The Brass Men could stand any heat or weather and were very hard to break, but everything they did seemed to cost them great effort, and they could not go on at all without mana fed to them regularly.
Fatima cared for her Brass Men deeply. It is said that the Brass Men carried the grief that Fatima never let herself feel.
Brass men turned up afterwards in many places and times, on Dominaria among them. Fatima herself, the tale says, is still in her city, keeping the world out with its fires, her anger and her sorrow.

chapters.title: The Fall of the Thran
sources: MTG Wiki, "The Thran" (summary of the novel by J. Robert King, 1999)
MTG Wiki, "Battle of the Null Sphere"

blocks.p: The last chapter left the Thran Empire two years from its end. Yawgmoth, the exiled healer who was called back to cure one man, now controls the Empire's health laws, the soldiers of its capital, and the defence of the floating city of Halcyon. The rebel Gix has sworn to serve him. Glacian, the great inventor and Yawgmoth's patient, is still dying of the powerstone sickness called phthisis. Rebbec, the architect who is Glacian's wife, loves both her husband and his doctor. Halcyon is about to hold a festival in Yawgmoth's honour.

The uninvited visitors who arrived on the day of the festival were ambassadors. They spoke for twenty-five nations of dwarves, elves, minotaurs, viashino and cat-people, for the human tribes of Gulatto Meisha, and for several of the Thran's own city-states. They had come to tell Halcyon who its saviour really was.

One after another the ambassadors set out what Yawgmoth had done during his five years of exile: the plagues he had loosed on whole peoples to see what would happen, the priestess he had ransomed and the healers he had returned dead, the ruler he had cut open alive. Their nations had joined together against him, and the ambassadors put their demand plainly. The Thran must strip Yawgmoth of his powers, or this alliance would make war on the Empire.

The Empire voted on the demand by its three stages. The eight city-states split evenly. Nyoron, Seaton, Phoenon and Orleason voted that Yawgmoth should stay. Chignon, Losanon, Wington and Halcyon itself voted that he should go. A tie among the city-states sent the question to the twenty-eight leaders, and the leaders divided too, thirteen against thirteen, until only two of them had not yet voted. One of the two was Rebbec. The other was Yawgmoth. Both voted that Yawgmoth should stay.
Yawgmoth did not wait to see what the Council would do next. He overthrew it the same day. He imprisoned the Empire's elders and the foreign ambassadors together.

Glacian, sick as he was, saw what had to be done, and persuaded his wife to do it. Rebbec called on Dyfed, the planeswalker who had visited them, and asked her to rescue the prisoners. Dyfed agreed, for Glacian's sake. She took the imprisoned elders of the Thran out of Dominaria altogether, and with them about two hundred of the goblins who had been Glacian's servants. She set them all down on another plane, called Mercadia. The elders became the ancestors of the Mercadian people, and the goblins became the ancestors of the goblins of Mercadia, the Kyren.

Yawgmoth answered by sending Glacian down to the Caves of the Damned. Glacian found the caves changed. The dripping holes where the outcasts had once been left to rot were now clean, bright laboratories, in which the sick were experimented on. The man in charge of the laboratories was Gix. Glacian could not decide whether this was an improvement.
Dyfed had kept her earlier promise to Yawgmoth as well. She had searched the worlds for an empty one, and she had found something stranger than an empty world.

She had found a plane that somebody had built. It was entirely artificial. It consisted of nine hollow spheres nested one inside the next, and its surfaces crawled with things that were alive and were also machines. The being who made this world had died not long before, in the innermost sphere, and Dyfed could not discover the cause. A made world needs a mind to govern it. With its maker dead, this one was very slowly beginning to run down. Dyfed proposed that Yawgmoth take the dead maker's place before the plane decayed.

In the caves under Halcyon, Dyfed set a charged powerstone on a pedestal and broke the stone in two. The breaking tore open a doorway between Dominaria and the artificial plane. The doorway, called a portal, stayed open.

Yawgmoth went through the portal. He had made his name fighting phthisis, a word that meant continual decay. He named his new world after the opposite idea, continual progress: Phyrexia. He went down to the core of the plane and bound his mind to it. From then on, whenever Yawgmoth stood inside Phyrexia, he had the power of a god there.

Yawgmoth began bringing his patients through the portal. In Phyrexia, empty powerstones were set into the patients' bodies, and the empty stones drew the sickness out. The patients were cured of phthisis. They were also changed. Over time their bodies grew longer, leaner, faster and stronger than human bodies. These altered people were the first Phyrexians.
Rebbec crossed into Phyrexia too, at Yawgmoth's request, and built him an infirmary there. It was the finest thing she had ever designed. Nine thousand years later it had grown into a city.

Yawgmoth also gave Rebbec what looked like a gift. He announced that he had finally discovered why her husband alone had never recovered: a sliver of the shard that Gix had stabbed Glacian with was still buried in the wound. Yawgmoth cut the sliver out while Rebbec watched. When Rebbec was not looking, he put something else into the wound in its place. He sewed into Glacian's body the two halves of the powerstone that Dyfed had broken to open the portal. Yawgmoth wanted Glacian dead, and the two half-stones would poison the sick man faster.

The alliance of nations now called itself the Thran Alliance. It struck first, and at first it did well. The city-state of Orleason fell to the Alliance almost without a fight, because Orleason's own artificers changed sides. Phoenon, the oldest of the Thran cities, held out through a short siege and then fell as well.

Yawgmoth struck back at Phoenon. He destroyed the Alliance's fleet of airships there. Then he bombarded the city itself until everyone inside it was dead, both the Alliance soldiers who had captured it and the Thran citizens who lived in it. Phoenon had voted for Yawgmoth.

Then Yawgmoth drew up his army in front of his capital. A desert plain lay between Halcyon and the rest of the continent. On the far side of the plain was a mountain pass called the Megheddon Defile. Any army marching on Halcyon had to come through that pass.
The army of the Thran Alliance came through the pass. It was made up of humans, dwarves, elves, viashino, minotaurs and cat-people, and its artifact soldiers marched among them.

Yawgmoth's forces were waiting where the Alliance could not see them. The Halcyte Guard lay hidden under canopies the colour of sand. Yawgmoth's caravels hung in the sky in front of the sun, where the glare hid them. Beside the Guard stood something the world had never seen before: the first Phyrexians, the people who had been remade in Yawgmoth's new world. Yawgmoth also had two enormous artifact war machines, called behemoths.

The ambush tore apart the front of the Alliance army at the foot of the pass. But the Alliance sent its own artifact warriors, which were shaped like mantises, against Yawgmoth's behemoths, and the Alliance line held. Yawgmoth saw that winning this battle would take longer than he had planned. He had a second plan ready.

parts.h: The Battle of the Null Sphere

blocks.p: Yawgmoth's second plan was to capture the Null Sphere, the giant hollow antenna that Glacian had built to command every artifact creature in the Empire. Whoever held the Sphere could give orders to the Alliance's artifact soldiers.
While the two armies fought at the Defile, Yawgmoth flew to the Null Sphere in a caravel full of Phyrexians. The bodies of these Phyrexians had been reworked until they resembled spiders.

The soldiers guarding the Sphere had two bombards, great guns that hurled burning rocks, and they used them well. Burning rock smashed into the caravel as it approached. The caravel fired back with its ray cannons. The rays melted one bombard together with its crew, and blew a hole in the wall of the guard post. But the second bombard holed the caravel's hull, and the ship began to tip over. Yawgmoth and his Phyrexians abandoned the ship. The caravel's gunner stayed at his cannon and destroyed the second bombard as the ship fell, and the gunner died when the ship struck the ground and exploded.

The spider-shaped Phyrexians went in through the hole in the wall. The defenders shot them with powerstone crossbows whose bolts punched clean through their bodies, and the Phyrexians kept coming anyway. When the fight inside the guard post was over, nobody in it was alive on either side.

Yawgmoth himself led a party of the Halcyte Guard to the Sphere. The Guard fastened a ring of powerstones around the Sphere's middle and blasted away the pylons that held it in its crater. The Null Sphere rose into the air. Yawgmoth spared the artificers who worked inside it, because he needed them to operate the controls.

By the third morning at the Megheddon Defile, the Alliance army was dug in behind walls built of its own dead. The Alliance soldiers could not retreat, because Yawgmoth's airships held the sky over the pass behind them. They could not advance either.

Up in the Null Sphere, Yawgmoth killed the captive artificers one at a time until one of them gave in. That artificer did what Yawgmoth told him to do. Every artifact creature in the Alliance army turned round and attacked the soldiers it had been fighting beside.
The Alliance's dwarven commander, Curtisworthy, fought on to the end. The last thing Curtisworthy saw was a weapon falling from the Sphere. It was a stonecharger.
The rest of this story depends on that weapon, so it is worth being exact about it.

A stonecharger was the most terrible weapon the Thran possessed. A single one could destroy an army together with the ground the army stood on. The stonecharger that Yawgmoth dropped at the Megheddon Defile wiped out the Alliance army, and the mountain pass itself ceased to exist.
A stonecharger also left something behind after the blast: a cloud. The cloud was white, and it consumed everything it touched. It lingered where the weapon had fallen, and whatever it reached died.

Yawgmoth meant to use more stonechargers close to his own capital. The white clouds would then be a danger to Halcyon itself. His protection against them was the Null Sphere. Floating near the city under his control, the Sphere could draw the clouds' energy into itself, and so keep the clouds from reaching Halcyon. Everything Yawgmoth did next relied on the Sphere continuing to do that.
The people of Halcyon were still cheering the victory at the Defile when two more Alliance forces appeared on the horizon.

Yawgmoth made a speech to the city. He told the citizens to go down through the caves, pass through the portal into Phyrexia, and be made new there, where they would be safe. About half of the citizens went. The other half locked themselves in their houses.

It was at this point that Dyfed came looking for Yawgmoth in the world she had given him. She had been thinking about the war and about what she had learned. Phthisis had never been contagious, she told him, and Yawgmoth had always known that. He had used a lie about a disease to bury his enemies and reward his friends. Dyfed was sorry she had ever helped him. She ordered Yawgmoth to give up his power, surrender to the Alliance, and release the Alliance's ambassadors.
Yawgmoth appeared to give way. He agreed to release the ambassadors, and he took Dyfed down into Phyrexia to see them.

Yawgmoth had been experimenting on the ambassadors, and what had been done to them was worse than anything Dyfed could have imagined. For a moment she simply stood and stared. In that moment Yawgmoth drove a dagger made of powerstone into the back of her skull.

The dagger did not kill Dyfed. It scrambled her mind so completely that she could no longer hold a thought together. A planeswalker moves between worlds by an act of will, and Dyfed could no longer will anything, so she could not escape. Yawgmoth handed her to his priests, who began to cut her apart while she lived. Yawgmoth reasoned that somewhere in Dyfed's body there must be an organ that gave her the power to walk between worlds. He wanted that organ for himself.

On the last night of the war both sides prepared. At dawn the Alliance sent two fleets of airships toward Halcyon. Yawgmoth took his favourite war caravel, a ship named the Yataghan, high above the two fleets and bombed them from above. The Yataghan had destroyed about two thirds of the Alliance's ships when it was rammed and then shot through with a ray. The Yataghan rolled over, and Yawgmoth fell out of the sky onto the sandy slopes below the city.
Yawgmoth survived the fall, because he was wearing a suit of armour that Glacian had designed.

From the ground Yawgmoth could see Alliance soldiers wrecking the great arrays of mirrors that stood around Halcyon. The mirrors fed the mana rig. Without them the city could make no more powerstones and no more weapons.

A creature climbed down the cliff to fetch Yawgmoth. It could walk on walls. It had tearing claws and a huge mouth full of teeth like razors. The creature was Xod, the healer who had once given Yawgmoth the idea for the serum. Xod had gone into Phyrexia and been remade. Yawgmoth looked at what his new world had made of the man, and thought Xod beautiful.

Xod carried Yawgmoth back up into the city. Yawgmoth then dropped stonechargers on the two Alliance armies in the desert below the walls, an army of dwarves and an army of humans. Both armies were destroyed. White clouds now hung over the desert on Halcyon's doorstep. The Null Sphere held them back from the city.

In the caves under the city, Glacian died. Rebbec was holding him. As she held her husband's body, she found the two halves of a powerstone hidden inside his wound, and she understood that Yawgmoth had put them there.

Yawgmoth learned that Rebbec knew. He drugged her and carried her through the portal into Phyrexia. There, with the power of a god, Yawgmoth poured his own mind into Rebbec's mind. He told Rebbec that the two of them would rule this world together.

Rebbec had one moment to prepare before his mind entered hers, and she used that moment to hide a single thing. Rebbec had loved Yawgmoth. She took that love and disguised it as hatred. When Yawgmoth searched her mind, he found only hatred for himself, and he believed it was the whole truth.
Yawgmoth found other things in Rebbec's mind as well. He learned where Dyfed had taken the Thran elders. He also learned that refugees were hiding in the stone silos of Halcyon.
Rebbec refused to rule with him. Yawgmoth was furious, but Halcyon was under siege, and he had to return to the city. He left Rebbec behind in Phyrexia.

Yawgmoth had forgotten one consequence of what he had just done. Phyrexia obeyed the mind of its master. Yawgmoth had joined his mind to Rebbec's, and so the plane now treated Rebbec as its master's equal. Nothing in Phyrexia tried to stop her as she walked through it.

Rebbec went down through the nested spheres, and she saw what the fine infirmary on the surface had been hiding. She found the Alliance's ambassadors, mutilated. She found Dyfed on the priests' table, still alive. Rebbec killed the priests. She drew the powerstone dagger out of Dyfed's skull, and Dyfed, released at last, died. Then Rebbec took up her husband's body and went back through the portal to Halcyon.

parts.h: The Null Sphere becomes a moon

blocks.p: While all this was happening, the artificers inside the Null Sphere had made a plan of their own. They were Yawgmoth's prisoners, working the Sphere under guard, and they knew that the Sphere was the only thing keeping the white clouds away from Halcyon.

The artificers told their guards that the Sphere had to rise higher in order to absorb so much energy from the clouds. The guards believed them. The Sphere rose, and went on rising, into air too thin to breathe. This was what the artificers intended. They had decided to die. When the artificers suffocated at their posts, there was nobody left who could work the controls, and the controls failed.

The Null Sphere kept climbing. With nothing to bring it down, it rose out of the sky altogether and settled into orbit around the world. It has been there ever since. Dominaria had one moon before that day and has had two since, and nearly every people on the plane has a legend about the night the small bright moon first appeared. It is called the Null Moon.
With the Sphere gone, nothing protected Halcyon from the white clouds drifting below it.
Yawgmoth, back in the city, now acted on what he had found in Rebbec's mind. He ordered the Halcyte Guard to bring down the stone silos in which the refugees were hiding.

When the Guard toppled them, the silos fell from the floating city into the desert below, where the white clouds from the stonechargers were still boiling. The falling silos struck the clouds and flung them upward. The clouds rose over the walls of the city.

Rebbec had made one last attempt to save people. She had fitted her floating crystal temple with an engine, so that the temple could carry citizens out of the city through the air. The Thran Temple very nearly escaped. As it flew clear, the edge of a white cloud brushed against it, and the crystal temple broke apart in the sky.

The whiteness rolled across the eight terraces of Halcyon, and everything it covered died. Yawgmoth called out to everyone still living to come down into the caves and go through the portal to safety. The people came, because there was nowhere else to go.

On the far side of the portal the people of Halcyon saw Phyrexia for the first time. They saw what was waiting for them and what they were going to be turned into. They tried to run back. Yawgmoth's servants killed them, and their bodies became the raw material from which the first full generation of Phyrexians was made.

Rebbec was now the last living person in Halcyon. She still had the two half-stones that Yawgmoth had hidden in her husband's body. She fitted the two halves together, and when they joined she heard Glacian's voice.

Glacian's mind was inside the stone. He had died with the two halves buried in his flesh, and as he died his mind had passed into them. So had something else. Glacian had carried a planeswalker's spark all his life without knowing it, the sleeping power that Dyfed had recognised in him. The spark had never awakened, but as Glacian died its energy flowed into the two half-stones and charged them.

Inside the stone, free of his sick body, Glacian could think clearly for the first time in nine years. He told Rebbec what the stone was. It was the same stone that Dyfed had broken to open the portal. If the whole stone were set back on the pedestal where Dyfed had broken it, the portal would close.

Rebbec carried the stone down to the chamber in the caves. She set it, whole again, on the pedestal. The portal began to close. On the other side of it stood Yawgmoth, a god inside his own world, and he begged Rebbec to stop.

Rebbec did not stop. The portal closed. Yawgmoth was shut out of Dominaria, together with Gix, the Phyrexians and everything else he had made. Rebbec had every reason to believe she had shut him out for ever.
Then Rebbec climbed the long stair out of the Caves of the Damned, up into the city she had built, and walked into the white cloud.

Yawgmoth had given his caravels standing orders to drop stonechargers on every Thran city that refused to surrender. The sources do not say what became of the other seven city-states. They say only that the Thran had lost too much to continue, and that the Empire was gone within a short time. Descendants of the Thran lived on in a few places, in Shiv and elsewhere, among ruins they no longer understood.

Halcyon no longer floated. Its wreck lay shining on the desert floor. The enormous forces released in that place left one thing behind: a being made of light, named Evra, who was the only witness to the city's end.

In Phyrexia, a god with a great deal of time set about improving the people who had trusted him. Gix stood beside him. Gix was among the first to be completely remade, and over the ages he became one of the most powerful of Yawgmoth's servants.

And under the desert, in the caves that would one day be called the Caves of Koilos, a single powerstone sat on a pedestal in the dark with a dead man's mind inside it. It stayed there undisturbed for five thousand years, until two brothers found it.

chapters.title: The First Vampires of Innistrad
sources: Colin Kawakami, "The Lunarch's Journal" (Wizards of the Coast, 13 August 2014)

blocks.p: The last chapter ended with the fall of the Thran Empire on Dominaria, about five thousand years before the birth of Urza. The age that follows is called the Time of Legends, and it runs from that fall to Urza's birth. For its first two and a half thousand years the chronicle records nothing at all.

When the record resumes, it is on another world. This chapter takes place on a plane called Innistrad. It tells how vampires came to exist there, and how one young man of that plane became a planeswalker, a being who can walk between worlds. That young man, Sorin Markov, will matter for the rest of the story.

Innistrad is a dark plane of forests, moors and small human provinces. In the age of this chapter, one of its mountain regions was ruled by a noble family named Markov. That region would later be called Stensia.

The head of the family was Edgar Markov. Edgar was a nobleman and an alchemist, and he was growing old. He had spent years searching for a way to stop ageing. He wanted to live for ever, and he wanted the same for his only grandson, Sorin.
Sorin Markov was born about -2440 AR. At the time of these events he was a teenager.

A demon set the events in motion. Innistrad has many demons, and one of the most powerful was a demon lord named Shilgengar. Shilgengar caused a great famine in the Markovs' lands. Crops failed and the people began to starve.

Then Shilgengar went to Edgar Markov with an offer. The demon knew a kind of magic that Edgar had not tried: blood magic, which is also called sangromancy. Shilgengar offered to teach Edgar a ritual. Those who went through the ritual would never grow old, and they would no longer need ordinary food. They would live on blood.

Edgar saw two answers in the offer. The ritual would give him the endless life he had been looking for. It would also solve the famine, in a terrible way. The few who were changed would be fed, because they would feed on other people. And as they fed, there would be fewer hungry mouths in the land.
Edgar accepted.

The ritual needed one ingredient above all: the blood of a living angel. Innistrad has angels, who protect its people. Edgar and his sons captured one of them, an archangel named Marycz. They hung Marycz up in Edgar's laboratory and drained her of her blood. From the angel's blood Edgar prepared the potion that the ritual required.

Edgar shared the potion with his own family and with other nobles of Innistrad. Everyone who drank it became a vampire: ageless, strong, and dependent on the blood of the living. Each noble who drank founded a line of vampires. One of those who took part was a wealthy and solitary noblewoman named Olivia Voldaren. Olivia became the founder of the Voldaren line of vampires, as Edgar became the founder of the Markov line.
This happened about -2424 AR. Some sources give the year as -2421.

A human priest of Innistrad discovered the truth of this origin thousands of years later, and what horrified him most was a single point. The vampires who preyed on Innistrad's people had not come from outside. Humans had made them, out of themselves.
Edgar wanted his grandson to share his gift. Sorin did not choose it. Edgar and the rest of the family held the boy still and forced him to drink the angel's blood.

The change into a vampire was an agony, and Sorin went through it held down by his own relatives. Sorin, though nobody knew it, had been born with a planeswalker's spark. A spark usually lies asleep until a moment of terrible shock wakes it. The horror of the ritual woke Sorin's. He became a planeswalker in the same hour that he became a vampire.

Soon afterwards Sorin left Innistrad, and left his grandfather, for the first time. He did not stay away. Sorin worried about what was happening to the world of his birth, and he returned to it again and again over the following ages.

Sorin lived on, as vampires do, for thousands of years. He travelled to hundreds of planes. By nature he followed his own pleasures and kept his distance from other people's troubles. But he never stopped caring about Innistrad, and he kept an eye on dangers that might one day reach it. About a thousand years after his transformation, that habit would lead him to the most dangerous creatures in the Multiverse. That story is told later in this age, in the chapter on the imprisonment of the Eldrazi.

On Innistrad the vampire families grew. They spread into the human provinces and hunted the people they had once been. In the ages that followed, the vampires became so many and so strong that humanity itself was in danger of being wiped out. If that happened, the vampires would starve as well.

Sorin could see this danger from his wider view of the worlds. When he put it to his grandfather, Edgar brushed it aside. The vampires had eternity, Edgar said, or something close to it, in which to find a solution. What Sorin eventually did about it belongs to a later chapter.

chapters.title: Arcavios: The Dragons and the Blood Age

blocks.p: This is a short chapter about one more world. The chronicle gives it a single line in this age: about -2438 AR, almost in the same years that vampires appeared on Innistrad, the first people appeared on a plane called Arcavios. Arcavios becomes important much later in the story, as the home of a great school of magic. This chapter tells how the plane began. It rests on the chronicle and on one encyclopaedia page, and it is brief because the sources are.

parts.h: A world made of two worlds

blocks.p: Arcavios was not always one plane. Thousands of years before the first people, two separate planes merged into one. Nothing like it is recorded anywhere else.

The two worlds did not fit together neatly. Every plane has leylines, which are channels that carry mana, the energy of magic. When the two planes merged, their leylines were laid on top of one another, and the lines did not match. A line carrying one kind of mana came to lie across a line carrying an opposing kind. The clash gave the magic of Arcavios a character found nowhere else. In certain small regions the clash is strongest, and the effects of mismatched mana can be plainly seen. Such a region is called a snarl.
The first age of Arcavios is called the Dawning Age. In that age no people yet walked the plane. Many forms of life adapted to the merged world, and many new forms of life came into being.

Five of the vortices of clashing mana were especially powerful. Each of the five became a shining sphere, and from each sphere a dragon hatched. These were the five Elder Dragons of Arcavios. They have no connection with the Elder Dragons of Dominaria who fell from the Ur-Dragon's wings. Each of the five was the first master of one kind of clashing magic, and each embodied one pair of opposed forces.
Their names are Beledros Witherbloom, Galazeth Prismari, Shadrix Silverquill, Tanazir Quandrix and Velomachus Lorehold.
About -2438 AR the first humanoid peoples arose on Arcavios, and the Dawning Age ended.

At first the five dragons were angry. Mortals were trying to use the wild magic of the plane, and the dragons thought that mortals had no business doing so. In time the dragons changed their minds. They came to see that magic would only ever be in safe hands if those hands were trained by long, disciplined study. That thought led to something, but not for a very long time.

What came first was war. The new peoples of Arcavios fought one another, and the age of their fighting is called the Blood Age. Its wars were so terrible that students of history on Arcavios are still shocked by them thousands of years later.

One of those wars is remembered by name. An orc leader called Golwanda the Bloodspiller led a fearless orcish cavalry known as the Thunder Riders, and she united the peoples of the steppe under a banner called the Crimson Glaive. Against her stood Xandril the Executioner, of the kor people, who rallied the hard, poor fiefdoms of a region called the Hordelands. The armies of Golwanda and Xandril met on battlefields soaked in blood.

The Blood Age lasted for a very long time. The five dragons finally brought it to an end by founding an institution to train mages for peace. That institution is Strixhaven, the school for which Arcavios is known. It was founded only about seven hundred years before the story's present day, and its founding is told in its own place.

chapters.title: Corondor: Sivitri's Dragons and the Forging of the Blackblade

blocks.p: The story now returns to Dominaria, the world of the Elder Dragons and the Thran. Two and a half thousand years or more have passed since the Thran Empire fell. Nobody on Dominaria remembers the Thran, and the great war of the brothers Urza and Mishra is still far in the future.

This chapter and the next take place on a single continent of Dominaria, called Corondor. Together the two chapters tell one long story of about four hundred years. The story has a villain, a planeswalker named Geyadrone Dihada, and it explains where one famous weapon came from: a sword called the Blackblade. That sword appears again at the very end of the story so far written, in the hands of Gideon in the War of the Spark.

These events were first told in comic books published in 1996. The chronicle cannot date them exactly. The comics only say that they happened thousands of years after the Thran and centuries before the brothers. The chronicle therefore gives each event a wide range of possible years, and the years in this chapter are those ranges.

Corondor lies in the northern half of Dominaria. A great chain of mountains called the Spine runs down the middle of the continent and divides it into three lands. Stonehaven lies to the west of the mountains, Casindral to the south, and Golthonor to the east. This chapter takes place mostly in Golthonor.

In the south-east of Golthonor, in the time of this chapter, there was a forest called Khone. The forest had a guardian. On Dominaria a wild place can give rise to a nature spirit, a living being that embodies the land and protects it. The guardian of Khone was a spirit of that kind, and its name was Sol'Kanar. In this age Sol'Kanar was gentle and cared for the health of the land.

The first trouble came from outside the world. A planeswalker named Sivitri Scarzam arrived in south-eastern Corondor. Sivitri was a human woman, though she carried some features of a dragon, and she commanded a breed of dragons that bore her name: the Scarzam dragons. She rode them from world to world as a conqueror.
Sivitri's dragons came down on the rich farmland like a swarm of locusts. The dragons were starving, and they ate everything in their path. The people fled before them.

As the dragons spread, the refugees began to band together to fight. Most of the refugees were farmers. Their weapons were made of iron and wood, and those weapons could not pierce a dragon's hide. The farmers tried to bury the dragons under rockslides. They tried traps of fire and traps of water. They tried what little magic they had. Nothing stopped the swarm.

Then an old healer found a flower. The healer had walked that region for years and knew its plants, and this was a poppy of a kind the healer had never seen before. It was new. The nature spirit Sol'Kanar had created it.

The healer ground the poppies into a potion and found that the potion was a poison of a very unusual kind. It killed Scarzam dragons, and it killed them by touch. A spear smeared with the poison did not need to break a dragon's skin. The spear only had to touch the scales, and the dragon died. The farmers killed dozens of dragons with poisoned spears.

Sivitri gave up the conquest. She mounted the largest of her dragons, a beast said to be able to level a mountain, and left Dominaria on its back to seek other worlds. The people destroyed the dragons she left behind, and the victors settled the land where the invasion had begun.

Two things should be remembered from this small war. Sivitri and her last and greatest dragon were alive, somewhere outside the world. And it was the spirit Sol'Kanar who had made the flower that beat her.
Shortly after Sivitri's War a second planeswalker came to Corondor, and this one was far worse.

Geyadrone Dihada was a demon and a shapeshifter, and she was already unimaginably old. In her own shape, the upper half of her body resembled a grey-skinned woman with long black hair and clawed hands, and the lower half ended in tentacles like those of an octopus. She could take other shapes at will.

Dihada wanted one thing: to have the most powerful beings in existence under her control. Her plans ran over thousands of years. When she found a being that was already mighty, she bound it to her service with spells. When she found a being that only had the makings of might, she shaped and corrupted it until it suited her. In Corondor she did both. This chapter tells how she corrupted two beings. The first was a blacksmith.

Dakkon was a mortal man, a master blacksmith and also a warrior. Dihada came to him with an offer. She wanted a sword: the most powerful blade in existence. If Dakkon made it for her, she would give him the power of a planeswalker.

Dihada was not lying about that part. When she first met Dakkon she sensed that he had been born with a planeswalker's spark, the sleeping gift that lets a person walk between worlds once it wakes. Dakkon did not know that he had it.

Dakkon agreed. Dihada taught him the secret magic that the sword required. The sword was to be a soul-drinker: a blade that takes the life-energy of everyone it kills and keeps that energy as its own strength.

The forging took ten years. By Dakkon's own account he stood at his anvil every day of those ten years. A smith cools hot metal by plunging it into water. Dakkon cooled this blade differently. Each time he heated the sword, he cooled it by killing a slave with it. In his hunger for the power he had been promised, Dakkon was even willing to give his own son to the blade.
At last the sword was finished. It is known simply as the Blackblade.

Dakkon could not stop himself from trying it. He went into battle with the sword in his hand, and with every person he killed he felt himself grow stronger. He killed so many, so fiercely, that stories of the slaughter spread across the land, and people gave him a new name: Dakkon Blackblade.
The stories reached Dihada, and she returned. She kept her promise. She woke Dakkon's spark, and Dakkon became a planeswalker.

In the same moment she took the Blackblade and drove it into Dakkon's shadow. The sword drank Dakkon's soul, though it left him alive. Dakkon's shadow and soul were now inside the blade, and the blade was in Dihada's hands.

Dakkon did not understand. Dihada had given him enormous power and, in the same breath, had made him her enemy. He could not see why anyone would do both. He set out across the planes to find her. For three hundred years he searched and did not find her. All that time Dihada was on Corondor. Why Dihada had done it becomes clear in the next chapter.

Dihada turned next to the spirit Sol'Kanar. She corrupted him as she had corrupted Dakkon, and the gentle guardian became a monster and her servant. As Sol'Kanar changed, the land he embodied changed with him. The forest of Khone sank into a vast marsh. The poppies that had killed Sivitri's dragons vanished from the land. Sol'Kanar was called the Swamp King from then on.

Dihada gave the Blackblade to Sol'Kanar to carry. Sol'Kanar made war on the countries of Corondor in her name. From the bones of the enemies he killed he built her a fortress, the Unholy Citadel, which crept across the land on giant legs of bone like a spider. With her corrupted champion and her walking castle, Dihada spent three centuries conquering the south of Corondor.

While Dihada was conquering the south, another tyranny grew in the north of Golthonor, in the mountains called the Wolf's Hackle. It had nothing to do with Dihada at first, but the two stories join in the next chapter.

It began with a boy named Xarl in the city-state of Balthesa. Xarl was the son of a temple prostitute and grew up on the streets. A wizard named Skule took him in as a spellsquire, which is a wizard's apprentice and servant. Xarl learned magic from Skule and came to despise him. In secret Xarl obtained an object called a Horned Halo.
Xarl rose to the rank of archmage and entered the service of a barbarian warlord, Mandek Ironfist. Then Xarl forced his old teacher Skule to perform a summoning. What Skule summoned was an angel.
The angel's name was Trine. She was one of the Serra angels, a kind of angel that mages can call to their side by magic. The story of Serra, for whom those angels are named, is told later.

As soon as Trine appeared, Xarl set the Horned Halo on her head. The Halo bound Trine to Xarl's will. She became a fallen angel, an angel turned to evil, and Xarl's slave. Xarl also used magic to make Trine forget that she had ever been an angel of Serra, so that she would never try to return to what she had been.

The warlord Mandek rewarded Xarl with a castle in the Wolf's Hackle. It came to be called Angel Keep, and Xarl took the title of Angel-Keeper. With Trine's power at his command, Xarl became the most powerful man in Corondor, and possibly in all Dominaria at that time. He used magic to stretch his own life far beyond a human span. He took many wives, among them a woman named Eska from the land of Thetia, and fathered a huge family, the House of Xarl. His countless descendants called him the Great Father.

The rule of Xarl and Trine was a bloody one. Over the years of her slavery Trine killed thousands of people, perhaps far more, in war and in sacrifice. Her slavery lasted three hundred and twenty-six years.

So for three centuries Corondor suffered under two tyrannies at once: Xarl and his fallen angel in the north, Dihada and her Swamp King in the south. And all that time Dakkon Blackblade wandered the other worlds, looking for Dihada in the wrong places.

chapters.title: Corondor: The Death of an Elder Dragon

blocks.p: This chapter finishes the story that the last chapter began, on the continent of Corondor on Dominaria. Three hundred years have passed. In the north of Corondor the archmage Xarl still rules through Trine, the angel he enslaved with a Horned Halo. In the south the demon planeswalker Geyadrone Dihada still rules through Sol'Kanar, the nature spirit she corrupted into the Swamp King. Sol'Kanar carries the Blackblade, the soul-drinking sword that the smith Dakkon forged for Dihada. Dakkon's shadow and soul are trapped inside that sword. Dakkon himself, now a planeswalker, has been searching other worlds for Dihada for three centuries.
As in the last chapter, the years are wide ranges. The chronicle knows the order of these events and how long they took, but not exactly when they happened.

Xarl the Angel-Keeper had stretched his life with magic, but he could not stretch it for ever. In his old age Xarl took a new spellsquire, as the wizard Skule had once taken him. The apprentice he chose was one of his own descendants: a boy named Eskil, the great-great-grandson of Xarl through his wife Eska. (The chronicle's short summary calls Eskil an adopted son instead.)
After three hundred and twenty-six years of rule, Xarl died of old age. The House of Xarl passed to Eskil.
With Xarl dead, the angel Trine had no master and no purpose. She fled Angel Keep and flew back to the place where Xarl had first set the Horned Halo on her head.

Eskil was nothing like his ancestor. He was pure of heart, and he wanted to undo the evil that Xarl and Trine had done. Eskil knew how to summon, and he called a second Serra angel into the world. Her name was Rahel. Rahel and Trine had once been sisters among the angels.
Rahel sensed that Eskil's purpose was good, and she agreed to help him. She hunted Trine down, and the two angels fought. Rahel killed Trine.

Trine died in a burst of light. Eskil was standing close, and by one account Trine's blood splashed over him. Eskil was blinded, and his skin and his hair were bleached white. And in that moment Eskil's own sleeping spark woke, and he became a planeswalker.

Rahel then forgave Trine for everything Trine had done as a slave. That forgiveness is the absolution for which the event is named. In death, Trine turned back from a fallen angel into a Serra angel, and she was carried away to Serra.

Eskil lived on as a planeswalker, which in that age meant that he did not grow old. He became one of the kindest planeswalkers Dominaria has known. He was called Eskil the White. In later ages he made his home in a forest in the south of Corondor called the White Woods, and guarded it.
In the south, Dihada had not finished. Among her conquests was a city and kingdom called Carth, which she destroyed.

One survivor of Carth was an orphan boy who lived as a thief. His own name is not recorded. He is called the Son of Carth, after his lost home. The boy fell into Dihada's hands and was thrown into her dungeons.

In his cell the boy met another prisoner, a monk. The monk helped the boy to escape. The monk also set the boy on a quest and told him how to get revenge on Dihada. There was an object called the Amulet of Ti-Fu, and with it the boy could summon a mighty warrior and bind that warrior to his service.
The boy used the amulet. The warrior it summoned was Dakkon Blackblade.

The amulet bound Dakkon to the boy. While the bond held, Dakkon could not walk away to another plane. Dakkon was a violent, short-tempered man and had no intention of serving a child. He attacked the boy at once, meaning to kill him and end the bond. The amulet protected the boy, and Dakkon found that he could not harm him. Dakkon had no choice but to serve.
Then Dakkon learned who the boy's enemy was. It was Dihada, the very being he had hunted across the planes for three hundred years. After that Dakkon served willingly.
Dihada heard that the two were coming for her. She sent her champion, Sol'Kanar the Swamp King, to kill them both.
It did not go as she appeared to expect. Dakkon fought the corrupted nature spirit and beat him.

Dihada then showed herself. She was laughing. The fighting, she let them know, was being staged for her pleasure. She treated the boy as beneath her notice and turned her attention to Dakkon. Against Dakkon she summoned two servants far greater than the Swamp King.

The servants were Elder Dragons. The Elder Dragons were the first dragons of Dominaria, who fell from the wings of the Ur-Dragon when the world was young. Only a handful survived the war that the Elder Dragons fought among themselves. Those survivors were among the mightiest creatures alive, nearly as powerful as planeswalkers.

One of the two was Chromium Rhuell, an older brother of Nicol Bolas. The other was Piru, a female Elder Dragon who was Chromium's mate. Between them Chromium and Piru had bred whole nations of lesser dragons. At some time in her long hunt for powerful servants, Dihada had bound both of them to her will with spells. How and when she did it is not told.

A note on Piru. The older tellings of the dragons' war name five surviving Elder Dragons, and Piru is not one of the five. For a long time readers argued over whether Piru was a true Elder Dragon or only a child of one. The later comics called her a sixth survivor, and her own card, printed in 2021, names her an Elder Dragon. This story follows the card.

Dakkon first tried to seize control of Chromium's mind and to order Chromium to kill Piru. The attempt failed, because an Elder Dragon's will is too strong. Chromium began to drain Dakkon's strength away. At the last moment Dakkon used a different power, the power to banish a creature, and hurled Chromium away to some unknown place.
That left Piru. And the boy, whom Dihada had ignored, had been busy. While the great ones fought, the Son of Carth crept close enough to steal back the Blackblade. He brought the sword to Dakkon.
Dakkon fought Piru with his own sword in his hand again, and he stabbed her with it. The Blackblade killed the Elder Dragon.
The death of so great a creature released a blast of energy that tore the land open. The gash it left is called the Dueling Chasm of Golthonor.
Dihada was not dismayed. Piru's death was exactly what she had planned.

Here is the whole of her scheme, in order. Dihada wanted the power of an Elder Dragon for herself. That power can only be taken at the moment when such a dragon dies. But an Elder Dragon is almost impossible to kill. So Dihada needed two things: a weapon that could kill one, and a warrior strong enough to use it. Three hundred years earlier she had caused both to be made. She had Dakkon forge the Blackblade, and she made Dakkon a planeswalker. She took his shadow so that he would hate her and come for her when called. And she had bound Piru as a servant, so that the dragon would be on the battlefield when the time came.
As Piru died, Dihada drank in the power of the dragon's soul. The power was so great that Dihada lost her hold on her own shape for a time and showed her true demonic form.

Then Dihada told the boy the last part. The monk in the dungeon, who had helped him escape and had sent him to find the amulet, had been Dihada herself in another shape. The boy's whole quest for revenge had been her doing.

Dakkon struck at her before she finished speaking. Even with the Blackblade, Dakkon was no match for Dihada with an Elder Dragon's power in her. She held him off long enough to set her mark on him. By that mark, she said, Dakkon would be her champion and would serve her for all eternity, and she would summon him when she had need of him. Then she left Dominaria. The fighting between Dakkon and Dihada is called the Blackblade-Dihada War, though it lasted only a few days.
Dakkon cursed the boy for ever having summoned him. But the boy had noticed something that Dakkon had missed. Dakkon's shadow had come back.
During those days of destruction, Eskil the White came south. The planeswalker who had ended his ancestor's tyranny protected the children of southern Corondor from the war.

Dakkon and the boy stayed together. Dakkon gave the boy a name: the Lion of Carth. The two of them left Corondor and crossed the world to a distant land called Terisiare. There the boy founded a family. The family took its name from him, Carthalion, and descendants of that line appear in the story for thousands of years afterwards.
Dihada did not return to Dominaria for a very long time. Dakkon still bore her mark.

Dihada had no more use for Sol'Kanar. She had a new champion marked, and she simply left the Swamp King behind when she departed. Sol'Kanar remained what she had made him. A legend of Corondor says that he will turn back into the gentle spirit he once was on the day Dihada dies.

Left alone, Sol'Kanar made himself a king. He showed himself to the peoples of the region from time to time and encouraged them to believe that he was a god. Two kingdoms lay near his marsh, the Kingdom of Khone and the Kingdom of Shikar, and only one road joined them. Sol'Kanar rose beside that road, declared that the swamp was his, and sank the road into the bog.

Then he made his demand. On one day of every year, both kingdoms were to send him tribute: food, slaves, goods and knowledge. If the tribute did not come, he would destroy them. That yearly day was called the Date of Tribute, and it went on for more years than anyone counted.

Among the knowledge that reached Sol'Kanar was an old piece of history. Centuries before, the planeswalker Sivitri Scarzam had left Corondor with one dragon still alive, the greatest of the breed, and that dragon still existed somewhere beyond the world. Sol'Kanar wanted its power for himself. He changed the tribute. From then on each kingdom was to send him one thing only: a spellcaster, to work on summoning the last Scarzam dragon.

The spellcasters whose work finally succeeded were two women: Gydolien Mor of Khone and Chondaeh of Shikar. Chondaeh was secretly plotting against the Swamp King. After years of attempts, working with Sol'Kanar, the two of them opened a portal and brought the last Scarzam dragon through it.
The dragon was not alone. Sivitri Scarzam was riding it.
Sivitri looked at Sol'Kanar and recognised him. Changed as he was, he was the spirit who had made the poppies that killed every one of her other dragons. She attacked him.

The fight threatened to grow out of all control. Gydolien Mor ended it. She cast a charm on the dragon and commanded it to leave. The dragon turned and went back through the portal by which it had come, carrying Sivitri away with it.

Gydolien had saved the Swamp King. Sol'Kanar did not understand that. In his rage he blamed the wrong kingdom, and he ordered Khone, Gydolien's home, to be laid waste. Shikar, the home of the real plotter Chondaeh, was left alone and grew into a glorious kingdom. Gydolien Mor swore that she would have revenge on Chondaeh. The sources do not say whether she got it.

That is the end of the old tales of Corondor. Their people come back into the story much later: Dihada and Dakkon, the line of Carth, Eskil the White, and above all the Blackblade, which had now done something that no other weapon had done. It had killed an Elder Dragon. That fame is the reason the sword is carried against Nicol Bolas, the last and most dangerous of the Elder Dragons, at the end of the story.

chapters.title: The Imprisonment of the Eldrazi
sources: Kelly Digges, "The Lithomancer" (Wizards of the Coast, 29 October 2014)

blocks.p: The last two chapters stayed on Dominaria. This chapter leaves it, and it is one of the most important in the whole early story. It tells how three planeswalkers found the greatest danger in the Multiverse and locked it away. A planeswalker is a person who can walk from one world, or plane, to another. The Multiverse is the whole collection of planes.

Two of the three have been met before. The first is Sorin Markov, the young nobleman of the plane Innistrad who was forced to become a vampire and became a planeswalker in the same hour. A thousand years have passed since then, and Sorin is now old, powerful and cold. The second is Ugin, the Spirit Dragon: the twin brother of Nicol Bolas, born on Dominaria, who died and came back as a being of spirit, and who spends his endless life studying the deep workings of the Multiverse. The third is new to the story. Her name is Nahiri.
Nearly everything in this chapter comes from one short story published by Wizards of the Coast, which is told from Nahiri's side.

Nahiri came from a plane called Zendikar. Zendikar is a wild world, rich in mana, the energy of magic, and thinly peopled. Nahiri belonged to the kor, a grey-skinned people of Zendikar. She was a lithomancer, which means a mage of stone. Nahiri could feel rock and the metal inside rock, and she could shape both with her will. She could raise a wall out of the ground, or draw a finished sword out of a boulder.

Nahiri was born with a planeswalker's spark. When her spark woke, it threw her across the Multiverse without warning, as a first planeswalk does, and she landed on Innistrad, confused and alone. Innistrad was Sorin Markov's world. Sorin might have driven the young stranger off. He chose to teach her. Sorin explained to Nahiri what the Multiverse was and took her to see many planes. An unlikely friendship grew between the ancient vampire and the young kor, and Sorin came to regard Nahiri almost as a daughter. Nahiri, for her part, trusted Sorin's judgment, though she was often annoyed at being treated as the child in the room.
Nahiri saw herself as the protector of Zendikar. It was her world, and she had decided to take responsibility for it.
About -1440 AR, Sorin and Nahiri were together on a plane whose name has been lost, because nothing of that plane survives.

The plane was being eaten. Swarms of monsters had overrun it: writhing creatures in sickly colours, with tentacles, snapping jaws and bone-white heads that had no eyes. The smallest were the size of dogs and the largest the size of buildings. Neither Sorin nor Nahiri knew what the creatures were.

For weeks the two planeswalkers defended a band of about a hundred human refugees in a camp above a valley. Every night Nahiri raised walls of stone around the camp. The two disagreed about the point of it. Sorin thought they should be fighting the enemy, and that nursing a few refugees was a waste of two planeswalkers. Nahiri could not bear to stand by and watch people suffer.

Among the refugees was a girl of fifteen named Lian, who watched the two planeswalkers with cold eyes and did not expect to be saved. Nahiri answered her with a gift. Nahiri reached into the living rock and drew out of it a finished sword, and gave the sword to Lian. This world was Lian's, Nahiri told her, and Lian could fight for it herself if she did not trust strangers to do it. Sorin remarked quietly that this was false hope. Nahiri replied that any hope was better than none.
Then the ground shook, harder than it had in all those weeks. The monsters in the valley went strangely still. All of them turned to face the setting sun and began to sway.

Behind the hills on the far side of the valley, something rose. It was the size of a mountain, a shape of white bone and ropes of tentacle. It began to move towards the camp, and as it moved, the swarms in the valley surged forward with it, the way iron filings follow a magnet.

The refugees stood frozen, staring. It was Lian who shouted them into motion. The swarm hit the stone wall and piled up against it, the creatures climbing over one another to reach the top. Sorin, Nahiri and Lian fought side by side. Sorin withered a dozen creatures to dust with a gesture. Nahiri sank dozens more into the ground. More kept coming. And the huge thing on the horizon pulled at everything. Clouds spiralled in towards it, and pieces of the land rose into the air around it and broke apart. Nahiri felt her own mana being dragged out of her as fast as she could gather it.

Then a crack opened and split Nahiri's wall, and a terrible light shone out of the crack. Nahiri tried to close it with her power over stone. Nothing happened, because the crack was not in the stone. It was in the world. The plane itself was coming apart.

The light grew until it was unbearable. The refugees screamed, and then the screaming stopped. Sorin called to Nahiri that it was over, and planeswalked away. Nahiri reached for Lian's arm, but the girl was already gone. Only Lian's sword still hung in the blazing air. Nahiri seized the sword and left the plane as it ceased to exist.

Sorin and Nahiri had agreed beforehand to meet on Zendikar if things went wrong. They met in Akoum, a region of volcanic highlands, at the edge of a kor camp. Nahiri sat holding Lian's sword, which was now the only thing left of an entire world.
A third planeswalker appeared beside them: a huge, ghostly dragon about twelve metres long, glowing blue-white, with mist pouring off his body. It was Ugin.

Ugin had been on the dying plane too. He had not fought. He had watched, in order to learn what the creatures were. Nahiri was angry that anyone could treat the death of a world as a subject of study. Ugin answered that he had been learning how to stop the creatures for good, which was more than a single battle could do. Then he told them what he had learned.

The creatures are called the Eldrazi. To understand them, one fact about the Multiverse is needed. The planes do not touch one another. Between them lies a formless, chaotic space called the Blind Eternities. Ordinary living things cannot survive there. Planeswalkers pass through it briefly when they travel. The Eldrazi are the only creatures known to live there. The Blind Eternities are their home.
The Eldrazi move from plane to plane and consume each one: its mana, its life, and finally the plane itself.
