Ugin then explained why the Eldrazi are so hard to fight. What Sorin and Nahiri had seen on the horizon was not really the creature. The true body of an Eldrazi stays outside, in the Blind Eternities. What appears on a plane is only the part of itself that it pushes in. Ugin compared it elsewhere to a man who puts his hand into a pond. The fish in the pond see a hand. They do not see the man. In the same way, the mountain of bone and tentacle was only the hand.

There are, Ugin said, only three true Eldrazi. They are called titans. The thousands of smaller creatures in the swarms are not separate animals. Each swarm is an extension of one titan, part of its body and its will.

That left a hard problem. To fight the titans in the Blind Eternities would mean facing their whole strength in a place where even a planeswalker can barely stay alive. To destroy only the parts that reach into a plane would be very difficult, and it would achieve nothing, because the true bodies would be untouched.

Sorin said that a way must be found to destroy them. Ugin replied that this might be impossible, and that it would be unwise even if it were possible. Nobody knew what the Eldrazi were for, or what place they held in the workings of the Multiverse, or what would follow if they were removed from it.
Ugin had another answer: a prison.

The plan had three parts. First, lure all three titans to a single plane. Second, once they had pushed themselves into that plane, bind them there, using the very parts they had pushed in as anchors to hold them. Third, force them into a sleep without end. The same device that caged the titans would keep them dormant. The plane that held them would be damaged but would survive. If the plan failed, the plane would be destroyed. But every plane, Ugin pointed out, was already in that danger.

The plane had to meet certain conditions. It had to be large and rich in mana, so that it would attract the titans. It had to be thinly peopled. It could not be under the protection of some other planeswalker who might object. And one of the three had to be able to stay there and keep watch over the sleeping titans, for ever.
Ugin was looking at the landscape of Akoum as he listed these things. He meant Zendikar.

Nahiri refused. She asked what gave the three of them the right to put a whole world and all its peoples in danger. Sorin's world Innistrad did not meet the conditions, and Ugin said that his own home world did not either. They could search for another plane, Ugin said, but worlds would die while they searched. And if that plane had a protector, they would have to win that protector over, by force if needed.

Nahiri asked whether they meant to force her as well. Ugin said no. He needed her. The work required skills that he did not have, and it was too large for any one planeswalker. And he had chosen Zendikar for exactly the reason that troubled her: it had a guardian who had already taken its fate into her own hands, and who could be trusted to do the right thing.
Nahiri knelt and put her hand to the ground and felt the whole of Zendikar through the stone. Then she agreed. Zendikar would be the prison, and Nahiri would be the jailer.
The building of the prison took forty years of almost unbroken work.

The prison was made of stones. Nahiri drew them out of the earth of Zendikar one at a time, each one carefully shaped: huge eight-sided blocks, like two pyramids joined at the base. Ugin called them hedrons, and the name stayed. Nahiri made them in their thousands and filled the skies of Zendikar with them. Ugin carved each hedron with runes in the language of dragons. The runes held the hedrons in the air, and the runes were what would bind the Eldrazi to the plane.

The hedrons were linked to one another by invisible lines of mana, so that all of them together formed one enormous network across the whole plane. The network did two jobs. It was the cage. It was also the bait. The hedrons sent out pulses of magical energy into the Blind Eternities, and those pulses drew the Eldrazi as the smell of blood draws sharks.
Sorin's task was to watch the titans and guide them in. He reported that the three were slowly approaching Zendikar and were passing other worlds by on the way.

At the centre of the network, deep under the mountains of Akoum, the three built a chamber with crystal walls. It held a single stone that was linked to every hedron on the plane. Sorin and Nahiri named the chamber the Eye of Ugin. Sorin probably meant the name as mockery. For Nahiri it was a reminder to the dragon that all of this had been his idea.

Meanwhile Nahiri travelled across her world and warned its peoples of what was coming: the merfolk, the kor, the humans and the elves. Even the surrakar, an amphibious people of the swamps, passed the word among themselves that monstrous gods were on their way. The angels of Zendikar patrolled the skies among the floating stones.
About -1400 AR the Eldrazi came, and Zendikar was as ready as a world could be.
One titan seen from far away had been a horror. Three of them seen close were something the mind could hardly take in.
The first was the one Sorin and Nahiri had already seen: Ulamog, with a mask of bone and a lower body of tentacles. Ulamog turned out to be the smallest of the three.
The second was Kozilek. Where Kozilek's head should have been, great blades of black volcanic glass floated in the air.
The third and greatest was Emrakul, a tower of latticed flesh and reaching tentacles that floated above the broken ground, higher than the other two.

With the titans came their swarms. The peoples of Zendikar fought the swarms. Ugin breathed ghostfire on them. Ghostfire is Ugin's own weapon, a flame that cannot be seen. Sorin used the power of a vampire against creatures that drain life: he drained the Eldrazi's strength back out of them before they could take too much from Zendikar. Even so, the defenders would have been overrun if the fighting had gone on for long.
The titans paid no attention to any of it. They moved steadily and mindlessly towards the centre of the hedron network, the source of the call that had brought them across the Multiverse.

Nahiri was waiting in the Eye of Ugin. When the titans stood where they were meant to stand, Sorin and Ugin joined her there. The three planeswalkers turned all their power on the single linking stone.
Across the whole of Zendikar, every hedron lit up and moved into a new position. The network took its final shape, and the entire plane shuddered with the strain. Then it was finished.
The three sealed the Eye of Ugin with a magical lock. They made it so that only three planeswalkers acting together could open it again. One planeswalker alone, or two, could not undo their work.

Then they climbed to the surface. The land was half ruined. Above the highlands of Akoum the three titans stood turned to stone, wrapped in a web of floating hedrons. Nahiri knew that ground, and she could feel it already responding. The rock was growing up around the titans like a scab over a wound. In time the mountains of Akoum would swallow them completely.

The swarms that the titans had brought still had to be hunted down. After that, Sorin and Ugin would go back to their own affairs, and Nahiri would stay. All three agreed that if the prison was ever disturbed, they would return.
Nahiri looked up at the three silent shapes and thought that in a thousand years the peoples of Zendikar might forget them altogether. She would not forget, and neither would the land.

Both thoughts proved true. The peoples of Zendikar did forget. The titans slept under Akoum for nearly six thousand years. What woke them, and what became of the friendship between Sorin and Nahiri, are told much later.

The story is back on Dominaria, and it is nearly at the end of the long, thinly recorded age called the Time of Legends. The age closes with the birth of two brothers, Urza and Mishra, whose war fills the next part of the story.

Before that, the chronicle lists a handful of smaller events on Dominaria. They happened in different centuries and in different lands, and they have little to do with one another. What they share is that each one sets something in place that the later story uses: a kingdom, a city, a people, a man who will become a monster. This chapter goes through them in order of time. One of them is a proper tale, about three Elder Dragons, and it gets the most room.

Dominaria has many continents. One of them, far to the south of Corondor, is called Jamuraa. At some time between -2140 and -840 AR a kingdom took shape on the north-western coast of Jamuraa. Its name was Zhalfir.

Zhalfir was a land of coastal sands, forest and red-earthed scrubland. It was ruled by a royal family from a capital called Ki'pamu. It kept a large standing army, and it had a proud, quarrelsome class of nobles who were always at odds with one another. Above all, Zhalfir was strong in magic. The mages of Zhalfir are credited with being the first people on Dominaria to work out the system of five colours of mana, which every later mage on Dominaria uses.
Zhalfir lasted for more than five thousand years. It matters to the story because, thousands of years from now, it is the homeland of one of the story's most important people, a mage named Teferi.

parts.h: A boy on the Sarpadian coast

blocks.p: In -1850 AR a boy named Tev Loneglade was born on the coast of another continent of Dominaria, called Sarpadia. Tev had a sister, Tymolin, who looked after him as he grew up and protected him. Tymolin was a skilled fighter with a sword.

Tev was born with a planeswalker's spark, and in time it woke. That is why a man born in -1850 AR can still be alive nearly two thousand years later, as the chronicle says he was: in that age, a planeswalker did not die of old age. Tev became fiercely protective of his sister and used his new power to give her endless youth.

For now Tev was neither good nor evil. He refused to involve himself in other people's affairs. He is mentioned here because of what he later became. After Tymolin's death, long after this chapter, Tev Loneglade reshaped his body into that of a twisted dragon, took the name Tevesh Szat, and set out to bring silence to all living things.

This tale comes from a comic book of 1996. It happened after the events on Corondor told two chapters ago, because one of the dragons in it is in mourning for a death that happened there. The chronicle places it somewhere between -1300 AR and the start of the brothers' war.

Three Elder Dragons take part. The Elder Dragons were the first dragons of Dominaria, and only a few of them outlived the war they fought among themselves. All three of these were survivors of that war, and all three are relatives of Nicol Bolas.

The first is Palladia-Mors, a savage, solitary dragon. In this age she lay asleep under a ridge of land, and the ridge was named after her: Mors Ridge. People lived there, and they knew what slept beneath them. Their ruling body, the High Council of Mors Ridge, kept one official whose only duty was to keep the dragon asleep. He did it by casting a spell called the tickery, again and again, so that Palladia-Mors stayed in a magical sleep and could not attack the people. The official was called the Tickery Man. In the time of this tale the Tickery Man was a man named Ham.

The second dragon is Vaevictis Asmadi, a cousin of Palladia-Mors. Vaevictis was under a curse. The curse had shrunk him from an Elder Dragon into a dragon whelp, a small young dragon. He believed that Palladia-Mors could lift the curse.

Vaevictis found a way to wake Palladia-Mors. She undid his curse, and Vaevictis was a full Elder Dragon again. Then the two dragons, with an army behind them, went on a rampage against the people of Mors Ridge.

At that point Ham the Tickery Man revealed what he really was. He was the third dragon: Chromium Rhuell, the brother of Palladia-Mors, in human shape. Chromium had the gift of taking other forms, and he had been living among the people of the ridge and keeping his own sister asleep. Chromium was the dragon in mourning. His mate Piru had been killed by the Blackblade on Corondor, as an earlier chapter told.

Chromium talked Vaevictis into changing sides and turning on Palladia-Mors. Palladia-Mors was ready for that. When Vaevictis cast a spell at her, she turned his own spell back on him. Vaevictis vanished from the battlefield and was never seen again.

Chromium did not finish the fight alone. A human leader of Mors Ridge named Red Donald had a daughter, Ad'Amra, who was both a warrior and a spellcaster. Ad'Amra had fallen in love with Ham, not knowing what he was. Together Chromium and Ad'Amra managed to cast the sleeping spell on Palladia-Mors once more, and she was bound again under the ridge that bears her name.
The cost was terrible. Countless people died in the rampage, and Red Donald was among them.

The sources do not agree on every point of this tale. The chronicle's one-line summary says that Chromium defeated both of the other dragons. The fuller account says that Palladia-Mors was the one who removed Vaevictis, and one summary of that account counts Vaevictis as dead while another says only that he disappeared. The sources also differ on where Mors Ridge lies: one places it on Corondor, another in a region of Dominaria called the Domains. The story given here follows the fuller account.

Far to the north-west of Jamuraa lies Terisiare, the continent to which Dakkon Blackblade and the Lion of Carth travelled, and the continent on which the Thran Empire once stood. In -912 AR a city was founded on the east coast of Terisiare, beside the sea. It was named Penregon.

Penregon became the capital of a country called Argive, and Argive became a land of scholars. Its people counted their years from the founding of the city. That calendar is called Penregon Founding and is written PF, so that -912 AR is the year 1 PF. The great clock in Penregon's Grand Court was said to be a machine of the Thran.
Argive is where the brothers Urza and Mishra will be born.
Urborg is a land of islands on Dominaria. In later ages it is a place of swamps, volcanoes and the walking dead. In this age it was a forest.

From about -300 AR the forest of Urborg was ruled by panther warriors, a people who are like great cats that walk upright. They ruled it in peace for three centuries. Their leader was named Windgrace. By his own account Windgrace began to make his name at the age of twelve and became the warrior chief of his tribe. He lived to see the forest destroyed, and what destroyed it left him with a lifelong hatred of machines. That destruction comes at the end of the brothers' war. Windgrace became a planeswalker, and he returns to the story many times as Lord Windgrace, the guardian of Urborg.

On the first day of one Dominarian year, in the land of Argive on Terisiare, a boy was born and named Urza. On the last day of that same year his mother bore a second son, who was named Mishra. The two brothers were born in the same year, almost a full year apart.

The brothers changed the world so completely that later scholars of Argive threw out the old calendar of Penregon and began to count all of history from the year of the brothers' birth. That system is called Argivian Reckoning, written AR, and it is the system this whole story uses. The year the brothers were born is the year 0. Everything told so far has carried a minus sign because it happened before them.
Here the Time of Legends ends.

One more world has an entry in the chronicle before the Time of Legends closes. The plane is called Ixalan. Much later in the story Ixalan is a world of jungles, dinosaurs, pirates and a golden city, and several of the story's main characters are stranded there. This chapter is about something far older and far deeper: the first people of Ixalan, and the god who tried to make them his own.
The chronicle says only that this war ended in -57 AR or earlier. Nobody knows how much earlier.
Ixalan is hollow. Deep beneath its surface there is an enormous round chamber, and people live on the inside of it. The chamber is called the Core.

The Core is about twenty-two kilometres across. In the middle of it floats a small sun. The land covers the inner wall of the chamber, all the way round, and everything on that land is pulled outward, away from the sun. A person standing in the Core therefore has the ground underfoot and the sun always directly overhead. There is no horizon. The land curves gently upward in every direction, fades into haze, and reappears high overhead on the far side of the sun. That land holds forests, mountains, plains, rivers and freshwater seas.
The sun has a name, Chimil, and the people of the Core hold her to be their creator.
The Core is the oldest place on Ixalan. Humanity was born there, and so were the gods of the plane.

parts.h: The last of the Fourth People

blocks.p: The people of the Core count the history of the world in ages. They themselves belong to the fifth age. Almost nothing is known of the four before it.

One story of the fourth age survives. When that age was ending, its last survivor was an ordinary mortal with an overwhelming fear of death. To live through the end of the world, he killed every other person who was left and drank their blood. The blood sustained him through what the people of the Core call the ending of all things, and he found his way into the empty, divine place where the next world was being made. His name, as later ages knew it, was Aclazotz.

At the dawn of the fifth age the new gods were born. They were the children of the sun Chimil, and they are called the Deep Gods. Before the last of them could come into being, Aclazotz killed that god, ate him and took his place among them. So one of the gods of the new world was a murderer left over from the old one, and he took the form of a monstrous bat.

The first humans of Ixalan woke inside the Core, under Chimil. They understood from her that the world was new and that they were new, and they called themselves the Komon Winaq, which means the Fifth People.

The Core gave the Fifth People everything they needed, so they had time left over for leisure and for study, and they loved knowledge. They set out to map their world. They invented writing to record what they saw and numbers to measure it.

The great hero of that work was an explorer named Tan Jolom, called the worldwalker. Tan Jolom was the first person to travel the whole way round the Core and come back to where he started. His journey proved that the world was a sphere built around a star.

Death held no terror for the Fifth People in those days. There was no hidden afterlife. The spirits of the dead, called Echoes, simply went on walking among the living, and the border between life and death was as thin as a cobweb.

To Tan Jolom, then, dying looked like one more country to explore. He chose to become an Echo and set off into the realm of spirits. He hoped to find the Deep Gods there and tell them that their people had mapped the Core and were waiting for the gods to come. A whispering voice guided him on his way and promised to show him the land of the Fourth People.
The voice belonged to Aclazotz. And when Tan Jolom passed into the realm of spirits, he left the door open behind him.
Dark things from the realm of spirits slipped through that open door into the Core. The worst of them was Aclazotz himself.

Aclazotz understood that fear could feed him. So he changed the nature of death. He hardened the thin border between the living and the dead until it became a wall. From then on the dead no longer came back as Echoes. They were simply gone. For the first time the Fifth People understood that they were mortal. Death became something to mourn and to dread, and Aclazotz grew strong on the dread.

Then he went hunting in secret. He sought out the people who were most terrified, most broken by grief, most desperate. When he had such a person cornered, he whispered an offer: give yourself to me, and you will live for ever.

Grief and fear spread through the Core, and with them spread the rumour that there was a way to escape death. Preachers and pilgrims swept through the cities and founded cults, whose rituals were meant to call Aclazotz out into the open. Those rituals horrified most of the Fifth People. When the elders and leaders tried to put a stop to the cults, the cults fought back. Fighting raged through the fields and cities of the Core. That civil war is the Whispering War, named for the whispers that began it.

parts.h: The coming of the Deep Gods

blocks.p: The war was ended by the other gods. The first to come was Ojer Axonil, the Deep God of fury and strength. The sound of battle was familiar to him, and it drew him to the Core. When Ojer Axonil saw what was happening there, he reached back and warned his elder sibling, the Deep God Ojer Taq.
Then Ojer Axonil went to war. He raised a company of a thousand champions to follow him. That company is called the Thousand Moons.

Aclazotz tried to kill Ojer Taq, and Ojer Axonil stopped him. Then Ojer Axonil and the Thousand Moons went down into the deepest lairs of Aclazotz and his blood-drinking followers and fought them there. In the last battle Ojer Axonil tore out one of Aclazotz's eyes and locked the bat god away in a prison.
With Aclazotz shut away, the wall between life and death grew thin again, and the honoured dead returned to walk as Echoes among the living.

The Fifth People laid the foundations of a capital city, Oteclan, on the shore of a great lake called Wachibal. Under the eye of Ojer Taq they built a golden age that lasted for thousands of years. It is called the Age of the Sun.

Three things from this chapter return when the story reaches Ixalan again. The Fifth People still live in the Core, and in later ages they are called the Oltec. The Sun Empire, a people of Ixalan's surface, descends from them. And Aclazotz is only imprisoned. A god who promises eternal life in exchange for blood, on a plane that will one day be full of vampires, has not finished with the world.

chapters.title: The Brothers and the Stone
sources: MTG Wiki, "The Brothers' War (novel)" (the novel by Jeff Grubb, 1998)

blocks.p: With this chapter the story reaches its first great, fully told tale: the Brothers' War. It is the story of two brothers, Urza and Mishra, whose quarrel grew into a war that wrecked a continent and changed the climate of a world. Almost everything that happens on Dominaria for the next four thousand years follows from it.
To follow it, three things from earlier chapters are needed.

The first is the Thran. Five thousand years before the brothers, the continent of Terisiare was ruled by the Thran Empire, a people who built wonderful machines. The machines ran on powerstones, which are crystals that store energy.

The second is Phyrexia. In the last days of the Thran, a healer named Yawgmoth turned a whole artificial world into his kingdom. That world is Phyrexia, a plane where flesh and machine are joined into one. Yawgmoth tried to conquer the Thran from it, and the war destroyed the Thran Empire.

The third is the door. Phyrexia was joined to Dominaria by a portal, a doorway between worlds, in a cave under the Thran capital, Halcyon. At the very end, a Thran woman named Rebbec closed that portal and locked Yawgmoth inside Phyrexia. The lock was a large powerstone. It had been cracked in two to open the portal, and Rebbec joined the two halves again and set the stone in place in the cave to close it. As long as the stone stayed where it was, the door stayed shut.
Five thousand years later the stone was still there, and nobody alive knew what it was for.

The tale of the brothers was told at full length in a novel by Jeff Grubb in 1998, and again in a set of short stories by Wizards of the Coast in 2022. This story follows the summaries of the novel and those short stories.

Terisiare in the brothers' day had three kingdoms along its eastern and southern coasts: Argive, Korlis and Yotia. West of them rose a mountain range called the Kher Ridges, and beyond the mountains lay a great desert, the home of a nomad people called the Fallaji. The ruins of the Thran lay scattered under that desert.

Urza and Mishra were born to a noble family of Penregon, the capital of Argive. Urza was born on the first day of the year and Mishra on the last day of the same year. That year is the year 0 of the calendar this story uses. Urza was therefore the elder by almost exactly twelve months. Early tellings called the two of them twins, but the settled version has them a year apart.
Their mother died when they were small. Their father married again, and his new wife had no love for her stepsons. At her best she ignored them, and at her worst she showed them contempt.
In 10 AR, when the boys were ten years old, their father fell ill. He sent both of them away to an old friend who owed him a favour. Two years later he died, and the boys were orphans.

The friend was Tocasia, an archaeologist of Argive who was already an old woman. Tocasia ran a dig in the desert, where she searched the sand for the machines of the Thran. Her camp was worked by Fallaji diggers, and it also served as a kind of school. Noble families of Argive sent their children there for a season. Most of those children went home again. Urza and Mishra stayed, and Tocasia raised them.

Tocasia taught the brothers what was known of the Thran and the basics of artifice, which is the craft of building machines. Both boys turned out to be brilliant at it, and they could hardly have been less alike.

Urza was a scholar. He was cold, exact and withdrawn. He seldom went out to the trenches. He preferred to sit with an object that the diggers had brought in and study it until he understood how it worked.

Mishra liked people. He was warm, quick-tempered and impatient. He went out on almost every dig and in time came to run all the digging in the camp. He lived among the Fallaji workers, learned their language and their ways, and made friends among them. One of those friends was a young Fallaji named Hajar, about Mishra's own age, the assistant to the foreman of the diggers.

The Fallaji had a saying about what a person is made of: stone and fire, sky and water, and a whole person holds them in balance. They said that Mishra had too much fire. Of Urza they said that he had too much stone: cold and unbending, a man who would sooner shatter than give way.
The brothers quarrelled often. What held them together was that they were curious about the same thing.

In 16 AR, when the brothers were sixteen, they dug up the remains of a Thran flying machine. It had wings that flapped like those of a bird. Such a machine is called an ornithopter. The brothers set about repairing it, and a year later it flew, with the two of them aboard.
From the air Mishra saw something that could not be seen from the ground: Thran signs laid out across the face of the desert.

Urza, working at his desk, noticed something else. When he marked on a map all the places where large numbers of Thran machines had been found, the places formed a ring. Something lay in the middle of the ring.

In 20 AR Tocasia, Urza and Mishra flew the ornithopter to the middle of the ring. On the way a roc attacked them. A roc is a gigantic bird of prey. The three were forced to land in a hurry in front of the mouth of a cave, and they ran inside to escape the bird.

They had found what they were looking for. Around the cave stood a few crumbling buildings, and inside it ran a network of tunnels full of Thran machines. Urza named the place Koilos, which is an Argivian word meaning secret. None of the three knew that these ruins were all that was left of Halcyon, the capital of the Thran Empire, or that the caves beneath Halcyon had once been called the Caves of the Damned.
Deep in the tunnels they came to a great chamber, the Hall of Tagsin. In it stood a Thran machine, and set in the machine was a powerstone far larger than any they had ever seen.
It was the stone that Rebbec had set there to lock the door to Phyrexia.

Both brothers went for the stone. Each wanted to be the first to hold it. There was a blast of light and force that knocked all three of them senseless. When the brothers woke, each of them was holding half of the stone. It had come apart along the old crack.

With the stone removed and broken, the door it had been holding shut came open. The portal to Phyrexia stood open for a short time and then closed again by itself. Nobody came through. But from that moment the lock was gone.
The cave had guards. They were su-chi, Thran machines shaped roughly like people, which had stood dormant for five thousand years. They woke and attacked the intruders.

Urza held up his half of the stone to stop the su-chi. It had the opposite effect. The su-chi grew stronger and faster. Mishra then held up his half, and the su-chi faltered and slowed. That gave the three time to run.

The roc was still waiting outside the cave. A Thran war machine lay half broken near the entrance, a thing with legs like a spider. While Tocasia and Mishra sheltered behind a rock, Urza hurriedly brought the machine back to life and fired its weapon at the bird. The roc burst into flames, fell, and crashed down on the su-chi as they came out of the cave, smashing them. The three patched up the ornithopter and flew back to camp. The brothers argued all the way home about which of them ought to have both halves.
The two halves were not alike. Urza's half made things stronger. A machine near it ran with more force than it had been built for. Urza named it the Mightstone.
Mishra's half did the reverse. It drained strength from machines, and from living creatures too. Urza named that one as well. He called it the Weakstone. The name stuck.

An earlier chapter told why the halves behave like this. When the stone was first split, in Thran times, Yawgmoth hid both halves inside the body of the dying Thran inventor Glacian, and they soaked up something of Glacian's genius with machines.

The stones also worked on their owners. In the months after Koilos the brothers, who had always bickered, became openly hostile. Each of them wanted the other's half, and each of them was sure that the other meant to take his. Mishra began to have dark dreams, in which something in the darkness called to him and tried to draw him back to Koilos.

Tocasia saw what was happening and tried to stop it. She asked both brothers to hand the stones over to her, so that she could study the halves together without the two of them fighting over them. Neither brother would do it. Each believed that she would give both halves to the other one.
It ended on a single night. Mishra had been drinking. He went to Urza's quarters to confront him and tried to take the Mightstone by force.

The brothers fought, and the whole camp heard it. Then each brother turned his stone on the other. Tocasia ran in and stepped between them to make them stop. The sight of her broke the concentration of both brothers at once. The power pouring from the two stones went wild, and there was an explosion.
Tocasia was killed.
Mishra, horrified and ashamed, fled into the desert in the confusion, taking the Weakstone with him.

The camp fell apart. Tocasia had held it together, and she was gone. The Fallaji diggers would have followed Mishra, who had lived among them for ten years. They would not follow Urza, who had hardly spoken to them. They left. Urza was left alone with the Mightstone, and he went east.
The brothers were twenty years old. Their teacher was dead by their own hands, each blamed the other, and each still wanted the other's half of the stone. They did not meet again for six years.

chapters.title: The Prince and the Wizard
sources: MTG Wiki, "The Brothers' War (novel)" (the novel by Jeff Grubb, 1998)
Miguel Lopez, "The Brothers' War, Episode 3: Sword One" (Wizards of the Coast, October 2022)

blocks.p: The last chapter ended in 20 AR with the death of the archaeologist Tocasia. Her two pupils, the brothers Urza and Mishra, had found a great powerstone in the Thran ruin of Koilos and had split it between them. Urza held the Mightstone, which strengthens machines. Mishra held the Weakstone, which weakens them. The stone had been the lock on a portal to Phyrexia, the world of flesh joined to machine, and with the stone gone the portal could be opened again. The brothers fought, Tocasia died trying to part them, and the two went separate ways.

This chapter covers the next eight years. In that time each brother rose, almost by accident, to stand beside a throne: Urza in the kingdom of Yotia, Mishra among the desert Fallaji. Then the two peoples went to war, and the brothers' private quarrel became everyone's.

Urza went to Yotia, the southernmost of the three coastal kingdoms. Its capital was Kroog, a city of red brick and tall, airy spires, where even the paving of the streets was laid in patterns. Yotia was ruled by a soldier-king who was known simply as the Warlord of Kroog.
Urza, who had grown up a nobleman and been trained by the best scholar of the Thran alive, took a job as the apprentice of a clockmaker named Rusko.

Within a year the Warlord announced a contest. The Warlord had a daughter, Kayla bin-Kroog, who was said to be the most beautiful woman in that part of the world. The man to whom she had been promised had drowned at sea. Now the Warlord wanted a strong son-in-law. In a courtyard of the palace stood a gigantic statue of jade. Any man who could move it across the courtyard, the Warlord declared, would marry the princess.

Urza had no interest in the princess. He was interested in her dowry, the treasure that would come with her. Among the things in the royal vaults was an ancient book of Thran knowledge called the Jalum Tome, and it would go to her husband.

Every strong man who tried the statue failed. Urza did not try to lift it. He built a huge machine, and the machine moved the statue. The Warlord saw at once that a man who could build such things would be worth more to Yotia than any strongman, and he kept his word. In 21 AR Urza married Kayla and became a prince of Yotia.

It was not, at first, much of a marriage. On their wedding night Urza left his bride in order to read the Jalum Tome. He was given the post of Chief Artificer, with a workshop and assistants of his own, and he buried himself in the work.

The work made Yotia strong. Urza built ornithopters for the kingdom, a whole flying corps of them. He built mechanical soldiers. And he built the avengers, tall fighting machines shaped like armoured men, each directed by a human operator.

About 24 AR a young man from the coastal town of Jorilin came to Kroog to ask for a place in Urza's workshop. His name was Tawnos. He was tall, broad-shouldered and fair-haired, and he had been trained by an uncle who was a master toymaker.
Urza was notoriously hard to pull away from his bench. Tawnos managed it by showing him a toy he had made, a mechanical snake that moved like a living one. Urza took him on.

Tawnos was the opposite of his master in temper: warm, loyal and easy to like. As a maker he had one particular gift. He studied living animals and copied the way they were built, and a number of Urza's later designs began as ideas of Tawnos's. Tawnos also became a close friend of Princess Kayla. In the years ahead he was often the only link between Urza and Urza's own family.
Mishra's road was much harder.

He had fled into the desert with the Weakstone. The dark dreams that had troubled him since Koilos grew stronger, and they pulled him towards the caves. He never arrived. On the way he was captured by warriors of the Suwwardi.

The Fallaji were not one nation. They were a number of tribes, and whichever tribe had the strongest leader led the rest. The Suwwardi were a warlike tribe from the part of the desert nearest Yotia, and they were the rising tribe of that day. Their chief bore the title Qadir, which means the all-powerful. The Qadir of the time was a huge, thick-necked man with a violent temper.

The Suwwardi took the Weakstone from Mishra and gave it to the Qadir. They made Mishra a rakiq, which is their word for a slave. For months the son of an Argivian nobleman did the lowest work in the camp.

Then his friend Hajar found him. Hajar, the young digger from Tocasia's camp, had since joined the Suwwardi to become a warrior, and he came across Mishra by chance. Hajar went to the Qadir and persuaded him that this slave was an educated man who could be put to better use. The Qadir made Mishra tutor to his young son, to teach the boy the language of Argive. Mishra remained a slave, but his life improved.

The Qadir's son was a cold, indifferent child. Mishra won him over with the old stories of Argive, and the boy grew eager and bold. After a few years this began to worry the Qadir. The Fallaji held that to lean on another person was weakness, and the boy plainly leaned on his tutor. The Qadir decided that Mishra would be killed after the boy's first campaign of war, and he gave the order to Hajar.

The order was never carried out. About 23 AR, one night in the Qadir's camp, Mishra dreamed again. This time he dreamed of a world that was a mechanical parody of nature. He woke screaming, with claw marks on his arm.

At the same moment a monster burst up out of the sand. It was a machine in the shape of a dragon, enormous, made of metal and moving like a living beast. It was a dragon engine, a war machine of Phyrexia. The Fallaji had an old word for the great dragons of their legends, mak fawa, and that is what they called it.

The dragon engine rampaged through the camp and killed many people, the Qadir among them. In the chaos Mishra and Hajar ran to the Qadir's body and took back the Weakstone. Mishra hoped that the stone would weaken the machine enough to stop it. It did something far better. Through the Weakstone, Mishra found that he could command the dragon engine. It obeyed him like a trained animal.
The dead Qadir's son became the new Qadir. He was still a boy. He freed his tutor and raised him from rakiq, slave, to raki, which means wizard. The two words differ by one letter.

A boy chief would normally have lost the leadership of the tribes to some stronger man. This boy had Mishra, and Mishra had a mak fawa. Over the next few years the two of them visited each Fallaji tribe in turn, and each tribe submitted. One tribe, the Thaladin, laid an ambush for them in the desert. The dragon engine killed every one of the attackers, and the Thaladin submitted too. For the first time the Fallaji were truly united, under the Suwwardi and their boy Qadir.

Power did not improve the boy. As he grew up he became spoiled, then reckless and foul-tempered, and finally a tyrant who had people executed for annoying him. Mishra was the only person who could manage him, and even Mishra had to be careful.
The Fallaji advance reached Zegon, a city on the southern coast. There the dragon engine stopped. It would not go near the walls.

That night a woman slipped into Mishra's tent. She had hair as red as a campfire, which the Fallaji considered an evil omen, and she wore trousers and close-fitting armour like a man. Her name was Ashnod. She was the chief artificer of Zegon, though she was not born there, and she had come to bargain for the city. She showed Mishra the device that was holding his dragon back. It was a staff of her own making, which drained the strength of whatever it was turned on.

Mishra was impressed. He agreed to spare Zegon on terms: the city was to take down its gates, submit to the Qadir, and give up its artificer. About 24 AR Ashnod became Mishra's apprentice. In time she also became his lover.

Ashnod was as gifted as Tawnos, and she was his opposite in every other way. She was brilliant, proud and without pity. She regarded living bodies as raw material, and she was soon called Ashnod the Uncaring.
So by 24 AR each brother stood next to a ruler, and each had an apprentice. Neither knew what had become of the other.

The Fallaji and Yotia shared a border and an old grievance. Between them lay a stretch of land called the Sword Marches. Three generations earlier it had been called the Suwwardi Marches, until Yotia drove the Fallaji out of it. Now the Fallaji were united and wanted it back.

In 26 AR a peace summit was called at Korlinda, an armed camp in the neutral kingdom of Korlis. Yotia, Argive and Korlis sent delegations, and the Qadir was invited. The Warlord of Kroog came in person, and he brought his Chief Artificer. He had more than peace in mind. He and the clockmaker Rusko planned to show the desert tribes Yotia's squadron of ornithopters, as a warning.

The Fallaji arrived late, on the third day. With the young Qadir came his wizard and his wizard's apprentice. The Qadir also brought the dragon engine. It was at this summit that he first called his people an empire.
So Urza and Mishra met again, for the first time since the night Tocasia died. The meeting was awkward and tense. But by every account the brothers were, at first, glad to see each other.

They were given no time. The Warlord and the Qadir could not agree about the Sword Marches. The talk turned to insults and then to threats. The Warlord gave a signal, and the ornithopters flew over the dragon engine and dropped bombs on it.
The Qadir drew his sabre and ran the Warlord through the chest. The Warlord of Kroog died where he stood.

One of Urza's avengers seized the Qadir by the throat and began to choke him. Ashnod turned her staff on the machine, and its grip slackened. Urza raised the Mightstone to strengthen his avenger. In the same instant Mishra raised the Weakstone against it. The two opposite forces met inside the machine, and the avenger blew apart.
The Fallaji fled, Ashnod dragging the half-strangled Qadir, and were chased back across the Kher Ridges by ornithopters and soldiers.

Kayla bin-Kroog was now Queen of Yotia, and her husband ruled the kingdom at her side. Urza blamed himself for the death of his father-in-law. Kayla saw that he did. Out of that shared grief the cold marriage at last turned into a real one. In later years Kayla gave the day at Korlinda a name: the Dawn of Fire.
After Korlinda, Mishra wanted more dragon engines. One would not be enough against a kingdom with a flying corps. He knew, or his dreams had told him, where they came from.

Mishra and Ashnod went to Koilos. In the Hall of Tagsin they found the portal and went through it into Phyrexia. Mishra saw the world from his nightmares, and in it he saw dragon engines. With the Weakstone he took control of three of them.

He was seen. A demon of Phyrexia attacked the two intruders: a tall creature with black skin like a lizard's, bones jutting out of its body, and teeth like razors. Mishra and Ashnod got back through the portal with their dragon engines and closed it behind them.

The demon was not so easily shut out. In the far north of Terisiare stood a monastery of monks who worshipped machines. They believed that machines had souls and an afterlife. Their order was named after a figure called Gix. The demon reached into the dreams of these monks, as something had reached into Mishra's, and called them. In 26 AR the monks left their monastery and walked to Koilos. There they opened the portal from the Dominarian side, and the demon stepped through into the world. The sources give the year as 27 or 28 AR.
It looked into the monks' minds, saw the name they worshipped, and announced that it was Gix.

An earlier chapter told of a Gix among the Thran: a rebel leader in the caves under Halcyon, sick with the powerstone disease, whom Yawgmoth remade into a Phyrexian demon. The encyclopaedia treats the demon of Koilos as that same Gix, five thousand years old. He was now one of the highest servants of Yawgmoth.

Gix wanted the two halves of the stone, and he wanted Dominaria prepared for his master's return. He ordered his monks, the Brotherhood of Gix, to go out and work their way into the courts of both brothers.
In 28 AR Mishra proposed a second peace conference, and he offered to come to Kroog for it.

He came with his new strength behind him, and he did not come for peace. During the talks Mishra turned his attention to his brother's wife. He persuaded Queen Kayla to take the Mightstone from Urza and bring it to him, and by most accounts to share his bed. The sources do not all agree that she did so. They agree about what happened next. Urza found his wife and his brother together in her rooms, with his stone.

Urza took the Mightstone back. Mishra fled the city. Urza sent his ornithopters after the dragon engine that had brought Mishra to the talks, and they destroyed it. That act was a declaration of war, and the Brothers' War is counted from it.
Ashnod did not get away. She was left behind in Kroog as a prisoner, shut in the rooms she had been given as a guest. Tawnos was put in charge of her. He treated her well and asked her few questions.
Soon afterwards Queen Kayla was with child. Everyone around her insisted, then and always, that the child was Urza's. Nobody could be entirely sure.
Urza now wanted one thing: to find his brother. He went west and spent months scouting the desert for Mishra's camp.
That was what Mishra had planned for. With Urza far away in the sands, Yotia lay almost undefended.

Four months after the talks, on a red morning in 28 AR, the Fallaji army fell on Kroog. Soldiers came up from the river in boats. Above them came the dragon engines, and Mishra himself rode the greatest of them, a monster named Traxos.

Tawnos was in command of what machines the city had. He had five of the newest avengers, a design so new that they were still packed for transport, each armed with a sword longer than a man. The only people in Kroog trained to direct them were five student pilots and their instructor. Tawnos sent them out. He also sent an ornithopter pilot named Rendall flying east with the Jalum Tome, so that the book at least would be saved.

The five avengers fought well. They cut down many Fallaji soldiers. Against the dragon engines they could do nothing. Three of the pilots' company died, including the instructor. Two of the students, Sanwell and Rica, escaped the city. The lesson of the day was plain to everyone who survived it: Urza's avengers were no match for Mishra's dragons.

As the dragon engines began to tear the palace apart, Tawnos went to Ashnod's rooms and let her out. He gave her back the Staff of Zegon. In return he asked one thing: that she help him protect the queen, who was four months pregnant. Ashnod agreed.

The three of them were making their way out of the palace when they ran into a band of Fallaji warriors. The Qadir himself was leading them. He looked at the three and ordered all of them killed, Ashnod included. He said that she was a crutch for Mishra to lean on, and a woman besides.
Ashnod raised her staff. She knocked the Qadir's guards senseless. On the Qadir she used the staff's full strength, and drained the life out of him until he fell bleeding and dead.

Then Ashnod took Tawnos and Kayla through the burning city to the river and put them in a boat headed downstream to the sea. She herself turned back to rejoin Mishra. Tawnos had freed Ashnod, and Ashnod had saved Tawnos, though they stood on opposite sides of a war. Neither forgot it. Ashnod had a mocking name for him. She called him Duck, because he followed his master about like a duckling.
Kroog was destroyed in a single morning. The Yotians called Mishra the Butcher of Kroog from that day.

The Qadir was dead. The Fallaji followed strength, and the strongest man among them was the foreign wizard with the dragons. Mishra, who had come to the Suwwardi as a slave eight years before, was made Qadir of the Fallaji Empire.

Urza came back from the desert to find his city in ruins, his kingdom overrun and his wife gone. He was twenty-eight years old. The war that carries his name and his brother's had thirty-six years still to run.

blocks.p: In 28 AR the Brothers' War began in earnest. Mishra, the younger brother, led the desert Fallaji with his Phyrexian dragon engines. He destroyed Kroog, the capital of Yotia, in one morning, and was made Qadir, the supreme chief, of the Fallaji Empire. Urza, the elder brother, had been Yotia's prince and Chief Artificer, and he was away in the desert when his city fell. His pregnant wife, Queen Kayla, escaped down the river with Urza's apprentice Tawnos. Mishra's apprentice, the red-haired Ashnod, went back to Mishra. And a Phyrexian demon named Gix had come through the portal at Koilos and had sent his monks, the Brotherhood of Gix, to worm their way into both camps.
Each brother still carried his half of the stone: Urza the Mightstone, Mishra the Weakstone.

This chapter covers the next seventeen years. No single battle decides anything in them. The two brothers build larger and larger machines, feed a continent into their furnaces, and get no nearer to winning. Meanwhile, in a city far from the fighting, a handful of scholars discover something that neither brother believes in: magic.
Urza, Kayla and Tawnos retreated north to Argive, the brothers' homeland. Argive needed Urza more than it blamed him, and it gave him what he asked for.

In 29 AR Kayla gave birth to a son and named him Harbin. He was brought up as Urza's son. Urza did not see the child until Harbin was more than two years old, and in private Urza was never certain that the boy was his and not Mishra's. Harbin grew up longing for his father's good opinion. It was Tawnos, more than Urza, who helped Kayla raise him.

Urza set up his workshops in a tower in the foothills of the Kher Ridges and went to work. In 36 AR the kingdoms of Argive and Korlis joined into one state, the Combined Kingdoms, and Urza was named its Lord Protector, with every resource of the east at his command.
Mishra ruled from a fortress in the west, with a foundry built inside the trunk of an enormous fallen tree.

Both brothers needed the same things: metal for machines, fuel for forges and powerstones to make the machines move. To get them, both stripped the land. Ancient forests were cut for fuel. Hills were dug away for ore. Year by year, Terisiare turned into mines, stumps and factories.

Ashnod found a new source of soldiers. She worked out a process for turning a living person into a thing that was part flesh and part metal. The result was a kind of manufactured walking dead: it felt no fear, never broke and ran, and obeyed simple orders. She called such a creature a transmogrant. Her raw material was living people.

In 32 AR Mishra gave Ashnod an army to test her invention and sent her to conquer Korlis, which had sided with Urza. The Fallaji war captains hated serving under her. She was a foreigner and a woman, she had the red hair they thought unlucky, and her transmogrants disgusted them. Mishra also gave her two dragon engines that he had built in his own foundry. They were poor copies of the Phyrexian originals, slow and loud, and they had to be left behind in a mountain pass after an enemy ornithopter spotted them.

Before Ashnod's army was clear of the Kher Ridges, a Korlisian army ambushed it. That army fought with Urza's mechanical soldiers, and with a new machine that Tawnos had designed for exactly this enemy: the clay statue, a soldier of clay built to fight transmogrants.

The transmogrants could not deal with them. Ashnod signalled her cavalry to charge. The Fallaji captains pretended not to see the signal and left her to it. Her transmogrants were destroyed to the last one, and she went back to Mishra beaten.

Mishra sent her away again at once, to the kingdom of Sarinth, to win it over as an ally. He did it partly to get her out of reach of his own captains, who might have murdered her. Sarinth refused her. In 33 AR Ashnod laid siege to it, and the siege lasted ten years.

The two brothers treated the monks of Gix very differently. In Urza's lands the Brotherhood had to work in secret. In Mishra's they were welcomed openly. The monks understood machines. Before long the Brotherhood supplied most of the artificers of his empire, and Mishra's own efforts to find and train talented young builders withered.

About 36 AR the monks brought their master to Mishra's fortress. Gix's first plan was simple. He would kill both brothers and take their stones. He tried Mishra first, at night, while Mishra slept. When the demon reached for the Weakstone, the stone defended itself and the man who owned it. It burned Gix's hand and hurled him back.

So Gix made a slower plan. If the brothers could not be robbed, they could be corrupted. He would bring the stones over to Phyrexia by bringing their owners over, and Mishra's court proved far easier ground than Urza's. From then on the monks worked patiently on Mishra. They made themselves his council. They also worked to separate him from the two people who truly cared for him: his apprentice Ashnod and his old friend and bodyguard Hajar.
One small story of 35 AR belongs here. It takes place in Almaaz, a land that Mishra brought under his rule in that year, and it comes from a novel of 1996 called Song of Time.

Almaaz had its own kind of magic, worked by singing. Its practitioners were called song-mages. In the city of Sumifa their leader was a man named Samor, known as the Collector. His strongest pupil was Porros, the crown prince of Sumifa. Porros stood to inherit both the throne and the leadership of the song-mages. He was too impatient to wait for either.

Porros regarded Mishra as a false king. He summoned a monster against Mishra's armies: a gigantic cockatrice, a creature part bird and part serpent, called the Beast of the Hours. It tore through Mishra's troops. Mishra ordered the song-mages to destroy it.

Samor and his companions sang a spell of destruction against the Beast. In the middle of the song, one voice sang a false note on purpose. It was Porros. The spell was spoiled, and all Samor could do was change it into a spell of binding. The song-mages locked the Beast of the Hours inside a great clock beneath a mountain called Sarraza.

Mishra was delighted. A bound monster was better than a dead one. He ordered Samor to write a second spell that would release the Beast and put it under command, so that Mishra could threaten Urza with it. Samor obeyed unwillingly. That was the moment Porros had been waiting for. He went to his master to take the spell, and the Beast's power, for himself.

The two fought. Porros cut Samor's throat with a shard of broken mirror. As he died, Samor cursed him. Porros's handsome body drained away, and he became a wraith of blowing sand with the clawed feet of a bird of prey. In his fury Porros rose into the air and pulled a cyclone of sand down on his own city. The people of Sumifa, Porros's two sons among them, fled to caves. When Porros's rage was finally spent, he looked down and saw that the city he had been born to rule lay under the desert.
With Samor dead and Sumifa buried, nobody knew how to let the Beast of the Hours out. It stayed in its clock for three thousand years.

Far to the west of all the fighting stood Terisia City, the oldest and most learned city on the continent. It was famous for its white towers and for an order of scholars and librarians named after them, the Ivory Towers. The head of that order was a woman known by her title, the Archimandrite.

In 33 AR the Archimandrite sent out invitations. She proposed a union of everyone who wanted no part of either brother: scholars, historians and artificers from every land that was still free. Its purpose was to find some way to resist both brothers' machines, or at least to outlast them. The union called itself the Third Path: a way that was neither Urza's nor Mishra's.
Those who came included the following.

Feldon was a scholar from the foot of the Ronom Glacier in the far north. He was a big, bearded man with a lame leg who walked with a cane, and a friend thought he looked like a bear that had been mistaken for a human being. He studied old objects that the glacier's meltwater washed out, and he had taught himself several languages in order to read them.

Loran was an Argivian noblewoman and an archaeologist. She had been one of Tocasia's best pupils and had known Urza and Mishra as boys in the desert camp. She crossed a continent at war to reach Terisia City.

Drafna and Hurkyl were husband and wife, the founders of a school called the College of Lat-Nam on an island off the west coast. Drafna was a talkative, argumentative man with an astonishing gift for machines. He could work out what a whole device had been from a few scraps of it. Hurkyl was quiet and shy, and in the first three years Loran heard her speak about one full sentence a year.

There were also a leader of the Yumok people and a chieftain of the Sardian mountain folk. And there was an abbot of the Brotherhood of Gix. The Archimandrite invited the monks in good faith. Nobody in Terisia City knew whom they served.
The great discovery of the Third Path was made by the quietest of its members.

Every morning Hurkyl sat still and thought about her home, the island of Lat-Nam. She pictured it as exactly as she could: blue waves, white with foam, hanging over the shore before they fell. Afterwards odd things happened around her. The first that anyone noticed was that her rooms were clean and tidy when nobody had cleaned them. The scholars cautiously called these happenings incidents.

What Hurkyl had found was mana. The land itself holds energy. A person who holds a place in memory, clearly and with feeling, can draw on that energy and shape it with the will. That is what magic is, in this story, and the method has not changed since: a mage calls on the memory of lands. Hurkyl taught her meditation to a growing circle of pupils, the Archimandrite among them.

Magic was not new to Dominaria. Zhalfir practised it, and Almaaz had its song-mages. But on Terisiare, a continent that had put all its trust in machines, nobody had studied it with care before. The scholars of the Third Path did. They found that mana came in different kinds according to the land it was drawn from, and they began to work out spells. One let a person fly. One let a person shatter an object at a distance. Feldon learned to draw on the mountains of his northern home. Loran tried for years and never managed it. Drafna, for all his brilliance, had little talent for it, though because he did the talking, many of his wife's discoveries were later credited to him.
Refugees and thinkers from every land gathered in Terisia City. For about ten years it was the one hopeful place on the continent.
In those same years, fishermen of the Yumok people pulled a strange thing up in their nets and sent it to Feldon to study. The sources date this to 34 or 36 AR.

It was a bowl of a copper-coloured metal that nobody could identify, about thirty centimetres across, standing on a thick foot, something between a bowl and a wide, squat goblet. The inside was carved with lines of writing that spiralled down to the centre. The writing was in several languages at once, the Thran script among them. The inscription called the object a sylex and said that it came from Golgoth. Feldon could not tell whether Golgoth was a place or a person. The thing is known as the Golgothian Sylex.
When Feldon and Loran first laid their hands on it, a darkness came over them both, as if the sun had gone behind an eclipse, and they heard something like a child screaming far away.
Feldon translated what he could. The inscription spoke of an ending: of wiping the land clean. It said that the bowl was to be filled with memories. Feldon understood enough to be afraid of it.

In the east the war went on. In 38 AR a group of people from Korlis were killed in occupied Yotia. They are remembered as the Martyrs of Korlis, and their deaths forced the king of the Combined Kingdoms to order Urza to act.

Urza gathered a great army and in 39 AR led it west across the Kher Ridges, for the first time since Kroog fell. In four years of fighting the Combined Kingdoms won back almost the whole of Yotia. Only the Sword Marches, the old disputed borderland, stayed contested. Yotia was not restored as a kingdom. It was absorbed into the Combined Kingdoms.

In 43 AR, encouraged, Urza pushed on into the desert towards Tomakul, the city of golden domes that served as the Fallaji capital. That same year Sarinth finally fell to Ashnod after its ten years of siege, and its people were forced into Mishra's armies.

By this time the fighting looked nothing like the wars of the brothers' youth. The armies faced each other from trenches that ran for miles, some of them twenty years old, with bunkers and underground hospitals. Ornithopters dropped bombs on clear days. Ordinary foot soldiers on both sides hoped that the next attack would be carried out by machines, or even by Ashnod's dead things, so that they themselves would not have to go.

In the winter of 44 AR the Argivian army came within ten miles of Tomakul. Some accounts say it came within one mile. Then the fresh troops from conquered Sarinth arrived. The Combined Kingdoms were overwhelmed within sight of the city and driven back.
In that campaign Tawnos was captured. He was taken to Tomakul and thrown into a dungeon beneath the city. The dungeon belonged to Ashnod.

Ashnod tortured him. She was Mishra's chief interrogator, and it was her trade. And then she helped him to escape. The two had not met since the morning Kroog burned, sixteen years before, when each had saved the other.
The monks of Gix found out. It was the opening they had wanted for years. They went to Mishra and laid it before him: his apprentice had freed his brother's right hand. Mishra banished her.
Ashnod went west, alone, into the Colekgan Mountains. Mishra's council now consisted of the Brotherhood of Gix and nobody else. Hajar still stood at his side as his bodyguard.

Tawnos got home to the Combined Kingdoms. In the same year young Harbin, now fifteen, began training as an ornithopter pilot. He had built his first glider at the age of six. He had no gift for artifice, and he feared that his father thought the less of him for it.
Stalled in the east, Mishra looked west. He had heard that the scholars of Terisia City possessed secrets, and he wanted them.
He tried diplomacy first, and the city council refused him. In 44 AR he sent an army under Hajar to take the city by siege.

Terisia City held. Its walls were high, and its defenders had magical artillery that shot dragon engines out of the sky. The city held for months. During that time the unarmed population was moved out, a few at a time, and the scholars searched desperately for magic that could be used in war.
The city might never have fallen to force. It fell to treachery. In 45 AR the monks of the Brotherhood of Gix, who had been honoured members of the Third Path for twelve years, opened the gates.
Mishra's army poured in, with juggernauts and dragon engines.

At the gate stood Hurkyl. The shy woman who had hardly spoken for years sank into her meditation one last time. Then she cast a spell that nobody had seen before. Three dragon engines that were bearing down on the gate vanished. The sources describe the effect in different words: the machines were unsummoned, or they disappeared, or they were turned to vapour. The spell is named after her, Hurkyl's Recall. It was the first great act of magic recorded on Terisiare, and it showed what the new art could do against the brothers' machines.
A moment later Fallaji spearmen killed her.

Drafna, mad with grief, tried to strike back and was driven into one of the towers. He took charge of what defence was left and ordered that every artifact in the city be gathered and carried out through the tunnels that ran under the towers.

Feldon did not want the sylex in that collection. He thought it too dangerous for Drafna's hands, or for anyone's. He gave the bowl to Loran. She was quick on her feet and he, with his bad leg, was slow, so they would go by different roads. They agreed to meet in a town called Ketha at the foot of the Ronom Glacier.

A fierce sandstorm blew up over the city and hid everything. Some said that the Archimandrite had raised it. Under its cover many people escaped through the tunnels. What became of the Archimandrite herself is not known.
Hajar's army pulled down every one of the ivory towers and burned the rest of the city to ashes.

Drafna survived. He went back to the College of Lat-Nam. Some years later, between 46 and 54 AR, the college was destroyed as well, most likely on Mishra's orders. Drafna lived through that too. With other survivors of the Third Path he founded a school whose first rule was to stay hidden. It was called the City of Shadows, and it lasted for thousands of years.

Loran got out of the city with the sylex and travelled north with a band of fleeing Yumok. In the Colekgan Mountains an avalanche of snow and rock came down on them. It crushed the right side of Loran's body.
The avalanche was no accident. Ashnod had set it off. The banished artificer was living in those mountains, and she took both the bowl and the woman.

Ashnod kept Loran prisoner for years and tortured her, as she had tortured Tawnos. From Loran she forced everything the Third Path had learned: what mana was, how the memory of land called it up, and what the sylex was for. Ashnod learned that the bowl was not a machine. It was set off by mana.

Loran eventually got free. The sources differ on how and when. One says she escaped in 57 AR, another that Feldon found her and rescued her, another that Ashnod let her go because she had nothing more to tell. Loran reached the Ronom Glacier in the end. She and Feldon were married and lived in a small house below the ice. Loran never recovered the use of one arm.

Ashnod kept the sylex. She told nobody that she had it, and above all she did not tell Mishra. The monks of Gix wanted it badly. To put them off the scent she made a copy by ordinary coppersmith's work and let them believe that it was the real one. A rumour went round that she had made the copy from the skull of the Qadir she killed at Kroog.

So by 45 AR the pieces were laid out for the end. Mishra was surrounded by the servants of a Phyrexian demon and had driven away the one person who might have warned him. Urza had an army, a tower full of machines and a son he hardly knew. Terisiare was stripped nearly bare. And a bowl that could end the world sat in the baggage of a woman who had served one brother and saved the other brother's apprentice.
