blocks.p: By 45 AR the war between the brothers Urza and Mishra had lasted seventeen years and had settled nothing. Urza, the elder, was Lord Protector of the Combined Kingdoms in the east of the continent of Terisiare. Mishra, the younger, was Qadir of the Fallaji Empire in the west. Each still carried half of the powerstone they had split as young men: Urza the Mightstone, Mishra the Weakstone. Between them they had cut down and dug up most of the continent to feed their war machines.

Three other things were in place. A Phyrexian demon named Gix was loose on Dominaria, and his monks, the Brotherhood of Gix, had become Mishra's only advisers. Mishra's former apprentice Ashnod, banished and alone, was hiding a mysterious bowl called the Golgothian Sylex, together with what she had learned about how to use it. And the scholars of the Third Path had discovered that a person can draw power, called mana, out of the memory of a land.
This chapter tells how the war ended. It ended on an island that neither brother had heard of when the war began.
For ten more years the war ground on. Both sides were running out of everything.

In 55 AR Urza's son Harbin was twenty-six years old and a pilot of ornithopters, the flapping-winged flying machines of his father's armies. He was married to a woman named Melana, who lived at the court in Penregon. Out over the sea to the south-east of Terisiare, Harbin was caught in a storm and forced down on a coast that was on no map.

He had landed on Argoth. Argoth was a very large island covered from shore to shore in forest. Nobody had ever cut it. It was rich in timber, in ore and in everything else that the mainland had used up.

Argoth was inhabited, and it was defended. Elves lived in the branches of its trees. In the middle of the island stood a settlement called Citanul, the home of an order of druids. These druids were human, and they had a remarkable ancestry: they were descended from Thran who had escaped the destruction of their empire five thousand years earlier and had sworn off machines for ever. The forest itself was aware. It could feel intruders and warn the creatures that lived in it.

The ruler of Argoth was Titania. She was not a human or an elf. She was the living spirit of the forest of Argoth, a being of the same kind as the guardian spirits met earlier in this story, and many of her people regarded her as a goddess.
Among the elves was a scout and druid named Gwenna, who came upon Harbin after his landing and helped him.
Harbin flew home and reported what he had found. For the Combined Kingdoms it was the answer to every shortage. Urza began to prepare an expedition.
Gix learned of the island through his spies, and he saw his chance. He passed the news to Mishra. The demon wanted the brothers in the same place at last, with all their strength, face to face.
About 55 AR Mishra fell ill. He was fifty-five years old. A disease of the lungs left him coughing constantly and bringing up slime.

The monks of Gix had a remedy to offer. The Brotherhood honoured machines above flesh. Its members cut off their own limbs and took out their own organs and put mechanical ones in their place, and they counted each such replacement as an honour. They explained their practices to Mishra, and he listened closely. He sent even Hajar out of the room so that he could talk with the priests alone.

Some time after that, Mishra was handed over to Gix, and the demon remade him. Phyrexians call this being compleated: the flesh of a person is cut away piece by piece and replaced with machinery until the person belongs to Phyrexia. Nobody knows exactly when it was done to Mishra. Ashnod's last words on the subject suggest that it had happened before he ever set foot on Argoth.
From the outside he still looked like a man. Under his skin he was something else.

In 57 AR both brothers invaded Argoth, separately, with everything they had. Harbin and Tawnos led the landing for the Combined Kingdoms. Mishra came with Hajar at his side and the Brotherhood behind him.
Neither brother had come for the island itself. They had come for what it was made of, and they began at once to cut and dig. Titania tried to bargain with each brother in turn. Neither would leave.

So Argoth fought. Elves, druids, the creatures of the forest and the forest itself attacked both armies at once and without pause. They could not stop the machines. For six years the two armies fought each other and the island together, and tore the forest down as they went. As the trees fell, Titania herself weakened, because she was the forest.

Ashnod came to Argoth too. She had learned that Mishra was going there, and she hoped that the secrets of magic she had forced out of the scholar Loran would buy his forgiveness. When she saw his camp, she understood that there was nobody left to forgive her. Hajar, who had stood at Mishra's shoulder for more than thirty years, had been pushed aside. Mishra now listened only to the monks. Ashnod did one decent thing before the end: she arranged for Hajar, and for the elf Gwenna, to board a ship for the mainland. Neither of them was on Argoth when it died.
About 63 AR Harbin's wife gave birth to a son, who was named Jarsyl.

Offshore, meanwhile, a ship lay at anchor. Its captain was a Yotian sailor named Crucias, who had built the ship in memory of a daughter who had died young, and who was by now so short of money that he had sold passage on it to rich nobles of Argive. He called the voyage an expedition to the end of the world. His passengers had paid to watch the last battle of the war from the water, as entertainment. Crucias hated them and hated himself for taking their money.
The final battle began in 63 AR. The sources place its end, and the explosion that ended it, in 63 or 64 AR.
Both brothers put everything into it. Every machine that had survived thirty-five years of war was on that island. The greatest of them was the Colossus of Sardia, a walking giant of metal.

Titania made her last stand. She gave herself up wholly to Gaea. Gaea is the name that the peoples of Dominaria give to the living soul of their world's nature, and they worship her as a goddess. Titania became Gaea's champion and her body on the battlefield. She fought the Colossus of Sardia, and the two destroyed each other.

Then Gix played his hand. The demon had power over metal, a Phyrexian corruption that he could send through any machine. He sent it through all of them. Every artifact creature in both armies went mad at the same moment and attacked whatever was nearest, friend or enemy or its own makers. The battle dissolved into slaughter without sides.
In the middle of that chaos Ashnod found Tawnos.
She had the sylex with her. She put it into his hands and told him what she knew. He was to carry it to Urza, whatever it cost. And Urza was to fill the bowl with his memories of the land.

Gix came upon them as they spoke. The demon had wanted the sylex for years. Ashnod turned and fought him, to hold him long enough for Tawnos to get away. Gix struck her down. In the novel of 1998 she dies there. The later stories say that she was badly wounded and somehow escaped with her life, and they show her alive years afterwards. This story follows the later version.
Tawnos ran.

Urza and Mishra had found each other at last. They met on a hillside, each at the head of what remained of his army, each with his stone. It was thirty-five years since the night at Kroog when Urza had found his brother with his wife, and forty-three years since their teacher Tocasia had died between them.

Mishra mocked his brother for having grown old. Urza was sixty-three, white-haired and worn. And as Mishra jeered, Urza noticed what he ought to have noticed long before. Mishra, who was younger by less than a year, did not look old at all. Mishra had not aged in years.

They fought, stone against stone. Mishra was wounded, and the wound showed what was under his skin. Where there should have been flesh and bone there was metal: rods and gears and wire, a machine wearing a man's face.

Urza understood then, in one moment, what had been done. His brother had been taken from him years ago, by something that had been at work behind the whole war. The enemy he had spent his life fighting was a puppet. Urza had never suspected that Gix existed.

Mishra cast off the last of his disguise. He joined his body to a dragon engine, so that the man and the machine became one creature: a serpent of metal with a screaming dragon's head, and Mishra's face, half torn away from the steel skull beneath, set in it.
A rockslide carried the thing down the hill and buried it for a moment. Then it dug itself out and began to climb again.
In that pause Tawnos reached Urza and gave him the sylex and Ashnod's message.

Something else had happened to Urza during the fight. In the rage and grief of it, a thing inside him that had slept for sixty-three years had begun to wake. Urza had been born with a planeswalker's spark. As it stirred, he felt what a mage feels and what he, the man of machines, had always refused to believe in. He felt the land. He felt the whole of Terisiare, stripped and mined and burned by himself and his brother, and he heard it crying out.

Urza ordered Tawnos to get to safety. Tawnos had brought a device of his own making to Argoth: a metal box about two metres long, built to hold a person in suspended sleep. He had made it so that Mishra might be captured and held instead of killed. Now Tawnos shut himself inside it.

Urza sat down cross-legged on the hilltop with the bowl in his lap. Mishra had cut him across the forehead, and the blood ran down and dripped into the bowl and filled the carved writing. He did not need to read the writing. He did what the scholar Hurkyl had taught the Third Path to do, the thing he had once dismissed as a fable. He made himself a channel for the memory of the land. He poured into the sylex all the places he had fought for and ruined, and all his grief, his love and his hatred with them. He was weeping, and Urza was not a man who wept.
The thing that had been Mishra reached the top of the hill. Its dragon head reared over him. What was left of Mishra's face was grinning in triumph, and he was shouting something.
A light began at the bottom of the bowl.

One strange thing must be mentioned here, though it belongs to a much later part of the story. According to the short stories of 2022, Urza was not alone in that instant. More than four thousand years in the future, a mage named Teferi, a master of the magic of time, sent his spirit back to this hilltop to learn how the sylex was set off, because his own age needed to use one. Teferi stopped the moment and spoke with Urza inside it, in an empty white place outside time, while Urza's body burned away and was woven together again out of light.

Teferi learned that there was no secret. There was no hidden spell and no mechanism. The sylex was set off by a person: one human being with nothing left, pouring a whole land's pain through himself. Urza would not remember the conversation. Why Teferi needed to know is told when the story reaches his time.
Then the light came out of the bowl, and Argoth ceased to exist.

The explosion is called the Sylex Blast. It turned almost the whole island to vapour in an instant. Both armies died where they stood: every soldier, every machine, nearly the whole fighting strength of the Fallaji people. Titania's forest and nearly everything that lived in it were gone. The plate of rock beneath the island broke apart. Where Argoth had been, only a few pillars of black stone were left standing in the sea. They are called the Shattered Isles.

A shock wave crossed the whole of Terisiare. It was felt at the Ronom Glacier in the far north, where the scholars Feldon and Loran, now married, understood what it meant. The war was over. Loran's only comment was that this was good.

The sea drew back from the coasts and then returned in waves the size of hills. The elf Gwenna was on the mainland, leading a raid on Urza's shipyards in Korlis. She felt the ground shake and heard Gaea cry out as her home died. Then she saw that the sea had gone, leaving bare mud, and she knew what that meant. She screamed at her warriors to run for the hills, and she was halfway up the nearest one when the first wave struck the shore.

In Penregon, the capital of Argive, earthquakes threw down most of the city's stone buildings on top of the people inside them. The king and his court had taken shelter in the Lion's Hall, a citadel on the cliffs above the harbour. The cliff gave way, and the hall fell into the sea with all of them. Then the waves came and scoured the lower city clean.
Far away, the forest of Urborg, which the panther warriors of Windgrace had ruled in peace for three centuries, was drowned and became a swamp.

Harbin was at sea, on a ship that had left Argoth for the mainland some time before. A mountain of water lifted the ship, and from the top of it Harbin saw, to the south, a red column of fire where the island had been. Then the ship came down. Harbin never reached Penregon, and his mother believed him dead.

Captain Crucias and his paying audience were less than a mile off the coast of Argoth. The blast killed every passenger but one and left Crucias blind. He did not die. Crucias, like Urza, carried a spark. He later became a planeswalker, and he returns to the story much later under the name Bo Levar.

Gix ran. The demon fled across the continent to Koilos and threw himself through the portal to Phyrexia barely ahead of the shock wave, taking a few human followers with him. His plan had failed. He had lost Mishra, he had failed to get either stone, and Dominaria was not ready for his master.
Urza and Mishra were both at the centre of the blast, and both bodies were destroyed.
Mishra was gone. Much later in the story there is a hint that something of him may have survived in Phyrexia, but it is no more than a hint.

Urza did not stay dead. His spark caught fire in the instant of his death. The two halves of the stone, the Mightstone and the Weakstone, which had been parted for forty-four years, came together in him. His body was woven again out of light, and the two stones became his eyes, one glowing red and one green. He was a planeswalker.

To be a planeswalker in that age was something very great. Such a being did not grow old, could take any shape, could cross from world to world at will, and commanded magic on a scale that ordinary mages could not approach. People called them gods, with some reason. Urza, the man who had not believed in magic, had become one of the most powerful beings in the Multiverse.

The blast did one thing more, which nobody understood for a long time. It tore the fabric of the Multiverse around Dominaria. In the years that followed, a kind of shell formed around Dominaria and eleven neighbouring planes and sealed those twelve worlds off from all the rest. It is called the Shard of the Twelve Worlds. Nothing could cross it in either direction. That included Phyrexia. For about three thousand years the Shard kept Yawgmoth's servants out of Dominaria, which no army could have done. It was the one mercy in the whole catastrophe, and it was an accident.

In 69 AR, five years after the blast, a metal box lay among the wreckage on a dead stretch of coast, in a tangle of uprooted trees and boulders that the waves had flung miles inland. It was Tawnos's stasis coffin. It had come through the end of Argoth unbroken, with Tawnos asleep inside it.
Urza appeared beside it, laid his hand on the lid, and let his apprentice out.

Urza told Tawnos what he now understood. Mishra was dead. But the brother he had loved and hated had not died on Argoth. The demon from Phyrexia had killed that man years before, and what Urza had fought on the hill was only what the demon had left.

Tawnos asked Urza to stay and help to rebuild what the two brothers had broken. Urza would not. He meant to leave Terisiare, and Dominaria itself, for a time. He asked one thing of Tawnos: to go to Kayla, and to tell her to remember her husband not as he was but as he had tried to be.
Then Urza was gone. Tawnos turned inland alone. He was an old man now, and it began to snow, on a coast where it had never snowed before.

The Brothers' War lasted thirty-six years by the usual count, from the fall of Kroog to the Sylex Blast. Its results governed the next four thousand years of the story, and they are worth setting out plainly.
The peoples of Terisiare were ruined. The Fallaji were almost wiped out, and their empire vanished. The kingdoms of the east did not survive the next few years.
The climate of the world was broken. The cold that Tawnos walked into did not lift. It deepened for centuries, into a Dark Age and then an Ice Age.
The people who lived through it blamed machines, and the men who built them, for everything. A hatred of artifice and of magic alike spread across the continent, and that hatred shapes the next age.
Dominaria was sealed inside the Shard, cut off from Phyrexia and from everywhere else.

And Urza, with the two stones for eyes, had learned what had really taken his brother. From this day until his own death, more than four thousand years later, he had a single purpose: the destruction of Phyrexia.

Kayla bin-Kroog outlived the war. Around 80 AR she finished a long poem about it, called The Antiquities War, and it is one of the few accounts of those years written by someone who was there. Her verdict on her husband and his brother was that they had burned the world down because neither of them was able to talk to the other.

blocks.p: The Brothers' War ended in 64 AR with a single explosion. Urza set off an ancient bowl called the Golgothian Sylex on the island of Argoth. The blast destroyed the island, both armies and Urza's brother Mishra, and it sent earthquakes and giant waves across the whole continent of Terisiare. Urza himself came out of it changed into a planeswalker, a being who can walk between worlds, and he left Dominaria.

The age that follows is called the Dark Age, or simply the Dark. It lasts from 64 AR to about 450 AR. It has that name for two reasons. The world grew steadily colder and poorer. And the knowledge of magic, which had only just been discovered on Terisiare, was very nearly stamped out.

This chapter covers the first sixteen years, and it follows the people the war left behind: Urza's wife Kayla, his apprentice Tawnos, Mishra's apprentice Ashnod, and the two scholars Feldon and Loran. Most of it comes from two short stories that Wizards of the Coast published in 2022.
Everyone on Terisiare saw or felt the blast, and everyone believed that the world had ended that day. Then they woke up the next morning, and life went on. It simply never got better again.

Spring still came, but it came later each year. Summers shrank from warm months to warm weeks. Harvests were smaller every autumn than the autumn before. Snow began to fall in places where it had never fallen. To the south-east, where Argoth had been, the sky at night did not quite go dark.

The kingdoms did not survive. Argive, Korlis and Yotia in the east fell apart within a few years, and so did the peoples of the north. Inland Terisiare came under warlords. Soldiers of both sides wandered home from the fronts in rags and begged for bread.

Scattered across the land lay the wrecks of the war's great machines. The worst of them sat in pools of black, oily water, grown over with a slimy growth that dripped and never froze. No bird nested in them and no animal drank near them, and scouts learned to mark a wide circle around each one.

Penregon, the capital of Argive, had been half destroyed. The earthquakes had thrown down most of its stone buildings. The king and his whole court had died when the citadel they were sheltering in fell from its cliff into the sea. The waves had finished what the earthquakes began.

When the water went down, one of the few nobles left alive in the city was Kayla bin-Kroog. She was a princess of Yotia by birth and the wife of the Lord Protector, and the rule of the city passed to her. She had lost her father at the peace summit of Korlinda, her home city of Kroog to Mishra's dragon engines, and her son Harbin, as she believed, to the blast. She had her small grandson Jarsyl, Harbin's son, to bring up. People called her the Lady of Penregon, and she is counted as the last Queen of Argive.
Kayla held the city together for fifteen years. Its gates were open to anyone on three conditions: give up your weapons, look after yourself, and work for the good of the city.

In the winter of 69 AR a visitor was shown into Kayla's council chamber. Kayla had thought him dead. It was Tawnos, Urza's apprentice and once her own close friend. He had slept through five years in his stasis coffin on a ruined beach until Urza let him out. He had walked to Penregon through the snow, and he arrived frostbitten, crooked and white-haired, looking very like his old master.

It was a hard meeting. Tawnos told Kayla that Urza had stopped a demon from taking the world, and that Mishra had been fused with a machine by that demon. Kayla wanted to know only about her son. It was Tawnos who had once persuaded her to let Harbin go to the war, and she told him that she would never forgive him for it.

Then Tawnos gave her Urza's message: that she should remember her husband not as he was but as he had tried to be. Kayla laughed at that. Urza and his brother, she said, had only ever tried to be princes of the world, and had burned it down because neither could speak to the other. She would remember Urza as he was.
Tawnos then had to tell her the rest. Urza was not dead. He had become something else, and Tawnos could not say whether it was a better man.

Tawnos had brought plans with him, Urza's designs and his own, and he knew where Argive's buried stores of powerstones lay. He offered to build machines again: no weapons, only tools to dig, to haul and to keep the city lit and warm. Kayla distrusted the offer, and she accepted it, because her city was dying. Tawnos set up a factory. Its machines were called civils. They cleared snow, hauled stone and rebuilt the city wall. Chips of broken powerstone were set in the street lamps, so that Penregon stayed lit through the worst winter storms.

That spring Kayla's scouts reported a vast column of people coming up from the south. The scout captain estimated ten thousand. When Kayla saw it for herself she thought it more like a hundred thousand. It was neither an army nor a migration but something of both: old people, children, men in scavenged armour from every side of the war. They flew plain black banners and carried pieces of dead machines as trophies. Among the trophies were Ashnod's transmogrants, the half-flesh soldiers of the war, carried in cages or bound in wire.
They called themselves pilgrims and penitents, and they belonged to a new religion.

Tal had been a minor sun god of old Yotia, with no temples or monuments of his own. After the blast, people turned to religion to make sense of what had happened, and two Yotian sun cults merged into one. That is why the symbol of the Church of Tal is two suns side by side, though the Church later wiped out the memory of how it began. Its teaching was simple. Machines were demons. Those who built them, and those who worked magic, had destroyed the world and would do so again if they were allowed to. Its holy book, the Book of Tal, put the conclusion in one line: a magician must not be suffered to live.

The leader of the march was Raddic of Kroog, a scarred veteran. He had been a Yotian, like Kayla. He had been conscripted for the campaign against Tomakul and had spent the rest of the war in a Fallaji labour camp. The Talites, as the followers of Tal are called, had begun their crusade in the far north by destroying the monastery of the Brotherhood of Gix. They had marched south through the desert to the ruins of Kroog and then east through Korlis. Their goal now was Urza's tower in the mountains, which they meant to pull down.

Raddic asked Kayla to join them, or at least to show them the way to the tower. Kayla felt the pull of it. She hated the machines as much as he did. But she had a city to keep alive. She offered trade and shelter for the unarmed, and the Talites appeared to accept.

The peace lasted one day. A group of Talites in the marketplace attacked one of Tawnos's civils and called it a demon. The civil had no weapons and did not fight back. The city guards did. Two pilgrims were killed.

Raddic returned to the gate at sunset. Kayla then learned what she had not known. Talite believers had been living quietly inside Penregon for years. They had watched her welcome Urza's own apprentice and set him to building machines. Raddic gave the city until dawn to drive its machine demons into the sea.

Kayla had fled one city in her life and had never gone back to it. She decided that she would not flee another. She asked Tawnos to arm the civils. Tawnos did not want to. Kayla told him that she was not Urza, and that she was asking only for the defence of the city. He agreed.

The Siege of Penregon lasted a single day in the spring of 69 AR. The civils had been built from the designs of war machines and only later turned to peaceful work. Armed and armoured again, they proved very effective. They threw back the assault on the walls, and they put down the Talites who rose inside the city at the same moment. Penregon held. The beaten march moved on towards Urza's tower.

For Tawnos it was the end. Everything he knew he had learned from Urza, and Urza had only ever designed machines for killing. Tawnos had told himself that his civils were different, and within months they were weapons. During the siege he tore a few pages out of his own old notebook, the designs of his youth: a mechanical snake, a bird, a mouse. Then he set fire to his office, and with it the only library of the brothers' knowledge left in the world.
In the morning nothing remained but ash and a few glowing chips of powerstone. Tawnos was gone, and Kayla believed that he had died in the fire. The age of artifice in Penregon was over.

The Talites went on to Urza's tower and destroyed every machine in it, though they left the tower itself standing. Then they marched against Mishra's old fortress and destroyed the machines there too. That fight cost them many lives. Raddic was among the dead.

Far to the north, below the Ronom Glacier, the scholars Feldon and Loran lived out the first years of the Dark in a small house. They had both been founders of the Third Path, the union of scholars that discovered magic, and it was they who had kept the sylex hidden for a time.

A few years after the blast a stranger visited Loran: a grieving widow, as it seemed. It was Urza in disguise. A planeswalker of that age could take any shape. Urza wanted to know where the sylex had come from, and he read the answer in Loran's mind. Loran never learned who her guest had been.
In 73 AR Loran died. She was old. She had never recovered from what Ashnod had done to her, and the lengthening winters wore her down. She died in her sleep with Feldon sitting asleep beside her.
Feldon could not accept it. First he built a mechanical copy of his wife. When he saw that the thing was not Loran, he took out its powerstone and stood it beside her grave as a statue.

Then he turned to magic. Feldon himself could draw only on the mana of mountains, which is the magic of fire and force. He set out to find mages of other kinds. A mad hermit in the ruins of Sarinth knew the magic of growing things, but it worked only on the living. A sorceress by Ronom Lake could make an image of Loran out of illusion, and nothing more. A mage in the swamps promised a true spell of return in exchange for Feldon's walking cane. Feldon paid, learned the spell and cast it, and understood too late that it had raised her as a walking corpse. He undid the spell before he could set eyes on the result. By then the swamp mage had vanished with the cane.

The last mage Feldon found was a scholar of the magic of order and healing. That man told him the truth. Magic can summon a likeness of a person, made from memory. It cannot bring a person back. Feldon used what the scholar taught him. He called up Loran one last time out of his own memories, said goodbye to her, and let her go.

Feldon's search is worth remembering for another reason. It is the first clear picture in the story of the five kinds of magic that every later mage on Dominaria uses, each drawn from one kind of land: mountain, forest, water, swamp and open plain.

A tiny story from about 70 AR shows the same thing from below. On the Terisian Isles a young woman named Annise, who worked for a man called Dumoss, broke with her lover, a gambler. He stole her magical pendant and used it to challenge Dumoss to a duel of magic. Annise appeared at the duel and distracted him, and he lost. The tale is a small one, but it shows magical objects and duels in ordinary hands only a few years after the blast.

About 75 AR a school was founded in the far north of Terisiare, near Ronom Lake. Its founders built it on the ruins of the monastery of Gix, which the Talites had emptied. It taught both artifice and magic, and it took in anyone the Church of Tal was hunting. It came to be called the Conclave of Mages.
Its two founders went by the names Nod and Duck.

Duck was Tawnos, who had not died in the fire. Nod was Ashnod. The woman once called Ashnod the Uncaring had survived the blast on Argoth, by means that nobody has explained, and had changed her name, her appearance and her manner. Urza himself searched Terisiare for her after the war, wanting to ask her about the sylex and about Gix. He was looking for a woman too proud to change, and he never found her. Duck had been her mocking name for Tawnos since the day Kroog burned.

So the two apprentices of the two brothers ended the war as partners, teaching in secret the art that their masters had refused to believe in. The scattered mages of the Third Path found their way to the Conclave over the years. Far to the west, a second hidden school, the City of Shadows, had been founded by Drafna, another survivor of the Third Path. Between them those two schools kept magic alive on Terisiare through the Dark.
Penregon lasted ten years after the siege. No enemy took it. The cold did.

First came a summer in which the cicadas of the city's gardens did not sing. A few winters later the harbour froze solid for the first time and trapped the fishing fleet in the ice. Storms began to bury the city in snow for a week at a time. Kayla's scouts reported that glaciers were breaking through the mountains to the north and growing every year.

The same scouts brought better news. Far to the west, past the southern end of the Kher Ridges, the grass still grew, and descendants of old Yotia had built new towns there. Kayla saw to it that everyone who wanted to go was given supplies and guards. Year after year the wagon trains left, and the city emptied.

In those years Kayla found that she could do magic. It came to her alone, one winter night in her shuttered house, in the worst of her grief and rage: a rush of heat through her body and a burst of sparks and fire from her hands. She laughed for the first time in years. Afterwards she had the city's libraries searched and found that refugees from Terisia City had brought books with them, among them the meditation of the scholar Hurkyl. Kayla practised in secret every night, using a stone from Kroog to fix her mind on her lost home. Learning to govern the fire and learning to govern her grief turned out to be the same work.

During one bitter blizzard the Talites came back, what was left of them after years of campaigning. Kayla opened the gates and let them look. There were no machines in Penregon any more. She told their new leader that the civils had one day simply walked away from the city across the ice. The Talites were satisfied, and they trudged off westward into the snow.

Kayla was among the last to leave, early in 79 AR. A few rich nobles and stubborn citizens refused to go, and stayed with their gold until the ice took them. That autumn Penregon was abandoned to the glaciers. It was the first city of Terisiare to be lost to the ice, and it was far from the last.

The last caravan crossed the Kher Ridges by the lowest pass and still lost a quarter of its people to the cold. It followed the river Mardun west, past the mossy wrecks of war machines, until it reached New Yotia, a wooden town on a height above the river. Most of Kayla's people settled there. The Church of Tal was already strong in the town.

Kayla stayed one winter. She had heard a story on the road. In the far west, people said, there was a flying man, the last of them, who had died in the great blast and been reborn as the herald of the wind. They called him a hero. Kayla thought of her son Harbin, the ornithopter pilot whose body had never been found. She no longer allowed herself wild hope. But she decided to cross the continent and learn the truth.

In 80 AR, on the evening before she left, her grandson Jarsyl came to her. He was a grown man now, and he looked very like his father. He too had found that he could do magic. He had heard of a school in the north where two teachers called Nod and Duck taught magic and artifice together, and he wanted to go. Kayla, who had always wondered whether Tawnos had really died in that fire, recognised the nickname. She told Jarsyl to go and to find teachers better than she was.

The next morning Kayla took a riverboat west, towards the drowned ruins of Kroog and the desert beyond. On the boat she worked at the last pages of a long poem: a history of the two men who had killed the world, written so that they would never be forgotten, or forgiven. It is called The Antiquities War. The sources do not say whether she found her son.
Jarsyl went north and became one of the first pupils of the Conclave of Mages. He lived an extraordinarily long time, and he and his descendants return in a later chapter of this age.

chapters.title: The Newt and the Planeswalker
sources: MTG Wiki, "Planeswalker (novel)" (the novel by Lynn Abbey, 1998)
MTG Wiki, "Shard of the Twelve Worlds"

blocks.p: The last chapter followed the people Urza left behind on Dominaria after the Brothers' War. This chapter follows the other side. It takes place mostly in Phyrexia, the artificial world of flesh joined to machine, which is ruled by the ancient Thran healer Yawgmoth. And it tells where Urza went.

Two things should be kept in mind. First, the demon Gix, one of Yawgmoth's chief servants, had spent the war on Dominaria corrupting Urza's brother Mishra. Gix fled back to Phyrexia through the portal at Koilos just ahead of the blast. Second, Urza came out of the blast as a planeswalker, with the two halves of the powerstone for eyes and one purpose: to destroy the world that had taken his brother.
The source is a novel of 1998, Planeswalker by Lynn Abbey, as the encyclopaedia summarises it.

Gix had failed to prepare Dominaria by corrupting its rulers. Phyrexia now tried a quieter way. It would grow spies that looked like human beings and plant them among the people of Dominaria. They would live there unnoticed, watch, and report, until the day of the invasion. Such a spy is called a sleeper agent.

The spies were grown in vats of flesh in a place called the Fane of Flesh, on the fourth of the nine layers, or spheres, of which Phyrexia is built. The Phyrexians called these creatures newts. About a thousand were made in the first batch, in groups of about twenty.

The Phyrexians had only a poor idea of what a human being was. Every newt of the first batch looked exactly like every other. They were neither male nor female. They were the height of a child of twelve, had no beards, and did not grow older. Unlike true Phyrexians, they had to breathe, eat and sleep. They were given no names. Each was called by a word for the place where it slept and fed.
One of these newts was called by a word that meant the lumps of slag and ash that pile up under a furnace. The word was xantcha. She was made about 65 AR.
Xantcha had a defect, by Phyrexian standards. She thought for herself. In Phyrexia every mind is meant to belong to Yawgmoth, and a newt with a will of its own was in great danger.

The overseer of the newts was Gix. When Xantcha met him, she noticed that this great demon spoke of himself as male. She had learned from her dreams that such a difference existed. She decided, privately, that she would be female, in order to be unlike him. It was an act of rebellion. Gix also began to use her word as her own name, as he used his.

Gix did not punish her for her oddities. He hinted that she had been made, in part, from special material. The story never says it outright, but its clues add up: Gix seems to have put some of the flesh of Mishra into the vat from which Xantcha was grown, and that was the source of her dreams. So the newt who would one day stand beside Urza may have been made from Urza's brother. Gix tried to break into her mind and take her secrets. She resisted part of it without letting him see that she had, and he lost interest in her.
About 80 AR Gix sent the first newts through to Dominaria. Xantcha was still waiting for her assignment when the sending stopped.

The plan had gone wrong almost at once. A village might overlook one small, beardless, sexless stranger. It could not overlook a number of them who all had the same face. The people of Dominaria found the newts unnatural and killed them.

A second batch was grown with more care. These newts were of full adult height, some male and some female, each with a face of its own, and they aged as people do. Once planted, their memories would be wiped, so that they would not themselves know what they were until they were needed.

Before the second batch could be sent, the way was shut. The Sylex Blast had torn the fabric of the Multiverse around Dominaria, and a barrier was slowly forming around Dominaria and eleven neighbouring worlds. It is called the Shard of the Twelve Worlds. Those inside it later described it as a wall of black ice. To the Phyrexians it was like a knife that cut their portals off. The sources date its closing to about 400 AR. Phyrexia lay outside it.
Yawgmoth blamed Gix for the whole failure and punished him terribly, in a public display. Xantcha watched it.

Xantcha, the leftover of a failed batch, was given other work. She was sent out with teams to other planes to hunt for old artifacts and bring them back to Phyrexia. In that work she was known as Orman'huzra.
By then she hated Phyrexia. She did her job backwards. The artifacts she found she quietly destroyed, or rigged so that they would kill whoever carried them home.
In the end she was caught. On a world whose name is not recorded, her fellow Phyrexians were about to execute her.
Urza had spent more than a hundred years hunting for Phyrexia and had not found it. He knew what had been done to Mishra. He did not know where the enemy's world lay.
About 180 AR he came to that nameless world and saw a pack of Phyrexian monsters about to kill what looked like a human girl. He destroyed them and saved her.

Urza did not understand what he had rescued. He believed that Xantcha was a human being whom the Phyrexians had kidnapped and emptied of her memories. For a very long time he went on believing it. Xantcha, in return for her life, gave Urza the thing he wanted most. She told him how to reach Phyrexia.

Urza took her with him. From that day the planeswalker and the newt travelled together, and they stayed together for three thousand years. Xantcha was not human, and she was not quite Phyrexian any longer either. She became the nearest thing to a friend that Urza had.

Urza did not attack at once. He spent centuries building a weapon: a dragon engine of his own, with eight legs. By about 450 AR it was finished. Xantcha went back to the world where Urza had found her, to keep watch for Phyrexians, so that Urza could follow them home. She watched for nearly two hundred years.

In those same years Urza found out what his own blast had done. He tried to return to Dominaria and could not. Whichever way he approached his home world, he met what he described as a darkness, cold and repelling. The Shard that kept Phyrexia out of Dominaria kept Urza out as well.
What happened when Xantcha's watch ended, and Urza rode his dragon engine into Phyrexia, belongs to the next age of the story.

chapters.title: Rabiah: The One Made of Five

blocks.p: This short chapter leaves Dominaria for a plane that the story has visited once before. Rabiah is a world of deserts, cities, genies and sorcerers, modelled on the tales of the Arabian Nights. An earlier chapter told how a woman of Rabiah named Fatima built the City of Brass there.

The chapter introduces one man, Taysir. He becomes a planeswalker, and in later ages he is one of the mightiest of them, a companion and in the end an opponent of Urza. His tale was told in comic books of 1995 and 1996, and the dates in it are rough. The chronicle places its beginning about 100 AR, a generation or so after the Sylex Blast on Dominaria.
Something happened to Rabiah that has happened to no other plane in this story. Rabiah was copied.

In a single mysterious event the whole plane was reproduced one thousand times. Every person, every place and every object on it was reproduced as well. Where there had been one Rabiah there were now a thousand and one, all of them nearly identical, each with its own copy of every man, woman and camel. The event is called the Thousandfold Refraction. Nobody has explained what caused it.

There was one exception. A child named Taysir had been born on Rabiah not long before. Taysir was not copied a thousand times. He was copied only five times, and the five were not alike. Each was bound to one of the five kinds of magic.
An old lore of Rabiah had foretold this. It spoke of the One Made of Five, and it said that if the five were ever joined in a single body, that person would be the most powerful sorcerer ever known.
The five grew up apart and lived five different lives.
The red Taysir became a nomad of the desert.
The green Taysir became a herder.
The white Taysir became a dervish, a wandering holy man. He took a servant named Raghib, a man suffering from leprosy.
The black Taysir became a sorcerer's apprentice.
The blue Taysir did not grow up at all. He remained a baby. A man named El-Hajjâj hid the child away.

El-Hajjâj had good reason. His own daughter was Nailah, the Sorceress Queen, a wicked and ambitious ruler. Nailah knew the prophecy, and she wanted the power of the One Made of Five for herself. Her father hid the blue child so that she could never bring all five together under her control.

The dervish's servant Raghib had a history with her too, which the white Taysir did not know. Raghib had once been Nailah's lover. When she had no more use for him, she had cursed him with his disease.

Nailah began with the black Taysir. She seduced him and set him on the others. At her urging the black Taysir killed the green Taysir, the herder, and absorbed him. Now two of the five were in one body, and that body was hers to command.

It did not stay hers. The Taysir who was now both black and green rebelled against her. He found the nomad and warned him of what the queen intended. He also gave the nomad a magical ring, the Ring of Ma'rûf, by which the other Taysirs could be traced.

The nomad used it. He found the dervish and merged with him. The two of them found the hidden baby and merged with him as well. Then the nomad, now three in one, came back for the last. He defeated Nailah and joined himself to the black and green Taysir.
The five were one. This is called the Unification of Taysir, and the chronicle dates it to about 130 AR. In the moment of it, Taysir's planeswalker's spark woke.

Nailah tried once more. She tried to seduce the new Taysir through the part of him that had been her black apprentice. He answered with a blast of power and walked away from Rabiah into the space between the worlds.

Nailah could not have his power, so she made sure that Rabiah would not have him back. She raised a magical barrier around all the thousand and one Rabiahs. Taysir, the mightiest sorcerer his world had ever produced, could never go home.

Taysir wandered. Some time before about 400 AR his wandering brought him to Dominaria, to the continent of Corondor, where the old tales of the Blackblade had taken place. There he met a woman named Kristina, a native of Corondor, who was called Kristina of the Woods. Kristina was a planeswalker too, though one source says that her spark woke only after the Shard had formed. They fell in love.

Not long afterwards the Shard closed. The Shard of the Twelve Worlds is the barrier that formed around Dominaria and eleven neighbouring planes as a late effect of the Sylex Blast. Any planeswalker who was inside those twelve worlds when it sealed was trapped inside. Taysir was now shut out of Rabiah by one barrier and shut inside the Shard by another.

He and Kristina made the best of it. For the long ages of ice that followed, the two of them travelled among the twelve planes they could still reach and helped the peoples there who were in trouble. What became of them when the Shard was finally broken is told in its place.

chapters.title: The Fallen Empires of Sarpadia
sources: MTG Wiki, "Fall of the Sarpadian Empires"
MTG Wiki, "Order of the Ebon Hand"

blocks.p: The Sylex Blast of 64 AR did not only ruin the continent where it went off. It cooled the whole world. This chapter shows what that cooling did somewhere else: on Sarpadia, a continent far to the south of Terisiare, alone in its ocean. The people of Sarpadia had taken no part in the Brothers' War and probably knew almost nothing about it. A hundred years after the blast, all five of their nations were destroyed within a few years of one another.

One person from an earlier chapter is at the centre of it. Tev Loneglade was born on the Sarpadian coast in -1850 AR. He became a planeswalker and gave his sister Tymolin endless youth. He is by now two thousand years old.

The story of Sarpadia was first told through a set of cards called Fallen Empires, published in 1994, and filled out in comics and short stories. Much of it survives only in pieces, and this chapter follows the encyclopaedia's reconstruction.

Sarpadia had been ruled long before by a single cruel empire, the Tchokta, which fed its gods with the lives of its subjects. The peoples who overthrew the Tchokta founded the five nations that stood in 170 AR.

Icatia was the largest. It was a nation of humans, with a capital called Windenby. It had elected officials, rich merchants, skilled doctors and a strong army. It also had a good deal of corruption among its officials. Its chief religious body was the Order of Leitbur, an order of clerics founded by Bethan Leitbur.

In the swamps of the west stood the Order of the Ebon Hand, a dark religious order and Icatia's sworn enemy. It had been founded by a man named Tourach, whom its members worshipped as a god after his death. New members cut off one of their own hands when they joined. That custom, and several other things about the Order, strongly resemble the Brotherhood of Gix, and the Order seems to have begun long before as a cult of Gix, perhaps founded by someone who fled the Brothers' War. By this time, however, the Ebon Hand counted itself an enemy of Phyrexia.
The north of the continent was covered by Havenwood, an immense forest. Elves lived there in scattered, fortified villages, as hunters, farmers and druids.
In the mountains called the Crimson Peaks lived the dwarves, in mining towns and strongholds.
And under the sea around the continent lay Vodalia, an empire of merfolk, ruled by the Empress Galina. The Vodalians worshipped Svyelun, a goddess of the moon.

After the blast the weather turned. Winters grew longer and harder. Crops failed. Food, iron and timber all ran short. Nations that had lived as neighbours began to quarrel over what was left, and each one turned inward.
Each nation looked for its own way out of the shortage. Two of those ways led directly to disaster.

The Order of the Ebon Hand had a wizard named Endrek Sahr. By a mixture of alchemy and the magic of death, Endrek Sahr learned to grow living creatures out of dead flesh. He called them thrulls. A thrull was alive, unlike a walking corpse, and it held a store of mana that was released when the creature was killed. The Order used thrulls as slaves and as victims for its sacrifices.
Endrek Sahr kept improving them. He bred thrulls to be worn as living armour, thrulls to fight, and thrulls clever enough to work magic.

His proudest creation was the derelor, a giant thrull. It needed so much mana to keep alive that it drained the Order's resources, and the Order's leaders sentenced its maker to death for it. Endrek Sahr vanished before the sentence was carried out. He appears to have fallen through a rift in time into the far future.
So the Order was left with a slave race that included strong breeds and intelligent breeds, and without the one man who understood them.

In Havenwood the elves' crops were failing. An elven druid named Thelon found an answer. With all the dying vegetation, fungus was growing everywhere. Thelon filled a fungus with the mana of the forest and made it into a living creature that could be farmed. The creature is called a thallid. Thallids budded off small growths called saprolings, and the elves ate them. It was plentiful food, if dull.

Thelon had a secret, which he shared with only two elder druids. He had borrowed his method from the Order of the Ebon Hand, and the thallids were made in part from thrull flesh. The elves were secretly trading with Icatia's worst enemy to get it.

The go-between in that trade was a human adventurer named Reod Dai. He had been born Robin Davies and had been a captain in the Icatian army. He changed his name when he joined the Order of the Ebon Hand, and he sold his skill in magic to whoever paid.

The elder druids of Havenwood hired Reod Dai for a second job. They needed Icatia to be looking the other way while the trade with the Ebon Hand went on. Reod Dai was to cause trouble on Icatia's southern border.

He did it thoroughly. In the Crimson Peaks lived tribes of goblins and orcs, who had always fought one another. Reod Dai made a truce between them and taught them how to make war. He showed the goblins how to blow up walls with explosive charges, how to fly over walls on kites, and how to throw an enemy into confusion with drums.

For a few years the united horde raided the Icatian border, and Reod Dai collected his pay. Then the elves ended the contract without warning. Reod Dai was left with no money and with an army of orcs and goblins that he had built and could no longer direct.

He went to Havenwood for revenge. With a cartload of explosive dragon eggs bought from a family of dwarves, he tried to blow up the elves' thallid farm. A magical ward around the farm twisted the blast. Nobody intended the result: the magic woke a dim intelligence in the thallids. Reod Dai was captured and escaped, and he set fire to an elven stronghold on his way out. Afterwards he found his way to the thrulls and urged them, too, to turn on their masters.
In the space of a few years one resentful mercenary had armed the orcs and goblins, awakened the thallids and stirred up the thrulls.

The cold drove the orcs and goblins out of their caves and warrens in search of food. The horde that Reod Dai had united fell upon the dwarves of the Crimson Peaks. The dwarven towns and strongholds were destroyed one after another, and one mining town was buried by a volcanic eruption that the Ebon Hand set off. The dwarven empire was the first of the five to fall.
In one of those attacks, in 170 AR, an orc stabbed a dwarf named Kaylen in the back and killed him. Kaylen was the husband of Tymolin Loneglade.
Tymolin Loneglade was the sister of the planeswalker Tev Loneglade. Her brother's magic had kept her young for two thousand years. The two could not have been less alike.

Tev lived alone in Havenwood. Absolute power had soured in him. He had found that for all his strength he could not change what people were, and his disappointment had hardened into contempt for everyone except his sister. He refused on principle to interfere in the world's affairs.

Tymolin threw herself into them. She was a fine swordswoman. She had married the dwarf Kaylen and lived among his people. During her marriage she had also had a love affair with an Icatian priest named Oliver Farrel, and she had left him to go back to her husband.
After Kaylen's death the dwarves cast Tymolin out, and Tev took her in. She begged him to use his power to stop the orcs and goblins. Tev refused.

Oliver Farrel had gone on to greater things. He had broken with the Order of Leitbur because he thought it far too soft on the Ebon Hand. He was a magnetic speaker. Preaching reform and coming doom in the poor quarters of the Icatian towns, he gathered a large and devoted following, the Farrelites. They worshipped the same god as the Order of Leitbur, but they dealt with their enemies by violence in the streets, and they accused anyone who stood in their way of serving Tourach.

Farrel had never forgiven Tymolin for leaving him. He now told his followers that Tymolin Loneglade was the living incarnation of Tourach. He chose one of his women, Sianna, as his champion and gave her a magical mantle that he had made.

Near the border of Havenwood and Icatia, Farrel and his followers ambushed the brother and sister. Farrel hurled a bomb at them. Tev struck back, killed several Farrelites and stripped the magic from Sianna's mantle. The Farrelites fled into the forest. In the confusion Tymolin, chasing them, was separated from her brother.
Alone and furious, Tev began to change. He had worn the shape of an old man. Now something more like a dragon began to show through.

Tymolin was captured by a priestess of the Ebon Hand named Vaylesh. She killed two of her captors before they drugged her. Vaylesh had a use for her. The Order wanted to draw Oliver Farrel out of hiding and into an open fight, and Tymolin was the bait. Vaylesh sent Farrel a letter.
Farrel came with his followers. He persuaded Vaylesh to let him speak with the prisoner. He offered Tymolin one last chance to come back to him. She refused. Farrel stabbed her to death.
Tev felt his sister die.

What was left of his humanity went out of him. He took a new body for good, the twisted shape of a serpentine dragon, dark-scaled and red-eyed. He flew into the Ebon Hand's camp, where the Farrelites and the Order had begun to fight each other, and burned everyone in it to ash with a single spell of fire: Farrel, Sianna, Vaylesh, the soldiers of both sides and a derelor that Vaylesh had summoned.
Then he gave himself a new name, Tevesh Szat, and a purpose. Civilisations, he had decided, led to nothing but decadence and corruption. He would bring them silence.

Tevesh Szat began at once. He opened a magical gate and brought the orc and goblin horde through it onto the Icatian town of Montford. Icatia beat that attack off. Szat was patient. One by one he arranged the death blows of the nations of Sarpadia.

The Ebon Hand was destroyed by its own slaves. The clever thrulls and the strong thrulls together led the whole race in revolt. An officer of the Order named Jherana Rure organised a resistance, and a thrull of the assassin breed killed her and ended it. The thrulls overran the Order's citadel.

Havenwood was destroyed by its own food. The thallids had begun to pick up weapons and build shelters. The elves split into two parties, one wanting to exterminate the thallids and one wanting to help them, and they were still arguing when the thallids rose. Thallids were almost impossible to kill, since their fungal roots let them grow back, and there were often more of them after a battle than before it. They far outnumbered the elves. The elven empire is said to have been crushed in a single day.

Icatia fell last. It had been weakened from inside by the Farrelites, who became more fanatical than ever once Farrel and Sianna could be called martyrs. It held off the orcs and goblins for a while. It could not hold off the orcs and goblins, the thrulls and the thallids together, with a planeswalker guiding them.

Vodalia was destroyed by an enemy of its own. Far to the south, in the waters around Dominaria's southern pole, lived the homarids: thinking creatures like huge lobsters that walk upright, between one and a half and two metres tall. Homarids need cold water. As the oceans cooled, they spread north.

The Vodalian army under Marshal Karel Volnikov beat the first invaders. But in the cooling sea the homarids bred faster than the merfolk could kill them. Vodalia ran out of food and medicine and had to be abandoned.

The Empress Galina led many of her people through a magical portal made by a mage named Akoroun. The portal was meant to carry them to a distant merfolk colony, Etlan Shiis. It carried them there, and it also carried them three thousand years into the future. Galina's story continues then.

When it was over, the thrulls swarmed across the whole continent. They destroyed the goblins. The orcs hid in the caves of the Crimson Peaks, and the thrulls bred a new kind of thrull for hunting in caves and killed the last of them. In the end only two peoples were left on the land of Sarpadia: the thrulls, and the thallids in Havenwood. The two left each other alone. They may have recognised that they were, in part, made of the same flesh. The homarids held the sea.
The thrulls never learned that there was any world beyond Sarpadia, and that was fortunate for the rest of Dominaria. They went on changing themselves and growing stronger for thousands of years.
Tevesh Szat left Sarpadia silent behind him and went looking for other civilisations to end. He is one of the great villains of the ages that follow.

Sarpadia's ruin was complete, and it was only partly the cold's doing. The cold made the nations hungry. What destroyed them was what each did about it: the slaves the Order bred, the food the elves grew in secret, the army a mercenary raised for pay, the mob a preacher gathered, and one grieving, all-powerful man who decided that the world deserved to die.

chapters.title: Tales of the Dark
sources: MTG Wiki, "Shard of the Twelve Worlds"

blocks.p: The Dark Age on Dominaria lasted almost four hundred years, from the Sylex Blast of 64 AR to the coming of the ice about 450 AR. Its two large stories have their own chapters: the ruin of the continent of Sarpadia, which has been told, and the tale of a young mage named Jodah, which comes next.

Between them the chronicle lists a number of smaller events. Most come from short stories and old magazine articles, and they do not connect with one another. They are gathered here in order of time. Together they give a fair picture of the age: a cooling world of small states, petty tyrants, hidden mages and persecuting priests. Two of them matter for the rest of the story, and they are marked as such.

parts.h: Agrippa and the sea dragons (c. 100 AR)

blocks.p: Off the coast of Argive lie islands called the Isles of Argive. About 100 AR they had a king of their own. A sailor of those islands, Agrippa, known as the Wayfinder, came from a family in disgrace, though his great-grandfather had once cleared the isles of raiders. Agrippa was shipwrecked and marooned on an island that belonged to sea dragons. He got away alive, and he brought back gold and a story that cleared his family's name. The sources give no more than that.
This tale matters later.

The elf Gwenna had been a scout of Argoth, the forest island that the Sylex Blast destroyed. She was on the mainland when it happened, and she lived. Elves live long, and a hundred years later Gwenna was still alive, in a village of other refugees from Argoth in a dark bayou. They called themselves the Survivors. Gwenna was eaten up by guilt over her part in the disaster. She had been the one who found Urza's son Harbin on the shore of Argoth and helped him, and the brothers' armies had followed.
The bayou had a master. A malevolent spirit of shadow lived in it, and it fed on despair. It drained hope and will out of everyone who lived there, and so nobody ever left.

An elven mage named Temken came to the bayou. Temken was travelling the land, gathering the scattered Survivors of Argoth to lead them west to a new home. He found Gwenna mourning Argoth, its guardian Titania and the goddess Gaea, all of whom she believed dead. Temken showed her that Gaea was not dead. Her magic was still in the land, even there. To prove it he made an orchid grow and bloom out of the swamp.

The shadow struck at him with a wave of darkness and dread, and weakened him. Temken reached the village and cast his spell of life a second time. The shadow rose against him again. This time Gwenna stepped in. She drew the spirit into herself and held it there, trapped, while the villagers gathered their things and walked out of the bayou behind Temken. It cost Gwenna her life. Temken told her, as he left, that the act had wiped out every fault she had ever blamed herself for.
Temken led the Survivors west. The forest that they came to and settled is Yavimaya, which becomes one of the great forests of Dominaria and an important place in the story.
This tale also matters later, for what it left behind.

Urborg, once the forest of the panther warriors, had been drowned into swamp by the blast. By 300 AR it held a city, also called Urborg, and the city was hellish. Its king was Nevinyrral. Nevinyrral was a necromancer, a mage who commands the dead, and he had made himself a lich, which is a sorcerer who has cheated death by storing his own life in an object. He wrote a handbook of his art that is regarded as the chief work on necromancy.

Nevinyrral wanted more. He sent his armies of the dead against Bogardan, a volcanic island nearby. Bogardan is ruled by mysterious beings of godlike power, and they took offence. They destroyed his armies and struck back. Dragons attacked the city of Urborg from the air. On the ground, Bogardan's masters of fire surrounded the city and beat on the earth with fists gloved in metal, until a volcano erupted in the middle of it.

Nevinyrral saw that the city was lost. He did not want his hoard of spells and artifacts to fall into his enemies' hands. The object in which he kept his life was a disk. He poured all his magic into it and set it off. The explosion wiped out everything for ten miles around: the city, the invaders and Nevinyrral himself.
Many later lords of Urborg have claimed to be his heirs.

parts.h: The war of Iwset and Jehesic (c. 300 AR)

blocks.p: On the west coast of Terisiare stood the city of Iwset, ruled by Lord Peemel, who dreamed of conquering the whole west. Offshore lay the island state of Jehesic, ruled by Lady Edara. Peemel asked for Edara's hand in marriage, she refused, and he went to war.

To keep Jehesic from finding allies, Peemel sent a blood witch named Sacumon north to set the neighbours against each other: the elves of a forest called Eln and the minotaurs of a valley called Urhaalan. Sacumon did it by tricking a third people, the Niroso, a young race of beings of liquid stone, into attacking both with golems made of coal.

The rest was palace murder. One of Peemel's advisers plotted with one of Edara's to force the marriage by magic, and Edara's secret lover, who was another of Peemel's advisers, killed the plotter. Jehesic kidnapped Iwset's chief general and sank its fleet. Peemel had Edara abducted, and was then assassinated by his own adviser before he could use her. Edara's lover killed the assassin. Peemel's heir refused the throne and smashed the city's seal. Edara and her lover were left ruling Iwset on a very thin claim, with enemies already plotting against them. But the war was over.

A rag man is a kind of minion, a servant made by sorcery out of a human being. About 300 AR one of them lived in the Bade Mountains, far from Terisiare, and fathered children on the women of a village. Those children grew up to be rag men in their turn. One of them was a girl named Mita. She became the first female Rag Man, and with the inheritance came a power: she could travel the world through dreams.
Jarsyl was the grandson of Urza's wife Kayla, and one of the first pupils of the Conclave of Mages. He lived more than three hundred years, which the sources do not explain.

In his long life Jarsyl found a portal to Phyrexia. It may have been the one at Koilos through which the demon Gix had come. He went through it and returned, and in a tower on his family's farm he wrote down what he had seen on the metal world, including descriptions of the Phyrexians. Much later he worked out how to open such a portal himself by magic. Soon after that, about 380 AR, he disappeared from Dominaria and was never seen again.
His journal survived him. It was nearly impossible to read, and it passed into dangerous hands. It matters in the next chapter, where Jarsyl's great-great-grandson is at the centre of events.

About 400 AR the barrier that had been forming since the Sylex Blast finally sealed. The Shard of the Twelve Worlds now enclosed Dominaria and eleven other planes completely. Nothing could pass in or out: no planeswalker, no portal, no Phyrexian.

Every planeswalker who happened to be inside was trapped there. Among them were the sorcerer Taysir of Rabiah and his love Kristina of the Woods, and Tevesh Szat, the destroyer of Sarpadia. Urza was outside, and could not come home. Those inside described the barrier as a wall of black ice.
The sources do not agree on the date. The chronicle gives about 400 AR, while the encyclopaedia's own page on the Shard says only that it closed some time after the Ice Age began.

A young king named Rogan ruled a small realm called Angremur. He led a crusade against the goblins of a region called the Flarg. It failed, and the goblins, stirred up, came down to burn the countryside.

Torya Longshanks was a farmer who had been called up as a soldier for that war. She came home to find her farm burned and her father and two younger sisters dead. While she was burying them, a healer appeared, bit Torya's hand, and used the blood to cast a curse on the king who had caused it all. A bolt of lightning killed the healer on the spot and sealed the curse.

Torya's wound would not heal. She learned that it never would until the curse made with her blood was lifted. She enlisted again and went to the king's citadel, which was being attacked night after night by some monster. Rogan turned out to be hardly more than a boy, and a humbler and more decent one than she had expected. She was made a guard in his bedchamber. That night the monster came. Torya fought it and scraped her wounded hand on its scales, and at once the attack was over. The king lay on the floor, bleeding. The curse had been turning Rogan into the monster every night, and her blood on it had broken the spell. Torya stayed to help him become a good king.

chapters.title: The Gathering Dark
sources: MTG Wiki, "The Gathering Dark" (the novel by Jeff Grubb, 1999)
MTG Wiki, "Fall of the Conclave of Mages"

blocks.p: This chapter closes the Dark Age. It is set on Terisiare, the continent of the Brothers' War, about three hundred and sixty-five years after that war ended. Its hero is a boy named Jodah. He matters because he does not die. Jodah is still alive more than four thousand years later, at the very end of the story so far, and he is present at many of its great events in between.
Four things from earlier chapters set the scene.

The Church of Tal is the religion that arose after the war. It teaches that machines and magic destroyed the world, and it hunts down and kills anyone who practises either. By this time it has an iron grip on the city-states of Terisiare. Its symbol is a double sunburst.

Magic survives in two hidden schools. The Conclave of Mages stands in the far north. It was founded about 75 AR by Tawnos and Ashnod, the apprentices of the brothers Urza and Mishra. The City of Shadows lies in the far west. It was founded by Drafna and other survivors of the scholars who first discovered magic.

Jarsyl was the grandson of Urza's wife Kayla and an early pupil of the Conclave. He found a way into Phyrexia, the metal world, wrote about it in a journal that nobody could decipher, and vanished about 380 AR.
And the world is still growing colder every year.
The story comes from a novel of 1999, The Gathering Dark by Jeff Grubb, as the encyclopaedia summarises it.

Jodah was born in 413 AR in Giva Province, the land that had once been Argive. His family were landowners, and they were proud of their blood. They descended from Kayla bin-Kroog, and therefore from Urza or from Mishra. Jarsyl was Jodah's great-great-grandfather.
The family's wealth was failing. The summers were shorter every year and the soil was worn out. While Jodah was still young, they gave up the estate.

Jodah had the gift of magic. At fifteen he was apprenticed to a wandering mage named Voska. Voska drew his magic from mountains. Jodah, at first, could draw only on the magic of the open plains, the magic of light and healing. After a year and a half Voska gave his pupil a present, a mirror with magical properties. Jodah kept that mirror for the rest of his very long life.

In 430 AR the Church of Tal arrested both of them. They were taken to the city-state of Alsoor and questioned by a priestess and inquisitor named Delphine, who held the rank of Primata. Delphine was an enormous woman, bigger than two guards together, with a heavy jaw and a permanent scowl. She had devoted her life to hunting people who cast spells. She cast spells herself, though the Church did not call them that.

Her questioning was harsh, and master and pupil saw only one way out. Jodah cast a spell that filled the room with blinding light. He and Voska went out through a window. Jodah got clear of the city. He had help that he did not understand: a strange ragged figure guided him out. Voska did not get clear. The Church's crossbowmen shot him full of bolts.
Jodah did not know that his teacher was dead, and for a long time he wandered the region trying to find him.

He came to a city just as it was closed off for plague. The sources name it as Alsoor in one place and as Ghed in another. To eat, he took work with an old woman called Mother Dobbs, selling her folk remedies. The remedies were ordinary ones. Jodah quietly improved them with magic, so that they really cured the sick.

Cures that work attract attention. A young woman in blue followed him and cornered him in an alley to ask whether he was the one behind the potions. Her name was Sima. She was a mage of the City of Shadows, a few years older than Jodah, and she had been sent out into the world to look for lost spells and for people with talent. She thought Jodah an idiot child. Guards interrupted them. Sima knocked Jodah flat with a spell and escaped alone.
The Inquisition was on his trail again. To get out of its reach Jodah joined the army of Ghed.

Ghed and Alsoor were at war over nothing very much. Each city had been bullying the farmers who lived between them to sell their harvest to it and not to its rival, and the bullying had grown into a real war.

One of Jodah's fellow recruits was a boy of thirteen from the town of Thorn, serving as a prison guard. His name was Tivadar. Young as he was, Tivadar had already come to a conclusion: these wars between human cities were pointless, and they distracted people from their true enemy.

The true enemy arrived while the two armies were fighting each other at a place called Pitdown. A horde of goblins, with giants among them, fell on both armies at once and slaughtered them. The survivors of both sides had to join forces to drive the goblins off.

Jodah ran. He fled into the ruins of the deserted city of Pitdown with goblin raiders behind him. To hide, he threw himself into the basin of an old fountain and lay under the water until they had gone.

It was no ordinary fountain. It was a Fountain of Youth, long abandoned and still working. Its water slowed Jodah's ageing almost to nothing. He did not know it. It was years before anyone noticed that Jodah had stopped growing older.
A week later the Church of Tal negotiated a peace between the two cities.

Delphine, meanwhile, had laid a trap. She spread a rumour that Voska was alive and held in Alsoor, hoping that his apprentice would come for him. The one who came was Sima, who had heard Voska's name from Jodah and hoped to recruit him for her school. Sima was arrested and condemned to death.

After Pitdown, Jodah saw her being carried in a prison wagon. He crept into her cell. Her wrists were locked in enchanted manacles of a metal called moonsilver, and she taught Jodah how to undo the enchantment on them. The two of them set a fire and let out all the Church's other prisoners.

Delphine caught up with them. She stunned Sima with a burst of holy light and called a sword of fire into her own hand to deal with Jodah. Jodah held up Voska's mirror. The mirror threw the fire back onto Delphine, and while the Primata rolled on the ground to put herself out, Jodah and Sima rode away on her horse.
By then Jodah had learned that Voska was dead. He had nowhere else to go. Sima offered to take him to the City of Shadows, where he could study in peace.

They sailed for the west. A storm struck the ship, and Jodah was swept overboard. He did not drown. Merfolk seized him in the water and carried him off. They had been hired. They handed Jodah over to the same ragged figure that had helped him out of Alsoor, and received in payment a magical helmet of coral.

The figure was a Rag Man, a minion made by sorcery, and somebody had sent it to find Jodah in particular. It led him by hidden ways across the continent to the north and delivered him to the gate of the Conclave of Mages.

The Conclave had grown in three and a half centuries into a citadel larger than most towns. It sprawled over the shoulder of a mountain, a great central keep with towers, iron balconies and flying bridges, parts of it hanging out over the cliffs. Around it lay an enormous unfinished maze of low, ivy-covered walls.

Jodah got past the gate by dazzling a guard with a spell. He was interviewed by the Conclave's chief artificer, a stocky, sharp-eyed, endlessly practical man named Barl, who seemed to know everything that happened in the place. Jodah told his story and mentioned his ancestor Jarsyl. Barl had never heard the name. He wrote it down and passed his notes up.

The master of the Conclave was Mairsil, an elegant man with a thin moustache, a golden cape, a skull-headed walking stick and a great ruby ring. The Conclave had no ranks, and Mairsil called himself only the First Among Equals. Mairsil knew the name Jarsyl at once. He had read it in Kayla bin-Kroog's poem on the Brothers' War, and he afterwards tracked down Jarsyl's unreadable journal.
Mairsil gave the new boy a place in the library and made sure he was comfortable. Jodah, who had been hunted for a year, made friends among the mages and believed that he had found his home at last.
Mairsil had a reason for his kindness, and the Conclave had a secret.

Mairsil was not its rightful master. The Conclave had been led by a great wizard named Lord Ith, the Magus Supreme, the builder of the maze. About fifteen years earlier, in 415 AR, Mairsil had overthrown him. Mairsil did not kill Ith. He had a better use for him.

In a cavern beneath the citadel there was a pit with no bottom. Over the pit, on chains, hung a cage. Barl had built it, of a metal called watersilver. Ith was inside it. The cage and its chains drew the magic out of the prisoner continuously, and that stolen power ran the Conclave's devices and fed Mairsil's own strength. Mairsil is remembered as the Pretender.

Fifteen years of it had driven Ith mad, and the cage was slowly killing him. But about 427 AR its magic began to weaken a little. In 430 AR, in one clear moment, Ith managed to push a single spell out through the bars. He summoned a Rag Man and begged it to go and bring help.
The Rag Man had found Jodah.

Mairsil's plan was a different one. He wanted to become a planeswalker. He believed that the beings of the Dark Lands, as he called Phyrexia, could make him one. He was entirely wrong about that, and it was lucky for him that he never found out how wrong. Jarsyl had opened a door to that world, and Mairsil hoped that Jarsyl's own descendant could work out from the journal how to open it again.

Jodah worked on the journal, and he did work the spell out. On his first attempt he used the wrong kind of mana, the white magic he knew best, and the spell failed. Then he understood that it needed the black magic of swamps and death. By that time he had begun to see what kind of man Mairsil was. He kept the discovery to himself and never completed the spell.

Sima had not given Jodah up for dead. She tracked him to the Conclave and presented herself there as a wandering mage. Her magic was the blue magic of the western school, and Barl suspected at once where she came from.
Delphine had not given up either. With the help of a wonder-worker named Betje she followed Sima's trail north. She raised an army from the local towns in the name of Tal and attacked the citadel.

The mages fought back with fire and with spells that drain life, and it was soon clear that the Church's army would lose. Delphine herself was wrapped in protective magic and no spell could touch her. She came face to face with Mairsil. He was carrying a wand that had belonged to Ith. With it he drained away every one of her protections. Then he ran her through and set fire to her body.
While that battle raged above, the Rag Man led Jodah and Sima down to the cavern. They broke Barl's Cage.
Ith came out of it insane with rage. He killed his own Rag Man. Then he rose up through the citadel floor by floor, smashing everything.

Jodah and Mairsil were facing each other when Ith burst into the room. Mairsil had taken Delphine's protections for himself, and Ith's spells slid off him. Ith hurled a ray of fire. Jodah caught it in Voska's mirror and turned it onto Mairsil. Mairsil's stolen protection did not cover that. He caught fire and ran screaming from the room, and he died.
Then Jodah turned the mirror on Ith, and showed the mad wizard his own reflection. Ith saw what he had become, and his mind came back to him.

Ith was sane again, and he was no more forgiving. He was determined that the place of his torment should not stand. He cast a spell of terror over every surviving mage, so that they all fled from the citadel. Then he pulled the Conclave of Mages down, stone by stone, until nothing was left but a heap of rubble on the edge of the pit. For Barl, who had built the cage, he had a particular punishment. He turned Barl into his new Rag Man.
Ith went away to be alone. The school that Tawnos and Ashnod had founded was gone, after three hundred and fifty-five years.
