One thing was overlooked in the ruins. Mairsil had taken a precaution that other dark wizards of this story also take. He had put his life into an object: the ruby ring on his finger. His body burned, and his spirit stayed in the ring, waiting for someone to pick it up.
It waited two thousand years. That ring does more harm in this story than Mairsil ever did alive, and it is still doing harm at the story's end.

Jodah and Sima gathered up the frightened mages of the Conclave and led them across the continent to the west, to the City of Shadows. From then on it was the only school of magic left on Terisiare. It later took the name School of the Unseen.
Jodah flourished there. He rose to be its Archmage, and he married Sima.

Then the gift of the fountain showed itself for the curse it also was. Sima grew old and Jodah did not. Some time after the Ice Age began she died, with Jodah sitting at her bedside. Everyone else he had known in his youth died too. The grief drove him towards madness. He saved himself with Voska's mirror. Jodah learned to store his memories in the mirror, wipe his own mind clean, and then take the memories back with the pain drained out of them. He did this again and again through the centuries. The mages came to call him the Archmage Eternal.

Tivadar, the boy soldier from Thorn, grew up to act on what he had seen at Pitdown. He became the leader of an order of warriors, the Knights of Thorn, and led them against the goblins and orcs that were overrunning Terisiare.

He did something else that shocked people. Tivadar took a sorcerer as his ally: Rasputin Dreamweaver, a former mage of the Conclave. Lord Ith, too, is said to have fought beside him. A knight raised among the Church's witch hunts was fighting side by side with wizards, and winning.

The crusade lasted from about 430 to 450 AR, and it succeeded. The goblin invasions were thrown back, and for a short time something like order returned to Terisiare. Tivadar later wrote a history of those wars.

His success changed the Church of Tal. As Tivadar's fame grew, the Church turned away from hunting witches and towards defending people against real enemies. About the same time it came out that many of the Church's own prayers and chants were spells of white magic. The Church had been casting magic all along. After that it grew more tolerant, and then it slowly faded from power.

It came too late to matter much. About 450 AR the long cooling that began with the Sylex Blast reached its end, and the Dark Age gave way to the Ice Age. Glaciers covered the north of Terisiare and went on spreading.

In Almaaz, the land where the prince Porros had once buried his own city, a people of living ice called the Rigida took power as the cold came. They looked like human beings with features of ice, and they were cruel. They founded a Glacial Kingdom that ruled most of Almaaz for the whole of the Ice Age.
The ice lasted nearly two and a half thousand years.

The Ice Age on Dominaria ran from 450 AR to 2934 AR. The Sylex Blast that ended the Brothers' War had started the cooling, and two planeswalkers who liked the cold later made it worse and kept it going.

It is the least recorded age in Dominaria's history. For most of those two and a half thousand years almost nothing was written down, and later scholars assumed that nothing happened. A good deal did. The nations that later ruled the continent of Terisiare were born under the ice, and magic was refined into the form it still has.

Throughout the age Dominaria was sealed inside the Shard of the Twelve Worlds, with eleven other planes. No planeswalker could get in or out. Those who were trapped inside had a small set of worlds to themselves, and they behaved accordingly.

This chapter walks through the age in order, from its beginning to about a hundred years before its end. Its last hundred years form one connected story, which has the next chapter to itself. Three people from earlier chapters are alive throughout. Jodah is the mage who stopped ageing after hiding in a Fountain of Youth, and he leads the hidden school of magic in the west. Tevesh Szat is the planeswalker who destroyed Sarpadia. Taysir and Kristina are the planeswalker lovers who wander the twelve worlds helping where they can.

parts.h: The keep over the pit (c. 470 AR)

blocks.p: In the far north of Terisiare there is a mountain shoulder with a bottomless pit in it. The Monastery of Gix once stood there, and after it the Conclave of Mages, which the wizard Ith tore down in 430 AR.

Twenty years into the Ice Age a third building rose on the same spot: a dank, grey fortress called Tresserhorn. Its builder and keeper was Chaeska, a huge figure the size of an ogre, with glowing red eyes and a voice like thunder. Chaeska looked like a living man but was one of the walking dead, a frame of bones covered with muscle and skin. Nobody knows who made him. He commanded an army of dead warriors, and he kept the fortress ready for a master. The master did not arrive for more than two thousand years.

One of the planeswalkers trapped inside the Shard was a schemer named Faralyn. He appears to have been meddling in Dominaria for a long time. It was Faralyn who had once cursed the Elder Dragon Vaevictis Asmadi into the shape of a small dragon whelp, the curse that led to the battle at Mors Ridge.

Faralyn had two companions. The first was the Elder Dragon Chromium Rhuell, the brother of Nicol Bolas and the mourning hero of Mors Ridge. Chromium had once been bound in service to the demon planeswalker Dihada. When he was free of her, he pledged himself to Faralyn.

The second was a boy named Ravidel, born on another of the twelve planes. Ravidel had magical gifts that his parents could not cope with, and Faralyn took him as a spellsquire, a wizard's apprentice. Ravidel had been sent away from his home with a stranger, and he was lonely. He found comfort in looking after the great dragon, and the two became true friends.
The three of them studied the Shard together, looking for a way through it. Their story ends in the next chapter, and it ends badly.

parts.h: The cult of the ice (c. 750 AR)

blocks.p: After a few centuries, life on Terisiare had settled into the cold. Near the Ronom Glacier a small order of wizards and scholars shut themselves up in a keep called Rimewind. They decided that fighting the winter was pointless, and they studied it. They found that the crystals of ice could be used like a lens: mana drawn up from the land through the ice came out magnified. They came to believe that the endless winter was good for the world. For the rest of the Ice Age the wizards of Rimewind lived quietly and comfortably and troubled nobody.

Almaaz is the land where the prince Porros once buried his own city, Sumifa, under the desert. After that disaster Almaaz fell into civil war. One side followed the memory of Porros, who was called the Raptor. About 1050 AR his followers formed themselves into an order, the Ninnites.

About 1300 AR a new city of Sumifa was founded close to the buried one, with the help of sages and wizards from Jodah's school. It grew into a great fortress town of ring-shaped walls. The first Sumifa was gradually forgotten. The new one is today the oldest city still standing on what was once Terisiare.

parts.h: The ruin of the Foulmere (c. 1600 AR)

blocks.p: The Foulmere was once a lush, living marsh at the mouth of a river called the Kron Lu. A tiny people lived in it, the Eub Hlut, gnomes about twenty centimetres tall. So did a hermit, Dr. Peter Langwynd, a sorcerer and former professor who had retired there to study its plants and animals.

One day a planeswalker named Vram arrived with her daughter Mao and demanded a tour. Langwynd showed them the marsh's great wonder, a gigantic frog. Vram tamed the frog and used it in a duel against another planeswalker.

A mage draws mana from the land, and a land can be drawn dry. In the heat of the duel Vram took everything the Foulmere had. Almost every living thing in the marsh died in a single burst of fire. What was left was a black, dead bog full of hostile walking corpses, and it never recovered. Both planeswalkers were hurled off the plane and could not return. Langwynd survived, with Mao, one gnome woman and a stray dwarf, and the old naturalist was left to bring up a planeswalker's child.
The story is a small one. It is told here because it shows plainly what the planeswalkers of that age were to ordinary people.

At some time during the Ice Age, on the continent of Aerona far to the east of Terisiare, several trading fleets formed an alliance. The alliance grew into a military state, the Sheoltun Empire, with its capital at Benfosa. Its most famous administrator, Tobias Andrion, spent more than thirty years destroying the pirates of the Spice Isles. Sheoltun matters because of what came after it. Many centuries later it gave way to Benalia, one of the great nations of the later story.
This is the most important event of the chapter.

In the Sardian Mountains of Terisiare, near the buried caves of Koilos, stood the kingdom of Storgard. It had taken in refugees from ruined Sarpadia long before, and it is sometimes called the last of the fallen empires. Five clans ruled it, each named for a gem: Ruby, Emerald, Onyx, Pearl and Sapphire. A great glacier was advancing on its capital.

A child had once come to Storgard alone out of the frozen wastes, seeking shelter. Her name was Freyalise. The shamans told the king that no ordinary human child could have survived out there. They were right, though Freyalise kept the reason secret all her life: she was half elven. She grew up in Clan Ruby, became a mage of fire, and rose to lead her clan. Her closest friend from childhood was a young man of Clan Emerald, Jason Carthalion. Jason was a descendant of the Lion of Carth, the boy who once summoned Dakkon Blackblade.

The leader of Clan Emerald, a shaman named Oriel Kjeldos, saw that the glacier would swallow the city and urged everyone to leave. King Miko refused. The king was not acting freely. Tevesh Szat had got hold of his mind. Szat wanted the whole kingdom to stay where it was and die.

Under Szat's influence the king ordered that the question be settled by a duel between the champions of the two sides. Jason Carthalion was to fight for those who wanted to leave. Freyalise was to fight for those who would stay. The two friends had to try to kill each other.

Freyalise was by far the stronger mage. Jason was barely trained. But Jason had a magical bow and a magical shield, and the nature magic of his clan, and against every expectation he won. He dealt Freyalise a mortal wound.

Freyalise did not die. She carried a planeswalker's spark, and the wound woke it. She became a planeswalker with the forest magic that had struck her down filling her mind, and she favoured that magic ever after. The change almost drove her mad. Jodah, the ageless archmage, helped her through it.

The duel was won, and those who wished to leave Storgard were allowed to go. Clan Emerald, part of Clan Pearl and others followed Oriel Kjeldos and Jason Carthalion out into the snow. The rest stayed. The glacier took them all, to Tevesh Szat's satisfaction.
Oriel Kjeldos died on the journey. Legend says that she was the first to tame an aesthir, one of the great birds of the frozen mountains that her descendants would ride into battle.

Her people went on, south and east. They settled on the buried foundations of Penregon, the old capital of Argive, the first city the ice had killed. There they built a new city and named it Kjeld after their dead leader. Around it grew the kingdom of Kjeldor, ruled by Oriel's descendants. Kjeldor is the great human nation of the late Ice Age. A second city, Krov, later became its capital, and a third, Soldev, was built on the ruins of Storgard itself.

Freyalise went to the elves. She helped the elves of two forests, Fyndhorn to the south of Kjeldor and Llanowar on another continent, to live through the ice. They came to worship her as a goddess. She also began to study the Shard, hoping to find a way to break it.
About the same time something terrible was put away under the ice.

Marit Lage is a being of immense power with a body like a vast sea monster. She has been called a demigod and a leviathan. She can cross between planes, though not in the way planeswalkers do, and nobody knows exactly what she is. About 2400 AR she had gathered great power. Then, by means that are not recorded, she was entombed in a crypt beneath the sea, deep inside the Ronom Glacier. Her worshippers hold that she is not dead but dreaming.

North-west of Kjeldor, beyond a range called the Karplusan Mountains, lay open steppe. The people of the steppe were the Balduvians, clans of hunters whom the Kjeldorans called barbarians. The Balduvians had always claimed the lands south of the mountains too. Those were the lands on which the refugees from Storgard had settled.
About 2500 AR Balduvia went to war with Kjeldor over them. The two peoples fought, on and off, for four hundred years.

parts.h: The tiger warriors of Scarwood (c. 2600 AR)

blocks.p: Scarwood is a jungle on the continent of Jamuraa. At its centre lay a place of power known as the Dark Heart of the Wood. A planeswalker named Terrent Amese wanted the Heart guarded. He made guards for it by fusing the natures of human and tiger, and so created the first tiger warriors.

He named the first of them Ojanen and made him leader of the tribe. On their maker's orders the tiger people built a great temple, the Tabernacle at Pendrell Vale, to worship him in and to watch over the Heart. They believed that he was a god.

Ojanen was the only one who dealt with Terrent Amese face to face, and he came to see the truth. His people were slave labour, and their maker was no god. Ojanen rallied the tribe to claim its freedom.

Terrent Amese took this as betrayal. He cursed Ojanen's line. Then he made a monster to wipe the tribe out: Ur-Drago, a creature cased in living rock, its face hidden behind a curved steel mask, with pincers for hands and feet. It did not need to eat or breathe. It existed only to kill. Having made it, Terrent Amese vanished and was never seen again.

Ojanen faced Ur-Drago alone in the halls of the Tabernacle while his people fled the forest. The tribe never learned how the fight ended. They settled in a desert and broke up into several bands. In time they came to remember their maker as a kindly god who had abandoned them because of Ojanen's sin, and they grew cautious and fearful of anything new. Elves moved into Scarwood, and centuries later giant apes drove the elves out in turn. The tiger warriors return to the story when a later bearer of the name, Jedit Ojanen, learns what really happened.

In a far northern land called Parma the cold became deadly. A war leader named Kradak led his people away from it. They came to a huge, solitary volcano that they called simply the Mountain. The Mountain seemed to call to Kradak. Many of his followers turned back. Kradak climbed to the summit.

There he formed a bond with the land and learned the secret of a magic of fire, which he called the Flame. He brought it down to his people, and it kept them alive. A second band of survivors, led by a man named Jezal, made a pact with him. From that union came the nation of Keld, and Kradak was its first warlord. Keld became a nation of fierce warriors, and it has a long part in the later story.

parts.h: A scribe leaves Kjeld (c. 2815 to 2834 AR)

blocks.p: About 2815 AR a boy was born in Kjeldor who grew up to be a scribe in the city of Kjeld. His name was Barrinalo. About 2834 AR he was present at the death of a wizard named Pharon. The dying man told the young scribe to become the most powerful wizard in all Dominaria, and taught him the secret of a mighty spell called the Blare of Doom.

The scribe decided to leave Kjeld for good. At the gate he was told to sign his name in the register of departures. The ink ran, and he could not finish the word. He took the accident as a sign and kept what he had written as his new name: Barrin.
Barrin lived an unnaturally long life. Four and a half centuries later he became the closest ally Urza ever had.

parts.h: The death of Arcades Sabboth (c. 2834 AR)

blocks.p: One more of the trapped planeswalkers must be introduced. Leshrac was a gaunt, floating figure who preferred the night and was famous for it. He and Tevesh Szat were the two who used their magic to deepen the Ice Age and keep it going, and they were allies.
About 2834 AR Leshrac fought a duel against Kristina of the Woods. To win it he did what Dihada had done long before him. He summoned an Elder Dragon by force and threw it at his enemy.

The dragon was Arcades Sabboth, brother of Nicol Bolas and of Chromium Rhuell. In the dragons' war at the dawn of history Arcades had been the lawgiver among them, the one who believed in order and good government, and after the war he had made himself a ruler and reigned for a very long time. Dragged into another being's duel against his will, he gave Kristina no choice. She had to kill him.

The old comics do not name the dragon outright, and readers long argued over which one it was. The encyclopaedia concludes that it must have been Arcades, since Nicol Bolas was himself a planeswalker and could not be summoned by another.

So by the last century of the Ice Age, two of the Elder Dragons who survived their own war had been killed in the quarrels of planeswalkers: Piru by Dakkon's sword, and Arcades by Kristina's hand. A third was about to follow.

chapters.title: Urza Against Phyrexia
sources: MTG Wiki, "Planeswalker (novel)" (the novel by Lynn Abbey, 1998)

blocks.p: About 450 AR the Ice Age began on Dominaria. It lasted almost two and a half thousand years. Throughout it, Dominaria and eleven neighbouring planes were sealed inside a barrier called the Shard of the Twelve Worlds, which nothing could cross.

This chapter is about the man who caused both the ice and the Shard, and it takes place entirely outside them. Urza set off the Sylex Blast that ended the Brothers' War. The blast made him a planeswalker, a being who walks between worlds and does not age. He learned at the same moment that his brother Mishra had been taken and rebuilt by Phyrexia, the world of flesh fused with machine that is ruled by Yawgmoth. Since then Urza had lived for one thing, which was revenge on Phyrexia.

His companion was Xantcha. She was a newt: a small, human-looking creature grown in a Phyrexian vat to be a spy. She had a mind of her own, had turned against her makers, and had told Urza how to reach their world. Urza believed, wrongly, that she was a human being whom Phyrexia had stolen and emptied.

By about 450 AR Urza had finished the weapon he meant to use: a dragon engine with eight legs, modelled on the war machines his brother once commanded. This chapter follows the summaries of the novel Planeswalker by Lynn Abbey.

Urza could not simply walk to Phyrexia. He needed to follow Phyrexians home. Xantcha therefore went back to the nameless world where Urza had first found her, a world the Phyrexians were known to visit, and waited there for them to come again. She waited for almost two hundred years.
About 650 AR they came. Xantcha warned Urza.
Urza struck without warning. He put on a suit that he had made to keep out Phyrexia's poisonous air, mounted his dragon engine, and walked straight onto the surface of the enemy's world.

Phyrexia is built in nine layers, one inside another like the skins of an onion, called spheres. Urza landed on the outermost and began to destroy everything in reach. Phyrexians died in their thousands. Then he turned his power downward and blasted a hole through the body of the plane itself: through the first sphere, the second and the third, down into the fourth.

Xantcha followed him in by a Phyrexian transport device, and she had an errand of her own. The fourth sphere held the Fane of Flesh, where she had been made. When a newt is grown, the Phyrexians take from it a small object that holds its life, and they keep it. Newts call the thing a heart. In the Fane there was a chamber with a pool full of them. Xantcha searched it until she heard her own heart, which seemed to sing to her. She waded in, took it, and ran back to find Urza.

She found disaster. Urza had badly misjudged his enemy. He had counted on his own strength, which was enormous, and had not understood how many Phyrexians there were, or what waited at the centre. His dragon engine had been broken. And his rampage had drawn the attention of the lord of the place.

Yawgmoth had once been a human healer of the Thran. He was not a planeswalker. But he had ruled Phyrexia for nearly six thousand years and had spent that time gathering power to himself, until he was something like a god within his own world. He reached out and touched Urza's mind.
That single touch was enough. Urza's world convulsed. He sat frozen in the cockpit of his wrecked machine while the Phyrexians closed in.

Xantcha climbed up into the cockpit, shook him and screamed at him until he heard her. Urza understood that he had lost. With the last of his control he walked the two of them out of Phyrexia, and left the broken dragon engine behind.

The assault failed in every way. Phyrexia repaired the damage. Yawgmoth now knew that he had a dangerous and determined enemy, and he began to plan against him. From that day Phyrexia hunted Urza. It sent out packs of killers bred to track and destroy him, and they followed him from world to world.

Worse, something of Yawgmoth's touch stayed in Urza's mind. Over the following centuries it worked on him, and he slowly went mad. He became confused about what was real and what was memory. More and more he relied on Xantcha to tell him which was which and to give his days a purpose.

The two fugitives fled from plane to plane. At last they settled on a world called Moag, a bright and gentle place of rich soil, forests and many peoples. Urza built a tower on an island in its largest sea. For about thirty years they lived there in peace.

About 680 AR Xantcha was travelling on Moag's southern continent and visited the temple of a fire god. She found traces of glistening oil there. That black oil is the mark of Phyrexia. It runs in every Phyrexian body. The cult of the fire god had been infiltrated.

Urza destroyed the temple and most of the Phyrexians in it. Then he and Xantcha left Moag and made sure that the hunters followed them away. Moag was rich in metal, and Phyrexia would have stripped it. Moag was spared for the time being, and its oldest trees still remembered the warning thousands of years later.

For two more centuries Urza and Xantcha ran. They could not stay anywhere for long before the hunters found them. About 880 AR they were hiding on a harsh, frozen world when a hunting pack caught them. Both were terribly wounded. Urza walked blindly away between the worlds, with no idea where he was going.
They came out in a place of golden light.

It was a small plane where the sky was a sunrise that never ended and came from all directions at once. There was no ground. Great islands of meadow floated through the air, each on its own path. Angels flew between them.

This was Serra's Realm, and its maker lived in it. Serra was a planeswalker of great age and power. Long before, she had visited Dominaria and made her first angels there, which is how angels bearing her name came to be summoned in the old tales of Corondor. Later she made this whole plane out of pure white mana, the magic of order, healing and light. She meant it as a refuge where nobody would ever suffer. She filled it with her angels and with human beings who loved her, and she lived among them in a palace of crystal and marble.

Xantcha had expected someone tall and distant. Serra turned out to be a plain, sturdy, pleasant-faced woman, who could have walked through any village without being noticed, except for the faint white light that flickered around her.

Serra healed Urza. It took five years, and she did it at some risk to herself. Xantcha had to be treated with ordinary medicines. She was Phyrexian in her flesh, and Serra's white magic would have killed her.

Urza learned two things in those years. He learned that a made plane such as Serra's cannot last unaided. It needs the constant care of its maker, or it slowly decays. And looking at this artificial world, he understood that Phyrexia was one too. Somebody had made Phyrexia. The Phyrexians must therefore have come from some other, natural world and been driven out of it.
Urza had a new plan. He would find that first world and learn where his enemy came from. The answer, which he did not learn for a very long time, was his own world.
Urza left Serra's Realm in peace. He did not know what he was leaving behind him.

The hunters had followed his trail. Phyrexia invaded Serra's Realm. The chronicle dates the invasion to about 2500 AR, long after Urza had gone, though other accounts say that it followed soon after he left. The angels fought the invaders and drove them out. It did not save the plane. The Realm was made of white mana, and the Phyrexians were creatures of black mana, the magic of death and decay. Their presence stained the fabric of the place, and the stain could not be removed.

Serra could not bear to live in it any longer. She proposed that everyone leave, took with her those who would come, and went away in sorrow. She left the Realm in the care of her chief angel, the archangel Radiant.
Radiant was proud, sharp-tongued and quick to judge, and she had none of Serra's mercy. What she did with the Realm, and how Urza came back to it, is told much later.
Serra wandered for a long time. Her own end, on a world called Ulgrotha, is also told later.

About 1500 AR Urza and Xantcha set out for the oldest world Urza had ever heard of, to ask their question there. The world is Equilor, which the very first chapter of this story described: a plane at the far edge of the Multiverse, so old that its people had already been seeking wisdom for a hundred thousand years.
Before they left, Xantcha gave Urza her heart, the one she had taken back from the Fane of Flesh. Whoever holds a newt's heart holds its life. It was her proof that she would never betray him.
Equilor is very far away. Even for a planeswalker the journey took far more than a thousand years. Urza and Xantcha were still on the road when the Ice Age ended.

chapters.title: Ixalan: The Night War

blocks.p: While Dominaria lay under ice, the plane of Ixalan had an age of darkness of its own. This chapter is the second about Ixalan. The first told of the Whispering War, and what it established is needed here.

Ixalan is hollow. At its centre is a great round chamber called the Core, with a small sun named Chimil floating in the middle and people living on the inner wall. Those people are the Komon Winaq, the Fifth People, the first humans of the plane. They hold Chimil to be their creator and her children, the Deep Gods, to be their guardians. Their dead stay among them as kindly spirits called Echoes. One god is an enemy: Aclazotz, a bat-like god who promises eternal life for blood. The Deep Gods defeated him and locked him away, and after that the Fifth People lived through a golden age of thousands of years, the Age of the Sun.
The chronicle gives only latest possible dates for what follows, so every year in this chapter means that year or earlier.
The Age of the Sun ended when visitors came from another world.

They arrived in ships. Each ship was a huge curved piece of dark metal, a shard shaped from a single casting. The ships hung in the sky of the Core, near the sun. A few days later one of them opened and let down a smaller vessel, and out of the vessel stepped a giant. He spoke the language of the Fifth People. He begged them to let his people shelter in their paradise.

These were the Fomori. They were grey-skinned giants with horns, with clawed hands as large as a human being, wearing armour the colour of rust. They were the people of an empire that had once reached across many planes. A scholar of much later times, who found its coin-shaped relics on world after world, called it the Coin Empire. The Fifth People came to call the giants the Kisik, a word that conveyed their terrifying looks and their greed for rule, or simply the Colonisers.

The plea for shelter was a way in. The Fomori took control of the Core and ruled it from their ships. More shard-ships arrived. One by one they took up places around Chimil, until they formed a complete shell around her. The sun was caged, and the Core went dark.
The darkness did a second harm. It cut the Fifth People off from the Deep Gods, who could no longer hear their mother or her people.

The sources differ on one point. The chronicle's short entry says that Aclazotz escaped his prison when the Age of the Sun ended, and that he began the war that followed. The fuller account speaks only of the Fomori. The words printed on one card suggest how the two fit together: the bat god laughed as the dark shards closed around the sun, and believed that his reign was about to begin.
The darkness lasted three hundred and twenty years, and the war against it is called the Night War.

The dead resisted first. The Echoes rose against the Colonisers, and then the living joined them. One name stands above the rest: Olanem Teq, a war leader who bore the title of the Nine Hundredth Moon. The title recalls the Thousand Moons, the company of champions that the god Ojer Axonil raised in the Whispering War. From a city called Oq'tinimit, Olanem Teq led raids on the Fomori's vessels and took Fomori agents prisoner. In the end the resistance carried the fight upward, to the cage around the sun itself.

Chimil had been fighting too. All that time she had lashed the inside of her cage with her power. The shards were weakening. They tried to mend themselves by some unknown magic and could not keep up. The raids across the Core had damaged the systems that the Fomori depended on. Then warriors of the Fifth People landed on the shards themselves and attacked the most important ones.

It was enough. Chimil broke one shard, then a second, and then the whole cage came apart. The substance of the sun, a shining metal called cosmium, burst outward. It blasted the Fomori away. The human warriors who stood on the shards at that moment were not destroyed by it. It filled them, and changed them into beings half divine. They were the first angels of Ixalan.
With the cage broken, the Deep Gods could hear their mother's cry and their people's prayers again, and they came.

The Fomori were driven out of the Core. The wreckage of their ships stayed in orbit around the sun, where it mixed with the spilled cosmium and became a glittering, dangerous reef. Other Fomori ruins and half-built works were left scattered over the Core. The Fifth People studied the war machines the giants had left and learned a good deal about armour from them.
According to the chronicle, the end of the Night War, in 2263 AR or earlier, was also the moment when Aclazotz was imprisoned once more.
The Coin Empire itself collapsed at some later time, on all its worlds, for reasons nobody has discovered.
The war had taught the Fifth People how large their world was. Below the Core, which to them means outward, lay a vast depth of caverns, and beyond the caverns an outer surface under an open sky.

An age of exploring followed, and then an age of settling. Over centuries, hundreds of thousands of the Fifth People left the Core. They built cities in the caverns, and some went on to the surface. Two other peoples are said to have fought beside them in the Night War and gone out with them: the merfolk, and the Malamet, a people of cat-folk.
Those who stayed behind in the Core began to call themselves the Oltec.
Many centuries after the exodus began, sickness broke out in Topizielo, one of the great human cities of the caverns.

The Oltec scholars in the Core studied it and found that it was a fungus, spread by spores, and far too sophisticated to be natural. It may have been a living relic of the Fomori, let loose outside the Core long before. This fungus was the beginning of the mycoids, which are walking fungal creatures. In time they came to share a single mind, and that mind is the Mycotyrant.

Nothing in the caverns could stop it. The people of the caverns and the Oltec fought the spread together and failed. Whole cities and cultures were lost, first to the infection and then to mycoids that grew larger and more cunning with every generation.

The survivors fled in the only direction left, upward and out. They came into the open on the surface, on the continent that would later be called Ixalan. They were the distant ancestors of the people who founded the Sun Empire.
Behind them the Oltec sealed every entrance to the Core, to keep the fungus out. The Deep Gods set angels to guard the golden gates. The chronicle dates the sealing to 2563 AR or earlier.

From that time the two halves of humanity on Ixalan lost each other. The people of the surface forgot that the Core existed. The Oltec lived on beneath their sun, shut in, for two thousand years. The Mycotyrant spread through the dark between them. And Aclazotz, by the chronicle's account, lay imprisoned once more, waiting for somebody to come and let him out.

chapters.when: 1943 AR or earlier, to about 2563 AR

chapters.title: The Eternal Ice
sources: MTG Wiki, "The Eternal Ice" (the novel by Jeff Grubb, 2000)
MTG Wiki, "Summit of the Null Moon"

blocks.p: This chapter tells how the Ice Age ended. It takes place on Terisiare, the continent of the Brothers' War, in the last thirty-five years of the ice.
These are the pieces on the board.

Kjeldor is the human kingdom in the east, founded five hundred years earlier by refugees from the doomed city of Storgard. Its capital is Krov. Balduvia is the nation of steppe clans to its north-west. The two have been at war on and off for four hundred years.

Tresserhorn is a grim fortress in the far north, standing over a bottomless pit. It was built on the ruins of the Conclave of Mages, the school that the wizard Ith tore down in 430 AR. In those ruins lies a ruby ring. The ring holds the spirit of Mairsil the Pretender, the usurper who caged Ith, who died in that fall.

Jodah is the man who brought Mairsil down. He bathed in a Fountain of Youth as a boy and has not aged since. He is now about two thousand five hundred years old and looks twenty-five. He leads the hidden school of magic in the west, the School of the Unseen, with the title Archmage Eternal. About once a century the weight of his memories begins to drive him mad. He then performs a ritual with his magic mirror: he stores his memories in it, empties his mind, and takes the memories back with the pain gone.

Several planeswalkers are trapped on Dominaria and its eleven neighbour planes by the Shard of the Twelve Worlds. Freyalise, born in Storgard, is the patron of the elves and wants to break the Shard. Leshrac and Tevesh Szat love the cold and have been making it worse. Faralyn is a schemer, served by his apprentice Ravidel and by the Elder Dragon Chromium Rhuell. Taysir and Kristina are lovers who try to help people.

The main source is a novel of 2000, The Eternal Ice by Jeff Grubb, with a comic series of 1995 that told part of the same story differently. Both are followed here through the encyclopaedia's summaries.

parts.h: The soldier in the blizzard (c. 2900 AR)

blocks.p: Kjeldor's most admired general in those years was Márton Stromgald. About 2900 AR Stromgald sent a squad of soldiers to wipe out what he said was a weak band of goblins. The goblins turned out to be well armed and in their prime. They slaughtered the squad.

One soldier ran away and lived. His name was Lim-Dûl. He was a wiry, fox-faced man of no importance. Fleeing, he was caught in a blizzard and came close to death. He stumbled into a cave near Tresserhorn, among the last remains of the Conclave of Mages. In the cave he found a ring with a great ruby, and he put it on.

The ring saved his life, and it took a share of him in exchange. Mairsil had been shut in that ruby for nearly two and a half thousand years. He gave the soldier a copy of his own magical power. He also began, slowly, to take the soldier over. The two became something like one being, part Lim-Dûl and part Mairsil. Lim-Dûl now had the powers of a necromancer, a mage who raises and commands the dead.

He made himself master of Tresserhorn. The fortress's ancient undead keeper, Chaeska, served him as his chief lieutenant. From Tresserhorn Lim-Dûl began to raise an army of walking corpses, and he grew into a power in the north. Kjeldor and Balduvia each regarded him as a lesser danger than the other. Lim-Dûl encouraged them to think so.
Lim-Dûl soon had a master of his own. The planeswalker Leshrac came to him and gave him still greater power, and in return took command of him.

Leshrac wanted an army, and he wanted it for a purpose that had nothing to do with Terisiare. The Shard that imprisoned the planeswalkers had one flaw. A plane called Shandalar drifts through the Multiverse in an unusual way, and its path carried it across the wall of the Shard, so that it was sometimes inside the twelve worlds and sometimes outside. Shandalar was also extraordinarily rich in mana. Leshrac and his ally Tevesh Szat planned to cross to Shandalar when it next came within reach, conquer it, and ride it out of their prison. Lim-Dûl's dead were to be the invasion force.

In the generation before the end, Kjeldor was weak and divided. Every decision had to pass through the monarch, and the factions around the throne fought one another for influence: the merchants of Krov, the army and the mages.

About 2910 AR a wizard named Zur broke with the kingdom's magical establishment altogether. He was a rival of Gustha Ebbasdotter, the royal mage. He was exiled for his mad attempts to make himself live for ever, and he came back with a following of mages and soldiers and made war on his homeland. Jodah helped to defeat him. Zur went off into the frozen wastes and vanished. Most people believed him dead. He was not, and he had found what he was looking for.

In those same years the kingdom was governed for a time by a regent, Lord Rothchild, from the southern city of Jornstad, until a queen took the throne. In 2933 AR that queen died and left the crown to her son, a young red-haired man named Darien.

About 2910 AR a girl named Jaya Ballard was born somewhere on Terisiare. She grew up a thief on the streets. One day she broke into the private rooms of the Archmage Eternal to rob him, and was caught. Jodah saw that she had a gift for magic and let her study at his school. Jaya learned a few spells and then left to make her living as a task mage, a wizard for hire who does small magical jobs for pay. Her magic was fire, and she was good at it, and she had a sharp tongue.

Two of her early adventures are recorded. About 2930 AR two poachers killed a lhurgoyf and stole its eggs. A lhurgoyf is a huge and fearsome beast of the frozen north. Its mate went on a rampage through a Kjeldoran village, and it was Jaya who stopped it.

Jaya also did a service for Kolbjörn, an elder of an order of druids. He rewarded her with an amulet that could summon the planeswalker Freyalise. Kolbjörn had an adopted daughter, an elven girl named Kaysa, born in 2924 AR. Kaysa bore a crescent-shaped birthmark, which marked her out as a future leader of the druids.
In 2934 AR the time came round for Jodah's ritual of memory. In the middle of it he vanished.

He had been sold. His second in command at the school, a mage named Gerda Äagesdotter, wanted his post. Her cousin was Gustha Ebbasdotter, the royal mage of Kjeldor. The two women wanted to be the leading mages of the continent, and they handed Jodah over to Lim-Dûl. Gustha kept his mirror.

Jodah woke in a cell in Tresserhorn with his mind in fog. Lim-Dûl kept him drugged with the pollen of a certain flower, which clouds the memory. He told Jodah that he was not really Jodah at all. He was only a magical copy that Lim-Dûl had summoned, and if he disobeyed he would be sent back to nothing. Jodah believed it.

The part of Lim-Dûl that was Mairsil enjoyed this very much. The enemy who had destroyed him was now his servant. Jodah was put to work in the fortress library on two questions. The first was the nature and position of the wandering plane Shandalar, which Leshrac wanted to know. The second was Lim-Dûl's own secret: how to kill a planeswalker. Lim-Dûl wanted to be free of Leshrac.

In the fortress Jodah met General Márton Stromgald. Lim-Dûl had killed the general who once sent him to die and had raised him as a walking corpse to serve him. Stromgald told Jodah that the necromancer kept near him only the people he hated most, so that he could punish them.

Leshrac found out what his servant was studying. Before Jodah's eyes he punished Lim-Dûl by reshaping him. He made horns sprout from the necromancer's forehead, to remind him that he was a beast of burden.

Jaya Ballard came back to the school to visit her old teacher and found him gone. Nobody could say where, and a few people plainly did not care. Jaya followed the trail to Tresserhorn, broke in, and found him.

She told him who he was. She destroyed the flower whose pollen was drugging him, and the two of them escaped, though Chaeska nearly stopped them. Jodah cut off one of Chaeska's arms and set him on fire.
Then Jodah collapsed. With the drug gone, two and a half thousand years of unpurged memory came down on him at once, and he began to rave. Jaya used Kolbjörn's amulet and summoned Freyalise.

Freyalise knew what was wrong with him and how to cure it. Jodah had once helped her through her own madness. She still wanted payment. She asked for the use of his mirror and of the resources of his school, for a great work she was preparing. Jaya had no right to promise either. She promised both.

Jaya went to Krov, broke into the royal mage's laboratory, and stole the mirror back. In doing so she discovered who had betrayed Jodah. She brought the mirror to the Balduvian camp where Jodah lay, and with it she restored his mind.

The Balduvians asked for something in return for their shelter: Jodah's help against Lim-Dûl. Their leader was a chieftain named Lovisa Coldeyes. Jodah answered that he could not beat the necromancer alone, and that nobody could. Kjeldor and Balduvia would have to do it together.

He and Jaya went to Krov to persuade the young King Darien. It looked hopeless. Refugees were pouring in from the countryside with tales of the walking dead, and the city still believed that the barbarians were the real enemy.

Jaya, nosing about the capital, found something worse. Many of Kjeldor's officers thought the new king weak and longed for a strong leader like the lost Márton Stromgald. They had formed a secret brotherhood, the Knights of Stromgald, and the army's supreme commander, Avram Garrisson, was at its head. They were about to overthrow the king. Jaya warned Jodah, the royal mage Gustha, and the army's second in command, a general named Varchild. Between them they stopped the coup.

Then the truth came out. The Knights of Stromgald had been Lim-Dûl's creatures from the start, founded through the dead general whose name they bore. The necromancer had sent them brandy to toast their victory. It was poisoned. Every one of the plotters died, rose again as a walking corpse, and marched north to Tresserhorn.

That convinced Kjeldor. Darien took firm hold of his kingdom and made the alliance with Lovisa Coldeyes. Jodah punished Gerda Äagesdotter in his own way. He left her in charge of the School of the Unseen, the post she had betrayed him to get, with Freyalise about to arrive at its gates demanding everything it had.

Lim-Dûl's armies came down into Kjeldor. The hinterland was emptied. Among the people who fled south into Fyndhorn were the druid Kolbjörn and his daughter Kaysa. The dead did not mind the winter, and every soldier they killed joined them. The allies held on until spring.
There was one more piece of bad news. An old Kjeldoran artificer, Arcum Dagsson, had built a machine for predicting the weather, and it told him that the Ice Age was getting worse.

parts.h: The Summit of the Null Moon

blocks.p: While the armies gathered, the planeswalkers held a meeting of their own.

Faralyn called it. He invited every planeswalker trapped in the Shard to come and work out together how to pierce it. The meeting place was the Null Moon. Dominaria has two moons, and the second is not a natural one. It is a hollow artificial sphere that the Thran launched into the sky in the last days of their empire, as an earlier chapter told.

Those who came were Faralyn with Ravidel and Chromium Rhuell, Leshrac, Tevesh Szat, Freyalise, Taysir and Kristina. Kristina had a hope of her own for the meeting, a treaty among all the planeswalkers of the Shard.

Three of them had a different plan. Faralyn, Leshrac and Tevesh Szat had worked out that the death of a planeswalker releases an enormous burst of energy, and that such a burst could punch a hole in the Shard long enough for someone to slip through to Shandalar. The summit was a trap. Its purpose was to set the planeswalkers fighting until one of them died.

There was plenty to work with. Kristina had killed the dragon Arcades Sabboth in her duel with Leshrac a century before, and Chromium Rhuell was that dragon's brother. The three plotters stirred the quarrels up, and the meeting turned into a battle.
No planeswalker died. Two others did. Chromium Rhuell, the Elder Dragon who had served one planeswalker after another for thousands of years, was killed. So was the apprentice Ravidel.

Their two deaths released energy enough. Faralyn used the life of his own apprentice as his way out and left the body behind. The way to Shandalar was open for him, for Leshrac and for Tevesh Szat. Freyalise fought Szat on one of the twelve planes, a world of islands called Azoria. The fight destroyed every island on that plane. Freyalise was left for dead and blinded.

Taysir and Kristina joined their magic and brought Ravidel back to life. He came back as a planeswalker. He was not grateful. They had saved him and not Chromium, the only friend he had ever had. His teacher had spent his life like a coin. Ravidel went mad with grief and swore undying hatred against Kristina. He becomes one of the great villains of the following age.

The plotters' escape went badly. Shandalar had a guardian planeswalker of its own, Kenan Sahrmal, who called up a dragon of the stars and killed Faralyn almost at once. Leshrac found that he needed his army after all, and went back for it.
Tevesh Szat stayed behind a little longer too, and Freyalise made sure that he would regret it. She could not fight him again herself. She chose a champion.

Jaeuhl Carthalion was a young and untested knight of Kjeldor. He belonged to the family of the Lion of Carth, and he was a descendant of the Jason Carthalion whose arrow had made Freyalise a planeswalker five hundred years before. The family had come down in the world since. Freyalise armed Jaeuhl with a sword, a staff and other magical gear and sent him against the destroyer of Sarpadia.

Jaeuhl fought his way through Szat's undead servants and found the thing he needed, a charm called the Amulet of Quoz. With the amulet he banished Tevesh Szat from Dominaria and flung him to Shandalar. There the guardian Kenan Sahrmal defeated Szat a second time.

In the spring of 2934 AR the allied army waited at the mouth of a pass through the Karplusan Mountains, north of Krov. Lovisa Coldeyes led the Balduvians and General Varchild led the Kjeldorans. With them stood Jodah, Jaya Ballard and the royal mage Gustha Ebbasdotter.
The day before the battle Freyalise appeared in the camp and asked for the last of her payment, the loan of Jodah's mirror. Jodah disliked it, and he handed it over.
Then the dead came out of the north, far outnumbering the living.

Gustha Ebbasdotter met Avram Garrisson, the traitor commander, now a walking corpse wrapped in protective magic. She spent every spell she had against him to no effect, and then the dead swarmed over her. She had betrayed Jodah, and she died fighting on his side. Varchild cut Garrisson down.

Jaya Ballard had to fight an old friend, a Kjeldoran knight of the air named Belenda Danisdotter, who had helped her escape from Krov and had since been killed and raised. Jaya hesitated, and then destroyed her.
Lovisa Coldeyes and her warriors charged too far ahead and were about to be cut off. Jodah summoned an order of knights out of Kjeldor's legendary past to stand around her.

Chaeska, the keeper of Tresserhorn, came against Jaya. He had replaced his lost arm with the sword arm of the dismantled Márton Stromgald. He knew that Jaya's magic was fire, and he was warded against fire. Jaya reached for a different magic, the blue magic of water, and cast a simple spell that sends a summoned creature back where it came from. Chaeska vanished from the field and reappeared in the halls of Tresserhorn.

Last of all Jodah faced the necromancer. By now Mairsil had the upper hand in that shared body, and he told Jodah who he was: the Pretender, whom Jodah had burned twenty-five centuries before. The duel was long and savage. It ended with both men drained of every spell and barely standing.
Before Jodah could finish it, Lim-Dûl called on his master.

Leshrac came, and he was furious. He had got through to Shandalar and needed his army there, and he found that his servant had thrown it away in a war against two nations Leshrac cared nothing about. He cut off Lim-Dûl's hand. Then he tore the rest of him apart, and kept him alive throughout so that he would feel it. He rolled what was left into a living ball of flesh, promised to remake it into a better servant, and carried it off the plane.

With their master gone the dead began to fall where they stood. The battle was over. It was the last battle of the Ice Age. Because Leshrac had stood behind one side and Freyalise behind the other, it is also called the Battle of the Planeswalkers' Proxies.
The severed hand lay on the field with a ruby ring still on one finger. Jaya Ballard picked it up as a trophy. She did not know what the ring was.

Freyalise had learned from the summit what would break the Shard: a burst of energy. She had learned from Lim-Dûl's stolen research where a large enough burst could be had. When the wandering plane Shandalar crossed the wall of the Shard, it sent out great waves of energy. Freyalise meant to catch that energy and use it for a second Sylex Blast, turned inside out, to undo what the first had done.

She invited Jodah to the forest of Fyndhorn to see it done. She had built a vessel for the spell, the Ice Cauldron, as a copy of the bowl that Urza used on Argoth. Into it she placed Jodah's mirror, to show the land its true self. About two dozen druids, elves and humans stood around her, with Kolbjörn and his daughter Kaysa among them.

Jodah saw at once what she had not said. A blast as great as the first would wreck Dominaria as the first had. Freyalise agreed. That, she said, was why he had been invited. All over Terisiare there were hidden refuges called safe havens, magical refuges that mages had long used to shelter in and to travel by, and Jodah knew them better than anyone. If he opened them all at once, the force of the spell could be vented through them to every corner of the continent and thinned out. There would still be floods and worse. Jodah had no real choice, and he did it. Every safe haven was burnt out. The one above Tresserhorn blew the mountainside down onto the fortress.
The spell worked. The Shard of the Twelve Worlds, which had enclosed Dominaria for two and a half thousand years, was destroyed. The Ice Age was over.

The older comic tells it differently. There the idea came from Kristina of the Woods during the summit, she and Taysir stood beside Freyalise at the casting, and the power came chiefly from the girl Kaysa and her birthmark, with the Ice Cauldron only held in reserve. The novel is the later version and is treated as the true one. Both agree that Freyalise cast the spell and that Kaysa was there.

Freyalise gave Jodah his mirror back. He could feel that the spell had changed it, and he never used it again. He was right to be wary. Before she returned it, Freyalise had placed an enchantment in it for a purpose of her own, which showed itself twenty years later.

One by one the planeswalkers left. For the first time in twenty-five centuries they could go where they pleased. Freyalise walked away between the worlds. Taysir wanted to go home to Rabiah and asked Kristina to use her power to help him through the barrier there. It would have meant both of them staying in Rabiah for ever. Kristina, who had the whole Multiverse open to her for the first time in her life, would not. The two parted, and the embittered Taysir took Ravidel as his pupil.
Jodah and Jaya stood in a world where, suddenly, mortal wizards were the most powerful people left.
Jaeuhl Carthalion met the druid Kaysa through Freyalise, and they later married. Kaysa became the leader of her order.

Far away, two witches named Tayva and Loria lost most of their powers when the spell went off. They fled north, carrying with them a dark spirit shut up in a severed head. The chronicle records it and says no more.

Dominaria was open again. That was good news for the planeswalkers. It was also good news for Phyrexia. For some two and a half thousand years the Shard had kept Yawgmoth's servants out of the world they meant to conquer. Now the door was open, and Urza, the one man who knew what was coming, was far away at the edge of the Multiverse and did not yet know it.
And the ice began to melt.

chapters.title: The Flood Age
sources: MTG Wiki, "The Shattered Alliance" (the novel by Jeff Grubb, 2000)

blocks.p: In 2934 AR the planeswalker Freyalise cast the World Spell. It broke the Shard that had sealed Dominaria off from the Multiverse, and it ended an Ice Age of two and a half thousand years. The age that follows is called the Thaw. Its first sixty-six years are the Flood Age, and they have other names too: the Age of Storms and the Age of Plagues.
This chapter stays on Terisiare, the continent of the Brothers' War, and covers the first twenty-two years. The people in it are those of the last chapter.
Jodah is the ageless Archmage of the School of the Unseen, the hidden school of magic in the west. He owns a magical mirror that Freyalise borrowed for her spell and returned changed.

Jaya Ballard is his former pupil, a mage of fire who works for hire. After the great battle against the necromancer Lim-Dûl she picked up his severed hand as a trophy. A ruby ring was on one of its fingers. The ring holds the spirit of Mairsil the Pretender, Jodah's enemy of twenty-five centuries, mixed now with something of Lim-Dûl.

Kjeldor is the human kingdom of the east, under young King Darien. Balduvia is the nation of steppe clans beside it, under the chieftain Lovisa Coldeyes. The two beat Lim-Dûl as allies after four hundred years as enemies.
The sources are the novel The Shattered Alliance by Jeff Grubb and the stories written for the card set Coldsnap, by way of the encyclopaedia.
Four great glaciers had lain on Terisiare for thousands of years. Now they melted, within a few decades.

The ice had ground the land down beneath it. Where there had been hills, valleys and whole mountain ranges, it left low, scraped ground, and the meltwater poured across it. A new sea formed in the middle of the continent. It drowned the great desert where Urza and Mishra had dug for Thran machines, and it drowned the fortress of Tresserhorn. It is called the Sea of Laments. Terisiare broke up into six large islands and many small ones, and it has been called the Terisian Isles ever since.

The forest of Fyndhorn, where the World Spell had been cast, went under the sea. So did the coastal city of Kelsinko, in spite of a band of mages led by Jaya Ballard who spent years trying to save it. The lobster-like homarids who had destroyed the merfolk empire of Vodalia long before now spread into the new waters. The people of Terisiare called them viscerids.
Warmth brought sickness. With no cold to check it, plague spread across the south, and the Kjeldoran capital Krov was hit worst.
There was another side to it. The steppes of Balduvia, which had been frozen hunting grounds, became rich farmland. Kjeldor's lands were sliding into the sea while Balduvia's turned green.

The elves and druids of Fyndhorn had to find a new home. Their leaders were Kaysa, the young Elder Druid who had stood beside Freyalise at the World Spell, and the knight Jaeuhl Carthalion, the man who had banished the planeswalker Tevesh Szat. The two had married. With knights of Kjeldor and with Jaya Ballard for company, they led the survivors of Fyndhorn across the water to the forest island of Yavimaya.

Yavimaya was the forest where the refugees from Argoth had settled long before. It was not welcoming. The forest had a will of its own, and after the World Spell its heart woke and began to kill the thinking creatures who lived in it, elves, humans and a people of intelligent gorillas alike, with strangling vines. Jaeuhl destroyed a Phyrexian war machine there, left over from some ancient time. Kaysa was carried off by a gorilla shaman. She talked a gorilla chieftain into an alliance instead, and gorillas, elves and humans together cleansed the Heart of Yavimaya. The newcomers made their peace with the forest. Jaya helped to deliver Kaysa's child, the next of the line of Carth.
Yavimaya's guardian spirit is named Multani. He is a being of the same kind as Titania of Argoth, and he becomes important when Urza comes home.
The alliance of Kjeldor and Balduvia did not survive its victory well.

About 2945 AR a Kjeldoran force and a Balduvian one met in a mountain pass called Balesh. On the Balduvian side an orc general, Groth Jonar, commanded the orc clans, and he had been saddled with a human mage named Elkan. Over Jonar's objections Elkan brought in goblins. Just before the fighting Elkan let slip that he meant to get the orcs killed. Jonar answered in his own way. He trapped the goblins between the two armies as a distraction, fell on the Kjeldoran knights and broke them. Then he called a truce, ran Elkan through with his sword, and let the surviving knights go home, keeping only their banner. It was his punishment for Balduvia as much as for the mage.

The worst of the trouble came from one person. Varchild was the Kjeldoran general who had led her country's army in the great battle. She hated the Balduvians. She had obeyed her king and fought beside them, and she never forgave it.

In 2949 AR Varchild and her whole troop were reported killed by orcs in the mountains. She was alive. She used her supposed death to gather a private army from among the poor, first a militia and at last a real war band. With it she raided the Balduvians year after year. The Balduvians naturally believed that Kjeldor was attacking them, hungry for their new farmland.

A small tale of about 2950 AR belongs to those years. A young apprentice named Damon completed his training as a wizard, and killed an agent of the Knights of Stromgald who attacked him. The Knights of Stromgald were the Kjeldoran officers who had plotted against their king and been poisoned and raised as walking dead by Lim-Dûl. They had outlasted their maker and were still at large.

Twenty years after the World Spell, Jaya Ballard turned up at the School of the Unseen. Jodah had not seen her since the battle. She showed him a blackened, shrivelled hand, the hand of Lim-Dûl. She said that she had found it in a market in the city of Soldev. One finger was missing. It was the finger that had worn the ruby ring.
If the ring was loose in the world, Mairsil was loose. The two set out on Jaya's aesthir, a giant bird of the north, to find it.

They went first to Tresserhorn. Lim-Dûl was not there. His old keeper Chaeska still held the fortress, and to give the dead something to rally to he had built a figure of corpse-flesh to sit on the throne, which he called the Lord of Tresserhorn. Outside the walls the undead Knights of Stromgald had been besieging the place for twenty years, since they considered themselves Lim-Dûl's true heirs. Jodah had to destroy the false lord when it attacked him, and he left Chaeska alone to mourn it. He noticed one odd thing. The bottomless pit beneath the fortress was gone.

Jodah had left the school in the charge of Gerda Äagesdotter, the deputy who had once betrayed him. While he was away some students found a cloud of black mana in the school's cellar. Gerda knew what it was, and said nothing. Twenty years earlier Lim-Dûl had offered to take Jodah off her hands on one condition: that she look after his bottomless pit. The pit was now under the School of the Unseen.

Looking for the ring, Jodah and Jaya went to the Balduvians. Lovisa Coldeyes told them about the raids. In a shaman's keeping they found Lim-Dûl's missing finger, worn as a charm, without the ring. Jodah used it to make a device that could tell whether a person was under the necromancer's influence.
They went on to King Darien. At court a monster of illusion attacked Jodah, and the device showed that Lim-Dûl had sent it. Then Jaya fell gravely ill.

Jodah took her to the Balduvian shamans for healing, together with a Kjeldoran princess named Alexandrite. They found Lovisa's settlement under siege by a Kjeldoran army. Lovisa's son Lothar and the princess flew for help on an aesthir. Jodah held the defences for days. Help came from both nations at once: a clan of Balduvians and an army sent by King Darien.
The besiegers fled, and Jodah came face to face with their commander. It was Varchild. His device showed that nobody was controlling her. She had done it all herself.

With her plot uncovered, Varchild was a traitor to Kjeldor and an enemy of Balduvia, and both nations turned on her together. Her soldiers melted away. And the common enemy did what the common victory had failed to do. Jodah sat down with Darien, Lovisa, Lothar and Alexandrite and laid the foundations of a union. In 2954 AR Kjeldor and Balduvia merged into a single nation. They named it New Argive, after the old kingdom on whose ground it stood. Zur the Enchanter's former followers, driven inland by the rising sea, were among its first citizens.
New Argive is still there at the end of the story so far.

The trail led at last to Soldev. Soldev was a city of artificers, almost independent of Kjeldor, built on the ruins of Storgard. Its leader was the old inventor Arcum Dagsson. Its pride was its steam beasts, great walking engines.

Soldev also had a secret society, the Adnates, who had the run of the vaults beneath the city. A stolen Soldevi guard machine had attacked Jodah on the road, and in that fight he found that his mirror no longer only reflected spells. It now threw them back with greater force. Jaya arranged a meeting with the Adnates. She also mentioned to Arcum Dagsson that Varchild's army had been seen nearby, and the old man took the steam beasts out of the city to hunt for it.

An Adnate guide led Jodah and Jaya down into the tunnels. They came into a great vault. In it stood eight huge machines of an ancient and hideous design. They were Phyrexian war beasts, ancient machines, and the models from which Soldev's steam beasts had been copied.
There Mairsil showed himself. He had been at Jodah's side the whole time. He was Jaya.

On the battlefield twenty years before, when Jaya picked up the hand, the spirit in the ring had moved into the deepest part of her mind. Over the following years it had made her its slave. The quest for the ring, the hand, the illness, the errand that sent the steam beasts out of the city: all of it was Mairsil's doing.
Jaya's hand drove a blade through Jodah's throat.

Mairsil needed the blood. Jodah was a descendant of Urza or of Mishra, and the war beasts answered to that bloodline. With Jodah's blood the Adnates woke the eight machines. The war beasts in turn took control of every steam beast in Soldev. Jodah was left to bleed to death on the floor of the vault.
In the last instant of his life Jodah threw his mind into his mirror, where time runs slowly.

He found Freyalise waiting there, or an image of her. She told him what she had done to the mirror. She had left a charge of power in it that would wake a planeswalker's spark. It was to be both his reward for his help and his punishment for the way he had spoken to her. Jodah had spent his whole life refusing to become the kind of being who plays with worlds, and she meant to make him one.

While she talked, Jodah thought it through. He had lived two and a half thousand years and had come close to death many times. If he had a spark, it would have woken long ago. He had none. But Freyalise could sense sparks. She must have sensed one near him and taken it for his. There was only one person it could be.
Jodah gathered what mana he could for a spell of healing, leapt back into his dying body and closed the wound with a moment to spare.
He climbed out of the vault into a ruined city. The machines were tearing Soldev apart. Over the wreckage stood Jaya, grown by magic to six metres tall, with Mairsil looking out of her eyes.

Mairsil offered his old enemy a choice. He ordered the war beasts to seek out the strongest source of black mana on the continent. That was the bottomless pit, under Jodah's school. The machines began to vanish, one after another, to reappear on the far side of Terisiare. Jodah could go and try to save his school and his pupils. Or he could stay and try to save his friend.
Jodah stayed. He fought the thing in Jaya's body, and at the right moment he smashed his mirror into her face.

The power that Freyalise had stored in it went into Jaya. Her spark woke. Jaya Ballard became a planeswalker, and the blaze of it burned every trace of Mairsil and Lim-Dûl out of her mind. Mairsil the Pretender had survived his own death by twenty-five centuries. This time he was gone. Only the ring itself remained, with a last sliver of the necromancer in it, and the ring passed on down the centuries to do one more harm.

Jaya carried Jodah across the continent in a single step. They were too late. The war beasts and steam beasts had appeared in the middle of the School of the Unseen and reduced most of it to rubble. The mages had destroyed some of the machines. Jaya, with a planeswalker's strength, destroyed the rest, and she cut the bottomless pit away from the world.

The school that had begun as the City of Shadows, the heir of the scholars who first discovered magic, was finished after nearly three thousand years. Gerda Äagesdotter gathered the survivors and led them east to found a new school, with herself as its founder at last. Jaya went with them for a while and then left Dominaria to see the Multiverse.
Jodah had lost his school, his mirror and the only friend who had known him for more than a few decades. He decided to disappear from history. He was not seen again for three hundred years.

In the same year, far away, two witches named Tayva and Loria betrayed each other. They were the pair who had fled north at the World Spell with a dark spirit in a severed head. The spirit claimed both their lives.
One group of people wanted the ice back.

The Cult of Rimewind was the order of ice wizards who had lived contentedly near the Ronom Glacier since about 750 AR. To them the Thaw was the end of the world. Their master, an old wizard named Gendrin, had a brilliant pupil, Heidar, whom he had found as a child out in the snow. Heidar was terrified by the warmth and by the refugees' tales of plague. He argued with Gendrin that the Thaw must be stopped, and in the argument he killed him, by accident. He took the old man's place without hesitating.

Heidar sent searchers across the land for anything that could turn back the Thaw. They found Phyrexian war machines buried in the ice of the glacier, left there since the Brothers' War. To wake them, Heidar made two alliances.

The first was with the Knights of Stromgald. Their leader was Haakon, an undead giant in black armour who had made himself lord of Tresserhorn. Haakon gave Heidar's scholars the run of Lim-Dûl's library, where they found the spells they needed. In exchange the knights were promised fresh corpses for their ranks.
The second was with Krov. That plague-ridden city had fallen under the rule of a vampire queen, Garza Zol. She lent Heidar her elemental mages, and he promised to help her break New Argive.
It worked. The Rimewind wizards brought the Phyrexian machines to life with hearts of enchanted ice, and their spells dragged winter back over the north.

Lovisa Coldeyes led a Balduvian force against Rimewind Keep. Heidar loosed the machines on it, and the battle became a massacre. Lovisa was taken alive and refused to surrender. Heidar had her executed.

The machines rampaged across the north. Haakon's dead marched on the city of Kjeld. The Battle of Kjeldor lasted four days, with the defenders' losses mounting each day. On the fourth day King Darien himself came into the fight and met Haakon in single combat. They fought from dusk until dawn. In the end Darien's own soldiers, afraid for their king, rushed the giant. Haakon cut many of them down before they overwhelmed him. With their lord destroyed, the dead army withdrew.

Then Heidar arrived with his machines. By this time the Phyrexian magic had driven him mad. He was attacking friend and enemy alike, and he had killed the woman he loved, Gendrin's daughter Lindra. Garza Zol saw that her ally had become a danger to her, and she already had assassins inside Rimewind. One of them killed him.

Without their master the machines ran wild. Help had come from an unexpected place. Elves and shamans of Yavimaya, the people of Kaysa, had come at New Argive's request. Their nature magic melted the ice that drove the Phyrexian beasts, and the beasts collapsed. Then the Yavimayans performed a ritual that ended Rimewind's winter for good.

The Thaw went on. The Order of Stromgald was finished. New Argive and Yavimaya were bound by friendship, and New Argive was secure. A relative peace settled over Terisiare, and New Argive kept its place there until Phyrexia came.

This chapter follows a loose thread from the end of the Ice Age onto another world. The thread matters because of where it ends: with an object called the Chain Veil, which one of the most important people of the story's last part picks up more than a thousand years later.

Four people left Dominaria for the plane of Shandalar in 2934 AR. Three were planeswalkers who had been trapped inside the Shard and wanted a way out: the schemer Faralyn, the night-loving Leshrac, and Tevesh Szat, the destroyer of Sarpadia. The fourth was Leshrac's servant, the necromancer Lim-Dûl. A necromancer is a mage who raises and commands the dead. Lim-Dûl had been a common soldier of Kjeldor until he found a ruby ring holding the spirit of the ancient wizard Mairsil. At the end of the last battle of the Ice Age, Leshrac cut off his hand, with the ring on it, tore his body apart, and carried what was left of him away.

One point of confusion should be cleared up first. The last chapter told how Mairsil, in the ring, took over Jaya Ballard and was finally destroyed in 2954 AR. This chapter is about the rest of Lim-Dûl, the part that Leshrac carried off. The two stories come from different books and do not fit together perfectly. Much later tales connect them by saying that a fragment of Lim-Dûl's essence stayed in the ring as well.
The story was told in a comic series and in the background of a computer game of the 1990s, and is followed here through the encyclopaedia.
Shandalar is a small plane with two peculiarities.

The first is that it wanders. Most planes hold a fixed place in the Multiverse. Shandalar drifts. During the age of the Shard its drifting carried it in and out through the Shard's wall, and that is why the trapped planeswalkers saw it as a door.

The second is that it is soaked in mana to a degree found nowhere else. Magic is so thick there that it has a kind of awareness of its own. Ordinary people use small spells every day as a convenience. Wizards of old made living creatures out of pure mana, and the descendants of those creatures, great dragons among them, still roam the land.

Shandalar had a protector, a planeswalker born there named Kenan Sahrmal. He was one of the few on his world who knew that other worlds existed. He also knew that Shandalar's happy isolation would end the day other planeswalkers noticed it.

Faralyn arrived first and declared the plane his own. He spent his first days there mocking his companions when he should have been learning. Shandalar's wild mana does not behave like mana elsewhere, and a mage who draws on it carelessly is in danger. Kenan Sahrmal summoned a dragon made of the plane's own magic. It poured so much mana into Faralyn that he burst.

Leshrac watched that happen and drew the right conclusion. On this world a planeswalker counted for less than he was used to. He had arrived with no army, because Lim-Dûl had wasted it on Dominaria. As a punishment he had shut what remained of Lim-Dûl up in stone.

Twelve weeks later Leshrac and Tevesh Szat met in the desert, with the stone prison between them. Both had found that their powers kept going wrong. Leshrac taunted his entombed servant and then, as it appeared, burned him to nothing.

Lim-Dûl was not destroyed. Shut in the stone for months with nothing else to do, he had studied the strange mana around him until he understood its rules. He slipped away and came out, with new powers, in a place called the Catacombs.

He then played a cruel game. Two sisters, Bani Bakur and Ravash Mog, were defenders of Shandalar and devoted followers of the absent Sahrmal. Lim-Dûl disguised himself, let them believe that he was their protector, and turned them against the other invaders. He used a magical jester's cap to work on their minds. He preyed on Bani's fears and on Ravash's doubts, and Ravash died of it. Bani, eaten up by guilt, swore to kill Tevesh Szat.

Szat had been brooding on the memory of Sarpadia, and had decided that Shandalar ought to be frozen as Dominaria had been. Bani's soldiers ambushed him. He was weakened by one of Lim-Dûl's spells, and he annihilated them all the same.

Then Kenan Sahrmal showed himself at last. Szat stunned him with a spell of darkness and was about to finish him when Leshrac came back with a warning: Lim-Dûl was alive and working against them both. Szat flew into a rage and attacked Leshrac. The two planeswalkers ended by fighting each other, and each of them, sick of a world where nothing worked as it should, gave up and left the plane.

That left Lim-Dûl. Sahrmal was badly weakened. As Bani swung her sword at the necromancer, Lim-Dûl cast a spell that exchanged his body with Sahrmal's. Bani's blade took the head off what had been her protector's body, while Lim-Dûl, wearing Sahrmal's shape, vanished.

Sahrmal did not die. His being escaped as his body fell. But it cost him nearly all the magic he had left. Shandalar believed that both its protector and its invader were dead, and it had peace for a few years.
Lim-Dûl spent those twelve years raising an army of the dead. In 2946 AR he came out with it, meaning to take the whole plane, as his master had once meant to.
City after city fell. After years of war only one was left, a city named Ardestan, and it was under siege.

Sahrmal was watching from a hidden sanctuary. He was too weak to fight, and he had been training two pupils to do it in his place. One was named Azar. The name of the other has been lost. Sahrmal told them to be patient. They were not yet ready.
Azar could not bear it. He could not sit and watch Ardestan die. He stole a spell from his master and went to the city alone.

It was a remarkable spell. It was made to seize the necromancer's spirit, lock that spirit inside a body, and then draw on the imprisoned spirit's power to raise a wall around the whole of Shandalar, a barrier like the Shard, which would keep every outside planeswalker away. Azar meant his own body to be the prison.
Lim-Dûl knew that he was coming and waited. He had survived his own beheading by moving his soul into another body, and he planned to do it again. This time the body would be Azar's.

Azar cast his spell. Lim-Dûl cast his in the same instant. Together the two spells did something that neither caster had intended. Both souls were locked inside Azar's body. The body fell limp and unresponsive, with the two spirits inside it fighting for control.

The wall around Shandalar had come into being. It is called the Great Barrier. It held only as long as Lim-Dûl stayed imprisoned. Sahrmal, who had arrived too late with his other pupil, grieved for Azar and buried the body in secret in a city of tombs.

Sahrmal finished training his remaining pupil. Then he poured the last of his own power into him and made him immortal, named him as his successor, and vanished. Nobody knows whether that last act killed him.

The pupil announced himself to the world as the Guardian, the immortal protector of Shandalar, and the people came to trust him as they had trusted Sahrmal. The Guardian founded five guilds of magic, one for each of the five colours of mana, to teach magic and to keep watch over its use. Each guild was led by a guildlord, chosen in a great contest whenever the last one died.

Inside the buried body the two souls fought for about two hundred years. Lim-Dûl won. He drove Azar's spirit out of Azar's own body, climbed out of the grave, and went to war for Shandalar a second time.

He had once come close to conquering the whole plane. This time he faced the Guardian and five guildlords at the head of five schools of trained wizards, and he was hopelessly outmatched. He killed the guildlord of the black guild. Then he was beaten.

The Guardian could not simply destroy him, because the Great Barrier ran on his imprisoned soul. So the Guardian took the necromancer's soul out of Azar's body and shut it into an object. The object was a veil for the face, made of fine golden chain worked so delicately that it hung like silk. It is the Chain Veil.
The Veil was hidden in ancient catacombs on Shandalar, built by a long-dead race of ogres called the Onakke. The Veil had its own dark history with them, which belongs to a later chapter.

One loose end remained. Azar's body, emptied now of both souls, had been steeped in the magic of death for two centuries. It got up by itself. It took the name Skavius Slan, called itself a lich lord, and claimed the empty seat of the black guild. It ruled that guild for ages.

Lim-Dûl slept in the Chain Veil for almost a thousand years. He was not entirely silent in it. In time his whispers reached a gifted young necromancer on Dominaria, a woman named Liliana Vess, and drew her towards it.

chapters.title: Ravidel and the Sages of Minorad

blocks.p: This chapter is about one man's grudge, and it sets up a war that breaks out more than a thousand years later.
