Ravidel was the apprentice of the planeswalker Faralyn. His one friend was the Elder Dragon Chromium Rhuell. In 2934 AR, at a meeting of planeswalkers on Dominaria's artificial moon, Faralyn and two others deliberately started a fight so that somebody would die and release the energy they needed to escape the Shard. Chromium was killed. So was Ravidel. Faralyn used his apprentice's death as his way out. The planeswalkers Kristina of the Woods and Taysir of Rabiah then brought Ravidel back to life, and he returned as a planeswalker himself. He hated them for it. They had saved him and let the dragon stay dead.
So Ravidel had four debts to collect: from Leshrac and Tevesh Szat, who had planned the killing with Faralyn, from Kristina, and from the world in general. Faralyn was already dead.

The story comes from comic books of the mid-1990s, some of which were never published, and it is told here from the encyclopaedia's account. It takes place largely on Corondor, the continent of the Blackblade tales.

After the World Spell broke the Shard, Kristina left Taysir. He wanted her to help him home to his sealed plane of Rabiah, which would have meant staying there for ever, and she would not give up the Multiverse.

Taysir was left bitter and alone. For reasons that puzzled those who knew him, he sought out Ravidel and took him as a pupil. Taysir was one of the mightiest planeswalkers alive, and under his teaching Ravidel's power grew enormously. Taysir hoped to mend the young man. He did not succeed.

Ravidel had a suggestion for his new master. Rabiah was sealed by the spell of the sorceress queen Nailah. Faralyn had pierced the Shard with the energy of a death. Taysir could do the same to Nailah's barrier. He need only kill a planeswalker or two, and there were two who richly deserved it.

Taysir let himself be persuaded. He hunted Leshrac and Tevesh Szat. Szat could not be found. Leshrac he ran down and defeated, on Dominaria, where Leshrac had come back and made himself master of a region. But when it came to the point, Taysir could not kill a beaten enemy in cold blood. He imprisoned Leshrac instead, in the worst place he knew, deep inside Phyrexia.
That left Taysir without the energy to go home and left Ravidel without his revenge. Ravidel began to go his own way.

Ravidel set out on a career of conquest among the planes, collecting magical objects and sharpening his skill at duelling. When he returned to Dominaria he went after the most dangerous object that world possessed.

The Golgothian Sylex, the bowl with which Urza ended the Brothers' War and began the Ice Age, had not been destroyed in its own blast. After the ice melted it came to light again, in the drowned ruins of a city on Terisiare.

Another planeswalker reached it at the same time. He was the Ash Warlord Embereck, a being of fire and one of the most powerful planeswalkers native to Dominaria. He and Ravidel fought over the bowl among the sunken ruins, and Embereck won.

Then Embereck made a mistake. Ravidel explained that he wanted the sylex only to avenge himself on those who had wronged him. Embereck was a creature of honour, and he sympathised. He let Ravidel take it.
In the far north of Corondor lies a sheltered valley called Minorad. After the Ice Age it became a refuge for survivors and then a seat of learning, with a great library.

In 3000 AR the wisest people of the continent gathered there to pool their knowledge and to begin a record of the new age. They declared that year the Year One of a new calendar. Among them were five planeswalkers, who had been inspired by the teachings of Taysir to swear themselves to the protection of the world. They were Kristina of the Woods, the Ash Warlord Embereck, Grenfell Mor of Golthonor, Altair of Coloni, who was called the White Mage, and Liana of Minorad.
Ravidel walked into the gathering with the sylex in his hands.

He threatened to use it. All the sages of Minorad would die, the last store of Corondor's learning would burn, and the new age would end on the day it began. He named his price, and it sounded modest. He wanted to be left alone. Whatever he chose to do on Dominaria from then on, none of them was to interfere.

Kristina was the leader of the five, and she may have felt some guilt for what Ravidel had become. She saw no way out but more bloodshed, and she persuaded the others to agree. Embereck alone refused. He vowed vengeance on the man he had armed and left the council.
Ravidel did not leave it at a promise.

He drove Kristina out of the White Woods of Corondor. He locked Grenfell Mor away in the sand seas of Golthonor. He laid a spell on Altair that stripped him of his planeswalker's powers, and Altair wandered Corondor for ages. Liana he handed over to his own apprentice, a man known as the Scarlet Vizier, who put her under a spell that controlled her mind.
Grenfell Mor had managed one thing before he was shut away. He had learned that the sylex could be destroyed, with the help of a certain pair of long daggers, and he hid the daggers.

The Scarlet Vizier, on his master's orders, worked his way into one of the great houses of Corondor, the House of Carthalion, and rose to be second in its command. This was the family founded by the Lion of Carth, the boy who summoned Dakkon Blackblade. It had produced powerful mages ever since. Ravidel meant to use its strength. The Vizier had a hope of his own that he kept from his master. He hoped that one day a child would be born to the Carthalions with a planeswalker's spark, and that the child would grow up to destroy Ravidel.

Ravidel now had the bowl, the silence of every protector Corondor had, and a servant inside its strongest family. He settled down to prepare, slowly, a revenge on everyone who had ever harmed him. Minorad was left in peace for almost thirteen hundred years. The reckoning comes in a much later chapter, and the child the Vizier hoped for is at the centre of it.

chapters.title: The Empty Quarter
sources: MTG Wiki, "Song of Time" (the novel by Teri McLaren, 1996)

blocks.p: After the floods, Dominaria had almost three centuries of comparative quiet, from 3000 to 3285 AR. Historians call the period the Empty Quarter, which is not quite fair. Several things happened in it that set up later stories, and one old threat from the Brothers' War was finally laid to rest.

The quiet was Dominaria's alone. On other planes these were years of catastrophe, and those have their own chapters after this one. So does the largest Dominarian event of the period, the return of Urza.
This chapter gathers the smaller Dominarian entries in order of time.

parts.h: The song of the hours (c. 3050 AR)

blocks.p: The first tale finishes a story begun during the Brothers' War, three thousand years earlier.

Almaaz is one of the Terisian Isles, the islands into which the floods broke Terisiare. Its people work magic by singing, and such a singer is called a song-mage. In 35 AR the song-mages of old Sumifa bound a monstrous cockatrice, the Beast of the Hours, inside a great clock beneath Mount Sarraza. Their leader, Samor the Collector, was ordered by Mishra to write a song that would release it and control it. Samor knew that a controlled Beast would mean the end of everything. He secretly wrote a different song. It would release the Beast and then use the crystals of a nearby valley, a place called the Chimes, to kill it. The traitor prince Porros murdered Samor before the instructions were complete, and was cursed into a wraith of sand, and buried Sumifa in his rage.
Porros was still there, as a wraith. He was called the Raptor, he had followers, and he still wanted the Beast.
In those years Almaaz began a new calendar of its own, counting from 3035 AR.

About 3050 AR an archaeologist named Javin was digging in the desert a little east of the new city of Sumifa. Javin was the last member of the Circle, the secret society that Samor had founded. He and his adopted son Cheyne were looking for the Collector's grave. They found old Sumifa itself, forgotten for three thousand years.
They also found a body carrying a small carved token, a totem, marked with symbols. Cheyne had owned one like it all his life and did not know why. He set out to learn who his parents had been.

In Sumifa an assassin tried to take Cheyne's head for the sake of his totem. A beggar tripped the young man at the right instant and saved his life. The beggar was Ogwater Rifkin, a small man with an enormous sunburnt nose, a drunk and a pickpocket. He had once been a song-mage. He picked Cheyne's pocket and then became his guide.

The two set out for the Chimes, with a map bought from a woman named Claria, a descendant of the Collector. Following them all the way came Riolla Hifrata, the chief criminal of Sumifa, who had once been Ogwater's lover and who worked for the Raptor.

Ogwater's lost power had depended on four magical gemstones, and on the road he gathered them again, one by one. He got the red one from an orc king. He got the white one from an elven healer, and the black one from Riolla herself. The blue one was the hardest.

It was in the hands of the last of the Rigida. The Rigida were the cruel people of living ice who had ruled Almaaz through the whole Ice Age. One was left, a queen named Drufalden. She had killed her two sisters and imprisoned her mother until the old queen died. She ruled from a palace of pure ice in the crater of a frozen volcano. The Thaw had nearly broken her power. The blue gemstone, a water sapphire, had restored it. With it she had frozen so much land that the sea itself dropped and the great river of the country nearly stopped, and the selkies of the river, a people who are part seal, were starving. Then Drufalden lost the stone while swimming, and it came to the selkies' king.

The selkie king gave the sapphire to Ogwater. Ogwater used it to sing a great spell that melted Drufalden's whole realm. The flood swept away the orc king's palace and set the river running again. The reign of the Rigida, which had begun in 450 AR, was over.

At the Chimes, Ogwater was forced to do what the Raptor wanted and release the Beast of the Hours. He used the music that Samor had left in a device of his own, his four gemstones, Cheyne's totem, the name-song of Claria and the humming of the crystal valley itself. The Beast came out of its clock and killed. Then Ogwater sang the rest of the Collector's song. The valley of the Chimes rang so violently that it shattered, and the Beast of the Hours was banished out of existence, back to wherever Porros had first called it from.

In the land of Kush, on another part of Dominaria, stood a city ruled by five noble Houses of fighting mages. Each House wore its own colour and kept its own school of magic. The mages of Kush tested their skill against one another in private, under a code of honour.

A man named Kuthuman changed that. He built an arena and turned the contests into a public festival, held once a year, with himself presiding as Grand Master of the Arena. The first Festival was held in 3071 AR, and Kush counted its years from it afterwards.
The Festival went on for a thousand years. Its end, and what Kuthuman really wanted from it, come much later in the story.

The floods reached other continents too. In Jamuraa, the glaciers of a range called the Blue Mountains melted almost at once. The hill tribes below were nearly wiped out by flash floods. Those who lived found that all the good soil of the hills now lay in the valley bottoms, which had become wonderfully fertile. Food became plentiful, the population multiplied, and a crowded city grew up there, called Tirras. It was shut in by mountains on two sides and by desert on the others, with a single river leading south.

About 3100 AR a ruler named Johan is recorded as Emperor of Tirras. The name returns. A Johan of Tirras, a horned and tattooed tyrant and a great mage of fire, later tries to conquer all Jamuraa by way of that river, and is opposed by a tiger warrior named Jedit Ojanen. That story is told in its place.

parts.h: The Sheoltun Occupation (c. 3234 to c. 3274 AR)

blocks.p: The Sheoltun Empire, the military state on the continent of Aerona, had by now conquered the whole of Aerona and the Spice Isles. It looked west across the sea to the Terisian Isles and saw the value of holding a town called Epityr, a mountain town of New Argive. About 3234 AR the empire invaded. One source gives the year as 3224. New Argive, the nation that Jodah had helped to found, was conquered and occupied.

It was the furthest that Sheoltun ever reached, and the occupation lasted about forty years. About 3274 AR Epityr rose in revolt. A song-mage of Almaaz named Thabit came to the rebels' help. He sang, and a flight of Serra angels answered him and fell upon the occupiers.

The Sheoltun were driven off the islands. The defeat began the empire's long collapse, and in the end the nation of Benalia rose in its place. The people of New Argive never forgot who had come to save them. The worship of Serra remains strong there, and it is one reason why Serra, who was a planeswalker and not a goddess, is prayed to on Dominaria as a goddess to this day.

chapters.title: Urza Comes Home
sources: MTG Wiki, "Planeswalker (novel)" (the novel by Lynn Abbey, 1998)
MTG Wiki, "The Shattered Alliance" (the novel by Jeff Grubb, 2000)

blocks.p: This chapter returns to the central thread of the whole story: Urza and his war against Phyrexia.

Urza was the artificer whose blast ended the Brothers' War in 64 AR. He became a planeswalker in that moment, with the two halves of the great powerstone for eyes. He learned that his brother Mishra had been taken and rebuilt by Phyrexia, the world of flesh and machine ruled by Yawgmoth, and he swore to destroy it.

About 650 AR he attacked Phyrexia with a dragon engine and was beaten. Yawgmoth touched his mind, and Urza has been going slowly mad ever since. He was hunted from world to world, healed for a time in the realm of the planeswalker Serra, and at last set out for the oldest world in the Multiverse to learn where Phyrexia came from.

His one companion in all that time was Xantcha, a small, human-looking creature whom Phyrexia grew in a vat to be a spy and who turned against her makers. The demon Gix, who corrupted Mishra, oversaw her making, and probably used some of Mishra's flesh in it. Urza still believes that she is a human whom Phyrexia stole. He carries her heart, the small object that holds her life, as her pledge.
Urza has been unable to return to Dominaria since the Shard of the Twelve Worlds closed around it. The Shard was a result of his own blast. In 2934 AR it was broken. He does not know that yet.
The source is again the novel Planeswalker by Lynn Abbey, in the encyclopaedia's summary.
Urza and Xantcha had been travelling towards Equilor since about 1500 AR. They arrived in 3110 AR.

Equilor lies at the far edge of the Multiverse, and it is the oldest plane known. The first chapter of this story described it. Almost everything on it looks worn and used up. Its mountains seem to have been flattened by nothing but time. There is one settlement, an unwalled town of graceful houses, reached by a road of grey stone so finely fitted that no grass grows between the blocks. A mist that never lifts lies over the land.

The people look human. They live for thousands of years. A toddler whom Urza and Xantcha met was more than eighty years old. They dress in silvery robes and live in rooms of pure white. Their minds cannot be read. They told Urza that he had found them only because they chose to let him. They have outgrown ambition, and even boredom.
In caves in the mountains live their elders, who seem to be spirits. Urza went up to them and stayed for nearly forty days at a time.

The elders knew a great deal about worlds they had never visited. They told Urza what the Shard was. That was why he could not go home. It was also why Phyrexia could not reach Dominaria. They told him too that the Multiverse is full of dark powers like Phyrexia, and that all of them fall in the end.
It calmed him. For the first time since Argoth, Urza believed that his war was over. His world was safe behind a wall that he himself had built by accident. He decided to stay on Equilor.

He could not stay quietly. He was amazed at how much the people of Equilor knew and astonished that they did almost nothing with it. Urza thought of many uses for their knowledge at once, and began to plan how to turn their ancient world into a paradise of machines. Most of the elders did not care for the idea.
They did not have to put up with him for long. They told him the rest of what they knew. The Shard had fallen. Dominaria lay open again, to him and to Phyrexia alike.
Urza and Xantcha left. The journey home took a hundred years.
They reached Dominaria in 3210 AR. Urza had been away for more than three thousand years.

The world he came back to had already been invaded, quietly. Phyrexia had taken up its old plan again. Its new sleeper agents were the improved kind: full-sized, male and female, each with a face of its own, growing older as people do, and with no memory of what they were until the day they were needed. They had worked their way into many organisations on Dominaria. Here and there they were starting small wars, to weaken the peoples who would one day have to resist an invasion.
Urza and Xantcha began to look for them.
They settled in a remote cottage in a mountain range called the Ohran Ridge, on Gulmany. Gulmany is one of the Terisian Isles.
Urza was no help to her for long.

The harm that Yawgmoth had done to his mind had been growing for two and a half thousand years. He sank into the past. He became so absorbed in the Brothers' War and in his brother's corruption that he no longer saw the present at all. He was eaten up with guilt over Mishra's death, and he had begun to hope that he could somehow find a way to undo it. He was giving up the defence of Dominaria for that hope.
Xantcha went on fighting alone for more than thirty years.
Then she had an idea, and it was a desperate one. If Urza would attend to nobody but Mishra, she would bring him Mishra.

On Gulmany lay a country called Efuan Pincar. It was tearing itself apart. A sect of religious fanatics, the Shratta, had burned the schools and libraries of its capital, and a force called the Red Stripes had been raised to stop them, and the fighting between the two had gone on for years.

In a market town Xantcha found a young slave who looked like Mishra. His name was Ratepe, and he was nearly eighteen. He was the son of a lecturer in philosophy in the capital, Pincar City, and had been born in 3226 AR. The Shratta had killed his whole family, and slavers had caught him afterwards. Xantcha bought him. She told him what she wanted. He was to pretend, to a mad and immensely powerful old man, to be that man's brother, dead for three thousand years.
Ratepe agreed. At his first sight of Urza's eyes, which were two glowing stones, he fainted.
Urza believed in him.

Ratepe turned out to have a gift that nobody had expected. The Weakstone, Mishra's half of the powerstone, was one of Urza's eyes. When Ratepe was near Urza, he could hear it. It whispered to him, and so he was able to show himself to Urza exactly as Mishra would have. More than once that saved his life and Xantcha's.
With his brother seemingly returned to him, Urza was shaken out of his stupor and began to come back to the present.

He had other help in that year. A stranger walked up through the mountains to the cottage. He looked about twenty-five. He was Jodah, once the Archmage Eternal, who had vanished from history three hundred years earlier after the destruction of his school. He was by now more than twenty-eight hundred years old, and he knew better than anyone what the weight of too many memories does to a mind.

Jodah was also family. He descended from Urza's wife Kayla through her grandson Jarsyl, so that he was a descendant either of Urza himself or of Mishra. He went into the cottage to tell the old planeswalker what had happened on Dominaria in the three thousand years of his absence. The chronicle says simply that Jodah visited Urza and brought him to his senses.
With his mind clearer, Urza turned to the sleepers, and he solved the problem as an artificer.

He designed a small machine in the shape of a spider. When it was set off, it gave out a sound pitched so high that no human being could hear it. To a sleeper agent the sound was deafening, and it went on until it killed. Ratepe helped to build the spiders. Xantcha carried them out and planted them around the cities where sleepers were at work.
They were all set to go off together, on the night when Dominaria's white moon, the Glimmer Moon, stood at its highest. In Efuan Pincar that night fell during a holiday called the Festival of Fruits.
In the course of that work Xantcha went down into a crypt in Pincar City. Something was living there. It was Gix.

The demon who had corrupted Mishra, who had fled the Sylex Blast through the portal at Koilos, was back on Dominaria and had made his lair under the sanctuary of the city's god. He recognised Xantcha. He made unsettling remarks to her about Urza, and she barely got away.

Urza announced that he would finish the business himself and gave his two helpers a few days of freedom. By now Xantcha and Ratepe were lovers, though a creature raised in the vats of Phyrexia understood little of the customs of love. Urza had noticed, and to their surprise he approved of the match between his brother and a Phyrexian, which suggests that by this time he knew what she was.

They used their holiday to go to Koilos. In the caves where the whole story had started, they learned the secret that Urza had crossed the Multiverse to find. The Phyrexians had not come from some other world. They were Thran: people of Dominaria, who had rebelled and been cast out five thousand years before the brothers were born. The enemy had been made at home. They decided not to tell Urza until the work was done.
On the night of the Glimmer Moon the spiders screamed. The sleeper agents died. The chronicle records that Urza killed every sleeper agent on Dominaria.

In Pincar City the sound brought Gix out. Urza attacked him. They fought briefly, and Gix fled across the sea to Koilos, the cave of the portal. Urza followed. He ordered Xantcha and Ratepe to wait outside, and went in alone.

It was a fight against the being who had taken his brother. At first neither could gain on the other. Then it came down to a contest of wills, in the form of a web of blue-white light stretched between the two of them, and Gix began to win it. He was cancelling the power of the two stones. The stones themselves started to pull loose from Urza's skull and drift along the light towards Gix.

Xantcha and Ratepe had not stayed outside. They saw that Urza was losing and understood what would follow. They went to either side of the web, and together they reached into the light to stop the stones.

It killed them both. It also broke the demon's concentration for one instant. The power rushed back into the Mightstone and the Weakstone, and it destroyed Gix. The Phyrexian who had once been a Thran rebel, the corrupter of Mishra, the overseer of Xantcha's making, was gone after five thousand years.
Urza woke after the battle and called for Xantcha. Nobody answered. He was the only one left alive.

He had lost the friend who had stayed at his side for three thousand years, and the boy who had been a brother to him for one. He thought for a while that he would have to carry on alone. Then he remembered that he still had her heart.

He made two decisions there. He would stop answering Phyrexia's moves and begin to lead the war himself. And he would find a way to reach into the past, to the time of the Thran, where the evil had begun.
Forty years later Urza founded a school on an island called Tolaria. Xantcha's heart he kept. In time he set it in the chest of a golem of silver, to be the core of its mind.

This short chapter visits a plane that the story has not been to before. Ulgrotha is a small, out-of-the-way world, far from Dominaria. Its name means garden, and its people later call it the Homelands. It was once very rich in mana and in living things.

Two people are introduced here who matter later: a girl named Ravi, and a boy who becomes the vampire Baron Sengir. The catastrophe at the centre of the chapter also touches two other worlds, Dominaria and a plane called Kamigawa, and the next chapter begins from that.
The story comes from the background written for the card set Homelands in 1995, as the encyclopaedia records it.

parts.h: The farm girl and the baron's son (c. 3180 AR)

blocks.p: The story begins on some other world, whose name is not given.
Ravi was a farmer's daughter in a village below a baron's castle. A swarm of plague-carrying rats overran the village and killed nearly everyone in it. Ravi's mother was among the dead.

At the funeral a richly dressed boy came up to her. He said that he was the baron's son, and he told her things that nobody in the village knew. The baron was practising black magic. He had brought the rats himself, because he wanted corpses for his work. He was trying to make himself immortal, and he had begun to do strange things to his son as well, such as making the boy sleep in a coffin.

The boy wanted his father dead. He believed that he would rule better. But by the law of that land a son who killed his father could not inherit. Somebody else had to do it. He taught Ravi a song, the one his father used to command the rats.

Ravi did not want to kill anyone. Then her father died of the plague too. She was alone in an almost empty village with nowhere to go. She sang the song, and the rats obeyed her, so readily that the boy was startled. Only a strong natural wizard could have done it.

That night the two children went into the castle with the swarm at their heels. In the baron's workroom Ravi faltered again, until she saw what lay on his table. It was her mother's body. She set the rats on him.

The baron knew the song as well as she did, and sang it back. The rats, pulled two ways, turned on the nearest other prey, which was the boy, and tore out his throat. The baron saw his son fall and broke off his song to hurl a spell at him. In that moment Ravi gave her order again, and the rats ate the baron.

She sent the rats away from the village for ever. Worn out, she opened a shuttered window to let in the morning. Behind her someone screamed. The boy was alive. His father's last spell had healed his throat and finished what the coffin had begun. He could no longer bear sunlight. He had become a vampire.

Crouched in the darkest corner, he told her that she must be a very powerful wizard to have beaten his father, and that he thought she would become a planeswalker one day. Only then did the two think to exchange names. She was Ravi. He had just become the new Baron Sengir.
They parted. Neither knew that they would meet again centuries later, on another world.

Ravi did become a planeswalker, with a magic rooted in living things and the land. She joined a band of young planeswalkers called the Tolgath. The Tolgath were at war with a rival group, the Ancients. Nobody now knows how long that war went on, or what it was about.
It reached its height on Ulgrotha, where the Tolgath had their citadel. The fighting grew so vast that one of the Ancients tore open a rift to a different world simply to draw more mana for spells.

Ravi's master had given her an object, a chime, and one instruction. She was to ring it only in the darkest of hours, and it would cleanse the world. He had also shown her a magical coffin in a place called the Basalt Spire, and told her to shelter in it afterwards. He did not tell her what the chime really did. Nobody who knew would have rung it.
In 3200 AR, hoping to stop the killing, Ravi rang the Apocalypse Chime.

The chime was tuned to the channels by which mana flows through Ulgrotha, and it shattered them all at once. A backlash of colourless fire swept the whole plane. Every planeswalker who did not flee in time was burned up. Almost every living creature died. The land itself died. Where the earth had once given mana, it now drank mana, and life with it, from anything that walked on it. That dead country is called the Dead Zone. Only the deep sea was safe.

One small region survived. It lay near the rift that the Ancient had opened, and the mana still pouring through from the other world kept it alive. Everything that happens on Ulgrotha afterwards happens there.

The damage did not stop at the edge of the plane. The shock was felt on distant Dominaria, and it weakened the walls between worlds, in particular the barriers between Dominaria and the plane of Kamigawa.
Ravi lay down in the coffin as she had been told. It protected her. Then she found that she could not open it. Her master had not told her how.

She lay there awake, unable to sleep or dream, aware of every second, for hundreds of years. Her magic had been the magic of living land, and she had felt every tie she had to that land torn away. Her mind did not survive it.

In the one living corner of Ulgrotha, the creatures and people who had been summoned to fight in the war were left stranded: warriors, healers, sorcerers of many kinds. Within twenty years they had begun to form a wandering people of the plains. Orcs and goblins that had lived through the ringing founded a kingdom in the Koskun Mountains about 3227 AR. The weather was violent and the seasons were unreliable. There was no shared written language, and within a few generations the Great War was only a grandmother's tale.

Ulgrotha's later history, with the coming of Baron Sengir, the planeswalker Serra and her husband Feroz, belongs to a later chapter. It is there that the Baron finds a coffin in the Basalt Spire and lets out the mad old woman inside it.

This chapter takes place on a plane that the story has not visited before. Kamigawa is a world modelled on old Japan, and it lies far from every other world in this story. It is connected to the last chapter by one thread. In 3200 AR, on the distant plane of Ulgrotha, a planeswalker rang the Apocalypse Chime. The shock travelled through the Multiverse and weakened a barrier on Kamigawa that should never have been weakened. A human ruler took advantage of it, and twenty years of war followed.
The chapter also ends by sending one man from Kamigawa to Dominaria, where his descendants do something that nobody else in the whole story manages.
The Kami War was told in three novels by Scott McGough, published in 2004 and 2005. This chapter follows the encyclopaedia's summaries of them.
Kamigawa has two halves. One is the world of flesh, where mortals live. The other is the world of spirit. The two together make up the plane.

The spirit world is the home of the kami. A kami is a spirit or small god, and on Kamigawa everything has one: every river and tree, every tool, every idea. Before the war, mortals did not think of the kami as living in another world at all. They believed that the spirits lived unseen among them and blessed those who led simple and devout lives. Now and then a kami would show itself, as a glow deep in a bamboo grove or a shadow that had nothing to cast it, and people built shrines and left offerings.

Between the two halves hangs a veil. Since everything on Kamigawa has a kami, the veil has one too. That kami is O-Kagachi, called the Great Old Serpent. O-Kagachi is the oldest of all the kami, as old as the plane, and the greatest. When it shows itself it has the shape of a serpent with eight heads, so large that it fills the sky, with eyes like stars. Without it there would be no difference between flesh and spirit.

The most powerful mortal on Kamigawa was Takeshi Konda. He had been born on the plains of Towabara and had proved a brilliant soldier. As a young man he built a great castle, Eiganjo, cleared the country of bandits, and brought a dozen warlords under his rule. As daimyo, which is the title of a great lord, he came to govern most of the plane.
By 3207 AR Konda was past fifty. He wanted the peace and greatness of his realm to last for ever, and he was prepared to change the nature of the world to make sure of it.

He had help. A wise fox-man named Eight-and-a-Half-Tails had done the research. Fox-folk are one of the peoples of Kamigawa, and they are called kitsune. Hisoka, the head of the great school of wizards at Minamo, lent his learning. So did the moonfolk, a tall, pale, aloof people who live in cities in the clouds, through their ambassador Meloku.

Behind the moonfolk stood a kami: Mochi, the Smiling Kami of the Crescent Moon, a small, cheerful and thoroughly treacherous spirit. Mochi wanted the veil weakened for reasons of his own, and he wanted his moonfolk to become the masters of the plane.

On the night when Konda's favourite concubine, Lady Yoshino, gave birth to his daughter, the ritual was performed. The birth itself was part of it. It released a surge of spiritual energy, and the ritual rode on that surge. Yoshino died in childbirth. The baby was named Michiko.

Konda broke through the veil, which the ringing of the Chime had already weakened. He reached into the spirit world and tore something out of O-Kagachi. It was the Great Serpent's child and at the same time its heart: the part of it that held its divinity and gave it purpose. Konda dragged that spirit into the world of flesh and locked it in the form of a disc of stone.

He set the disc on a stand in his innermost chamber. From that day he did not age. No kami could harm him. He had immense power. It cost him most of his own life-spirit and, by any decent reckoning, his honour. He spent more and more of his time shut in with the stone, staring at it and dreaming of the endless glory to come. His daughter he left to be brought up by a kitsune lady, Pearl-Ear, though he kept the girl closely guarded. She was tied to the stone by the hour of her birth, and he knew it.
The thing in the stone had no name. It is called That Which Was Taken.
O-Kagachi's rage moved the whole spirit world. The kami, who had blessed mortals since the beginning of time, turned on them.

Spirits began to appear in the world of flesh and to kill. Hardly anyone knew why. Konda's crime was a secret, and to ordinary people it seemed that their gods had simply gone mad. They fought back because they had no choice.

It was a war that mortals could not win. The kami were beyond counting. A spirit that was cut down in the world of flesh was not destroyed. It came back and fought again. The war went on for twenty years, through massacres and battles from the plains to the mountains to the forests, and Konda's people believed all that time that their lord was their shield against the wrath of heaven.
The man who ended it had no interest in ending it.

Toshiro Umezawa, called Toshi, came from a disgraced family and lived by his wits in a rotten swamp city. He was a masterless swordsman, a thief and a swindler. He also knew an almost forgotten kind of magic, which works by drawing written characters, called kanji. He often drew them with the point of a jitte, a short parrying weapon that he always carried.

In 3217 AR Toshi was one of a gang sent to kill an ogre sorcerer named Hidetsugu. The ogre killed all the rest. Toshi talked. He persuaded the ogre to swear a pact of mutual vengeance with him: anyone who harmed one of them would answer to the other. The pact became a brotherhood, the Hyozan Reckoners. In 3222 AR Hidetsugu took an apprentice, a young man named Kobo, who later swore the oath as well.

In 3227 AR, the twentieth year of the war, Toshi blundered into a secret meeting of moonfolk and had to kill two of them to get away. The moonfolk came after him. Hidetsugu advised him to seek the forest monks, and sent Kobo along as a companion.

Michiko Konda was twenty years old by then, the image of her dead mother. She had grown up inside the war and was tormented by her people's suffering. She wanted to know why the kami hated them, and she suspected that the answer had to do with the night of her own birth.

A friend of hers, a young wizard named Choryu, helped her to slip out of her father's castle. Choryu was secretly working for the wizards of Minamo and the moonfolk, and he meant to deliver her to them. That plan went astray, and Michiko's road led into the great forest of Jukai. There she met Toshi and Kobo.

All of them were captured by the snake-folk of the forest, the orochi. The orochi served one of the great kami, the Myojin of Life's Web, and they meant to kill the princess, believing that her death would end the war. When Toshi came to his senses he found Kobo hanging between two trees with his lungs full of water. Choryu had drowned him by magic.

Toshi got Michiko away to a cave. There the smiling kami Mochi appeared to them. He showed Michiko a vision of the night she was born, and so she learned what her father had done. Mochi also introduced Toshi to a far greater spirit.

The Myojin of Night's Reach is the great kami of darkness and secrets. She had found something in the war that she wanted to keep. With O-Kagachi distracted, the borders of Kamigawa itself had grown thin, and she had discovered that she could slip out between the worlds. She did not want the war to end. She wanted the stone kept away from the Great Serpent for as long as possible, and she needed a mortal to do it.

Toshi was cornered, with the orochi closing in. He took her blessing, though on terms rather different from those Mochi had in mind. With her power behind his kanji he defeated the Myojin of Life's Web when it appeared to claim the princess. Then he drew a character on Choryu that lifted the murderer into the air and sent him straight into Hidetsugu's home.
Later Toshi stole a treasure called the Shadow Gate from a crime lord, and the Myojin joined it to his body. After that he could step into any shadow on Kamigawa and out of any other.
Michiko hired him. When her father had her brought home and locked up, Toshi walked out of a shadow in her room and took her away again.

Hidetsugu took his time with Choryu and learned who had given the orders. Then the ogre went to war against the school of Minamo and the moonfolk's city in the clouds. He had enslaved a band of mountain warrior-priests to fight for him, and he called on his own dreadful patron, a demon known as the All-Consuming Oni of Chaos, which came in the form of a storm of disembodied jaws.

Michiko, against Toshi's advice, had gone to Minamo to question the wizard Hisoka about her birth. She and her friends were there when the ogre arrived. Toshi got them out. The school and the cloud city were laid waste.
By then Toshi's loyalties were shifting from the brotherhood to the goddess, and Hidetsugu knew it. The two old partners ended as enemies. In their last fight the ogre lost both his eyes.
In that twentieth year O-Kagachi itself came through the veil. Almost nobody on Kamigawa had even known that it existed.

Konda had sent three thousand warriors to recover his daughter from the thief. The Great Serpent's jaws came up out of the earth and down out of the sky together and swallowed the whole army in one bite, with a piece of the country. It brushed aside the All-Consuming Oni of Chaos, Hidetsugu's patron, with ease.

Then it appeared on the plains south of Eiganjo and rolled towards the castle like a storm front made of coils. The castle's guardian, a dragon spirit named Yosei, the Morning Star, flew up to meet it. One of the eight heads caught Yosei and tore him in half.
Konda waited in his tower, sure that the stone would protect him. O-Kagachi crushed his armies and broke his castle, which was guarded by some of the strongest spells on the plane, into ruins.
In the middle of it Toshi stepped out of a shadow in Konda's inner chamber, picked up the stone disc from its stand, and stepped back.
Toshi's idea, as far as he had one, was to set the Great Serpent against the smiling kami who had started it all. He left the stone beside Mochi. Later he took it back.

The Myojin of Night's Reach had forbidden him to carry That Which Was Taken through her realm of shadows. In the end, with O-Kagachi overhead and enemies on every side, he did it anyway. She was furious, until the thing in the stone struck at her and cracked her mask. She fled. Toshi was thrown out of the shadows stripped of everything she had given him, and of his own kanji magic too.

He had one thing left, which was what he knew. He brought the stone to Michiko in the forest of Jukai and told her what it was to her. She and the spirit inside it had come into the world of flesh in the same hour, by the same act. In every way that mattered they were sisters.
O-Kagachi was forming in the sky above the forest. Michiko laid her hands on the disc. Toshi wrote two words on it in his own blood: sisters, and united.
The stone shattered. The spirit that had been shut inside it for twenty years came out free. It took a shape like Michiko's own, with the features of a dragon, and it took a name, Kyodai.

The two joined together, a mortal woman and a kami as one being, something new in the world. Together they destroyed O-Kagachi and took its place. Since then the Sisters of Flesh and Spirit have been the veil between the two halves of Kamigawa and its guardians.

Konda arrived at the head of an army of his own dead warriors, who had risen as spirits, to take back his prize. Kyodai dealt with him herself. She put out his eyes. She turned his deathless body to stone and broke it into a million pieces. Because he could not die, he remained alive and aware in every piece. The fragments are said to lie in the forest of Jukai still.

Mochi came forward smiling to make friends with the new powers. The Sisters opened a gate into the realm of the All-Consuming Oni. Out of it came Hidetsugu. He had been sent to his patron's lair blind and beaten, and there he had merged with the demon as the Sisters had merged with each other. The thing that had been the ogre tore the Smiling Kami of the Crescent Moon apart and ate him, in payment for Kobo.

The war was over. Michiko refused the title of emperor. She spent the rest of her life trying to heal the plane, and she decided that this could not be done without the truth, so she told her people what her father had done. Many hated her for it, and for her union with the Serpent's child. Later ages judged that she had been right. She is counted as the first emperor of the Kamigawa that came afterwards.
Toshi walked away from the forest. A few miles on, a vengeful moonfolk woman named Chiyo ambushed him and ran him through the chest.
The Myojin of Night's Reach chose that moment to forgive him. He swore himself to her again, and his attacker was destroyed.

Her forgiveness had limits. By helping to make a new guardian of the veil, Toshi had closed the borders of Kamigawa again and had cost the goddess her freedom to roam the Multiverse. For that she took his eyes. Then she carried him out of his world altogether and set him down in another, one that she had found on her travels. She told him that she was planting him there.

The blind man stood on a strange shore. It was the coast of Madara, on Dominaria, near the place called the Talon Gates. That is the spot where, eighteen thousand years earlier, Nicol Bolas had fought the Demonic Leviathan. Toshi turned inland, towards the smell of swamps.

He founded a family there, the clan Umezawa. Centuries later a man of that clan, Tetsuo Umezawa, did what gods and planeswalkers had failed to do. He killed Nicol Bolas. That story has its own chapter.

chapters.title: Tarkir: The Fall of the Spirit Dragon
sources: Kate Elliott, "Chronicle of Bolas" (Wizards of the Coast, eight episodes, June to August 2018)

blocks.p: This chapter closes the age of the Thaw, and it returns to the two oldest characters in the story: the twin dragons Ugin and Nicol Bolas.

They were born on Dominaria about twenty thousand years before the brothers Urza and Mishra. Both became planeswalkers. Bolas became a conqueror who believes that everything exists to be ruled by him. Ugin became a scholar of the Multiverse, a dragon of spirit who keeps watch over dangers greater than his brother. About -15,000 AR Bolas killed Ugin in the Meditation Realm, the strange still place where the twins used to meet, and believed him gone. Ugin was not gone. He returned, and about -1400 AR he helped to imprison the Eldrazi on Zendikar inside a network of floating stones called hedrons.
Ugin has a second home, a plane called Tarkir. An early chapter said that he shaped it. He is bound to it so closely that he is called its soul.

This chapter needs one warning. Something happens in it that cannot be fully explained yet, because it is caused by a man who will not be born for more than twelve hundred years. The story tells what was seen at the time, and gives the reason when it reaches that man's own day.
Tarkir is a hard, wide world of steppe, mountain, jungle and desert. In this age five clans of people lived on it, each with a leader called a khan.

The Abzan were a clan of desert fortresses and families, who honoured the spirits of their ancestors. The Jeskai were monks and mystics of the high lakes. The Sultai were a rich and cruel empire of the jungle, served by the walking dead. The Mardu were a horde of mounted raiders. The Temur were hunters and shamans of the frozen mountains.
The clans had one enemy in common. Tarkir was full of dragons.

The dragons of Tarkir are not born from eggs. They come out of storms. Great tempests of magic roll across the sky, and when one breaks, living dragons fall out of it, full grown and hungry. The storms are tied to Ugin. They are a kind of overflow of his presence in the world. While Ugin lived on Tarkir the storms kept coming, and so did the dragons.

There were five great broods, each descended from one mighty dragon: Dromoka in the desert, Ojutai in the high cold places, Silumgar in the jungle, Kolaghan over the steppe and Atarka in the mountains. The clans did not fight one another much in this age. They were too busy defending themselves from the sky. Killing a dragon was the greatest deed a warrior could do.

Ugin had not left the clans helpless. He had taught each of them some secret of magic. To the shamans of the Temur he taught a way of sharing thoughts and visions, called the whisper. To the Jeskai he taught the use of his own invisible flame, ghostfire. He gave each clan something, so that none would outgrow the others.

parts.h: The sphinx and the trap (before 3179 AR)

blocks.p: Ugin had known for a very long time that his brother would have to be stopped. About a hundred years before the events of this chapter, he found an ally.

Azor was a sphinx, a great winged creature with the body of a lion and a bearded human face, and he was a planeswalker. He appeared earlier in this story as the lawgiver of the city-world Ravnica, the author of its Guildpact. Azor travelled from plane to plane imposing systems of law, and he and Ugin had a common enemy.

They made a plan. They did not mean to kill Bolas. They meant to cage him. Azor would build a device with one overriding power: no planeswalker could leave the plane on which it stood. Ugin would lure Bolas to Tarkir. Bolas believed that Ugin would never risk the world he loved, and so he would not expect a trap there. Ugin would hold him, and send a signal. Azor's device would then be used to trap Bolas, so that he could never walk between worlds again.

Azor built it. It was a great slab of stone, and he called it the Immortal Sun. To give it power enough, he put his own planeswalker's spark into it. That was a terrible price. It meant that Azor himself could never walk between worlds again. About 3279 AR he took the Immortal Sun to the plane he had chosen as the prison, a world named Ixalan, and waited there for Ugin's signal.
Bolas was making preparations of his own, and his way was to find somebody on the spot whose wishes he could use.

Yasova Dragonclaw was the khan of the Temur. She was a powerful shaman, and she went everywhere with a great sabre-toothed cat named Anchin. She had spent her life watching her people be burned and eaten, and she hated the dragons with her whole heart.

About 3279 AR she began to receive visions. A voice showed her a future Tarkir with no dragons in it: quiet skies, fields of dragon bones, no more storms. In that future the Temur ruled the world, and a woman of her own blood was khan over all the khans. The voice told her how it could be done. If the Spirit Dragon died, the storms would end, and the dragons would die out. The voice would do the killing itself. It asked only one thing of her. She was to follow the dragon storms, which always led towards Ugin, and to mark the trail.
Yasova did it. She tracked the storms across the mountains, and wherever she passed she burned a sign into the ground with her staff: two curves, like a pair of horns.

On that journey a stranger fell out of nowhere into the snow of the Temur country. He was a wild-looking man who talked to voices that were not there. He gave his name as Sarkhan Vol. On Tarkir the word sar means great or sky, and Yasova took the name as an insult and the man as a lunatic.

He followed her all the same. When she pressed him, he told her things that made her think again. Where he came from, he said, there were no dragon storms. There were no dragons at all. They had died out more than a thousand years before his time. He was a man of Tarkir. He had come back out of its future.
Yasova was delighted. It meant that her vision was true and her plan would work. She told him about the voice, and about the marks.

Sarkhan looked at the marks again, and understood what the two curves were. They were the horns of Nicol Bolas. He had known Bolas in his own time, and had served him, and had gone half mad in that service. Bolas was coming to Tarkir to kill Ugin, and he was coming now.
Sarkhan had a gift of his own. He could take the shape of a dragon. He changed, and flew for the heart of the storm.

parts.h: The battle in the sky (3279 AR)

blocks.p: Ugin was waiting in the eye of a tempest, as the plan required. The air split, and Nicol Bolas came through. The brothers faced each other and seemed to speak.
Then they fought. Ugin called the dragons of Tarkir to him. They were his own offspring, in a sense, and they gathered about him.

Bolas struck at his brother, and Ugin held him off. For a little while the fight was even. Then Bolas turned his brother's own strength against him. Bolas is, above everything else, a master of the mind. He reached into the dragons of Tarkir and gave them one command. On the ground below, Yasova cast a spell that carried the command further. Every dragon in that sky heard the same thing: kill Ugin.
Sarkhan heard it too, in his dragon's body, and felt it take hold of him. He could only escape it by ceasing to be a dragon. He threw off the shape in mid-air and fell.

The broods of Tarkir turned on their own source and tore at him. When Ugin was weakened, Bolas delivered the blow that finished it. The Spirit Dragon fell out of the sky and struck the mountains so hard that his body smashed a canyon into the rock. It had not been there before.
Bolas looked at his work and left, in a burst of golden light.
No signal was ever sent to Ixalan.

Yasova found the stranger broken on the ground and began to heal him. She wanted answers. Before she had finished he lurched to his feet, drove her back with fire, and staggered away to find the place where Ugin had fallen.
He climbed down into the new canyon. The Spirit Dragon lay at the bottom, dying.

Sarkhan begged Ugin to tell him what to do. He had spent years following a voice that he believed was Ugin's. Ugin spoke into his mind for the last time. He told Sarkhan that he would go on failing for as long as he sought guidance in place of truth.

Sarkhan had carried one thing with him all the way: a small shard of stone from another world. It was a fragment of a hedron, broken from the prison that Ugin had helped to build on Zendikar. He held it out and woke it. The shard unfolded. It grew into a great lattice of floating stones, and the stones closed round the dying dragon like a shell.
Then Sarkhan Vol vanished from the canyon, and from that age.
The shell held. Inside it Ugin was neither alive nor dead. He was preserved, exactly as the hedrons of Zendikar preserved the Eldrazi. And because something of Ugin endured, the storms did not stop.

Here is the one thing that can be said now about what really happened. In the first course of events there was no stranger. Ugin died in that canyon. The storms ended, the dragons of Tarkir died out, and the five clans lived on for twelve centuries in a world of dragon bones. Sarkhan Vol was born into that world. He found a way back, and he changed it. Everything after this point follows the changed course, which is the only one that anybody now remembers. The Temur shamans kept a tale of it: a dragon man, a khan of the sky, who came to save the Spirit Dragon and disappeared again.
Bolas did not know. He could not see through the hedrons, and his fire slid off them. He believed that his brother was dead at last.

parts.h: The fall of the khans (c. 3282 AR)

blocks.p: Yasova's bargain had failed. The storms did not end. They grew stronger. More dragons fell from the sky every year, and the five great dragons, who had been merely the mightiest of their kind, became the masters of the world. They are called the dragonlords.
Within a few years the clans faced a plain choice: give up their old ways, or die.

The Sultai broke first, from inside. Their khan was Tasigur, a pampered and vicious young man who had come to the throne at fifteen or sixteen, about 3279 AR. He was carried about his palace on a platform borne by the dead and amused himself with a whip. He insulted one of the demon cat-sorcerers on whose magic his empire depended. The sorcerers and the serpent-folk both abandoned him, and the Sultai lost command of their dead.

The Abzan were next. Their khan, Daghatar, decided to submit to the dragonlord Dromoka. Dromoka would not tolerate the worship of ancestors. As the sign of his submission Daghatar smashed his own mace, which held the spirits of his forebears, and the Abzan pulled up the sacred trees in which their dead were kept.

The remaining leaders met in secret at a stronghold called Dirgur to decide what could still be done. Shu Yun, khan of the Jeskai, was there, and Alesha of the Mardu, and Yasova of the Temur, and Reyhan, who led those Abzan who had refused to give in, and Tasigur. Tasigur had betrayed the meeting place to the dragons.

The broods of Silumgar and Ojutai fell on the fortress. Reyhan was killed. Shu Yun bought his people's survival. Ojutai demanded the death of every Jeskai who had ever killed a dragon, the khan included, and Shu Yun and the warriors of the ghostfire gave up their lives so that the rest might live. Alesha, Yasova and Tasigur got away.

Alesha had been born about 3260 AR, had earned her name at sixteen and had become khan at nineteen, and she was called Alesha Who Smiles at Death because she had once killed a dragon with a single stroke, smiling. She saw what the dragonlord Kolaghan was. Kolaghan cared for nothing but speed and the open sky. Alesha led the Mardu out behind her, to ride wherever the dragon flew.

Yasova saw that Atarka cared for nothing but eating. She dragged the carcass of a mammoth before the dragonlord, and it was accepted. As long as the Temur kept Atarka fed, they were allowed to live. Yasova gave up the title of Dragonclaw, which Atarka forbade on pain of being eaten. She hid her real staff in a cave and handed over a copy to be destroyed. She had helped to kill the soul of her world for the sake of a future without dragons, and she spent the rest of her life hunting to feed one.
Tasigur went back to Silumgar to collect his reward. The dragonlord kept him. In later ages a shrivelled body could be seen hanging among the ornaments on Silumgar's necklace.
That was the Khanfall. The clans were finished, and the word khan itself was forbidden. For the next twelve hundred years the people of Tarkir lived as servants of five dragons.
One more scene belongs here, though it happened eighteen years after the battle. It was told in the stories called the Chronicle of Bolas.

Yasova was by then an old woman leading a small hunting band. She had twin granddaughters, Naiva and Baishya. Baishya had the shaman's gift, which Atarka punished with death. Visions began to reach the girl, of the birth of the first dragons on another world, and Yasova understood who was sending them. Something of Ugin was still alive. She took her band to the canyon.
Nicol Bolas was there. He had come back to make sure. He still could not see through the hedrons. He set to work on the girl Naiva with his voice, and very nearly had her.

Yasova and Baishya walked out to face him and told him a lie. He was standing, they said, exactly where the hedrons focused their power. Ugin had tricked him after all. The Immortal Sun was aimed at this very spot, and in a moment it would seize him and carry him off to a prison for ever. They had only been keeping him talking.

It was half true. There had been such a plot. Bolas knew that there had. He could not take the chance. He left Tarkir in a flash of gold, bringing the canyon wall down behind him. He never learned that his brother was sleeping under his feet.
Two ends remain.

Azor waited on Ixalan for a signal that never came. He had given up his spark to make the Immortal Sun, and he could not leave. The lawgiver of Ravnica was stranded on a world he had meant to use as someone else's prison. What he did there, and what became of the Immortal Sun, are part of Ixalan's story.

Bolas went back to Dominaria. About this time he took a kingdom there. Madara is a group of islands west of the continent of Jamuraa, the very place where he had fought the Demonic Leviathan when the world was young. Three kinds of mana met at one point on the main island, and that made it a good foothold. An empire stood there, founded by a warrior queen who called herself a god-empress. Bolas killed her and took her place. He ruled Madara as its god-emperor for about four hundred years.
A blind man from Kamigawa had come ashore on those same islands some fifty years before, and had founded a family in the swamps. Its name was Umezawa.

chapters.title: The Tolarian Academy
sources: MTG Wiki, "Time Streams" (the novel by J. Robert King, 1999)
MTG Wiki, "Founding of the Tolarian Academy"

blocks.p: A new age begins here, and it is the longest and most eventful in the story so far. It is called the War with Phyrexia, and it runs from 3285 to 4206 AR. It begins with the founding of a school and ends with the invasion of a world.

The man at the centre of it is Urza. He is the artificer who ended the Brothers' War with a single blast in 64 AR and became a planeswalker in doing it, with two powerstones for eyes. He has spent more than three thousand years fighting Phyrexia, the plane of flesh joined to machine, whose lord Yawgmoth means to conquer Dominaria. Most of that time Urza fought alone and badly, half mad from a wound that Yawgmoth dealt to his mind.

In 3245 AR, in the cave of Koilos, Urza killed the Phyrexian demon Gix, who had corrupted his brother Mishra. It cost the lives of his only two friends: Xantcha, a Phyrexian creature who had turned against her makers and travelled with him for three thousand years, and Ratepe, a young man who had posed as Mishra to bring him back to his senses. From their deaths Urza took a resolve. He would stop reacting to Phyrexia and begin to prepare, with every resource the world could give him. He had also learned at last where the Phyrexians came from. They were Thran, people of ancient Dominaria, cast out five thousand years before his birth.
He still had Xantcha's heart, the small stone that had held her life.
The source for this chapter and the next is the novel Time Streams by J. Robert King, as the encyclopaedia summarises it.

Tolaria was an island in the middle of the ocean, far to the west of the continent of Jamuraa, ringed with coral reefs. It was tropical and lightly wooded, with palms on its shores. It lay far from every other land on Dominaria, and that was the reason Urza chose it.

In 3285 AR he founded a school there. His partner in it was a mortal wizard named Barrin. An earlier chapter told of Barrin's beginning as a scribe in Kjeldor at the end of the Ice Age. He had become a master of magic, and he was the first true colleague Urza had ever had. Barrin held the title of Mage Master. Urza did not use his own name. To the students he was Master Malzra, the headmaster, an odd and distant old man. Only Barrin knew who he really was.

The school gathered the most gifted young people from all over Dominaria to study artifice and magic. It took only children. Urza had a hard reason for that rule. Phyrexia's sleeper agents, its spies grown in vats to pass as human, never appeared as children.

Most of those children believed that they were simply at a very good school. Its real purposes were known only to Urza and Barrin. One was to train the mages who would lead Dominaria's defence when the invasion came. The other was a single enormous project.
Urza meant to build a machine that could travel into the past. He wanted to go back five thousand years, to the time of the Thran, and stop the birth of Phyrexia before it happened.

No living thing can survive a journey through time. Urza's experiments had shown that only one substance passes through the forces involved unharmed, and that is silver. So Urza built a traveller out of silver: a golem, an artificial man, well over two metres tall, modelled on the avengers that he had built for the kingdom of Yotia three thousand years before.

A machine was not enough. The traveller would be alone in the past and would have to judge and decide for itself. It needed a mind that could learn. Urza had one thing that could give it that. He set Xantcha's heart in the golem's chest. In 3307 AR the silver man opened his eyes.
Urza had built him to feel pain, and to have feelings. He did not at first feel much except indifference. He understood that he was a tool, and that tools are replaced.

Urza handed the new golem over to a student, to be taught about the world. The student was Teferi, a boy of fourteen from the kingdom of Zhalfir in Jamuraa. Teferi was the most gifted young mage in the school and its worst nuisance, a joker and something of a bully. He treated the golem as a wonderful toy. He named it Arty Shovelhead.

An older student put a stop to it. Jhoira was eighteen. She came from Shiv, a land of volcanoes and deserts, where her people, the Ghitu, live as nomads. She had left them to learn artifice and bring it home. She took the golem away from Teferi and taught him properly. She also gave him a real name: Karn, which is the Thran word for mighty.
Jhoira was Karn's first friend, and he has said ever since that she is his one true friend. Teferi, for his part, was hopelessly taken with Jhoira, who thought of him as a child.

The experiments went forward. Karn was sent back a few hours, and then a full day. Each journey burned him with terrible heat. Each one also left small tears in the flow of time around the school, and the students began to fall sick from them. The tears grew worse.
Jhoira liked to walk on the shore and think about home. One day she found a shipwrecked sailor there. He was a handsome man with golden hair and blue eyes, and he said that his name was Kerrick.

She did not report him. She was lonely among the schoolboys. She hid him in a cave on the beach and visited him at night by a secret way out of the school, and she fell in love with him. The only one she told was Karn. Karn had come upon the two of them while he was displaced a few hours into the past, and he promised to keep her secret.

On a later journey Karn saw a shadowy figure stealing from Urza's laboratory. A time traveller is not quite solid in the past he visits, and Karn was able to follow the thief unseen. It was Kerrick. Kerrick went out by Jhoira's secret way to a meeting in the woods, and there Karn heard him ask for a squad of negators to be sent. Negators are Phyrexia's killers, monsters bred to hunt and destroy.
Kerrick was a sleeper agent. Urza had guarded against every way a spy might get in except the kindness of a lonely girl.

Karn returned to his own hour and ran to warn Urza. He was too late. The negators were already inside the school, slaughtering students and teachers. Karn fought his way to Jhoira's room. He found her body on the floor, torn in half. He killed the thing that had done it.

Urza appeared beside him. Barrin was dead as well, he said, and so was the boy Teferi. There was one thing left to try. The machine was close to breaking. Urza asked Karn to go back once more, further than before, and stop Kerrick before any of it happened.
Karn went. He found Kerrick in the past and broke his leg, and the attack never came.

That saved Jhoira, Barrin and Teferi, and it changed far too much. The machine could not bear the strain of so great an alteration. Karn was wrenched back to the present as it began to tear itself apart. Rays of time poured out of it, and whatever they touched aged to dust in a moment. Then it exploded.
Urza had an instant. He turned the fourteen people nearest to him to stone to protect them, Barrin among them, and walked away between the worlds with them.

Wave after wave of blinding light blew the Academy to pieces. Hundreds of students and teachers died. The island was left broken into regions where time itself ran at different speeds. In some, time raced. In others it almost stood still. Anybody who stepped across the edge of such a region without knowing it was killed by the change. A rift in time was also torn in the sky above the island, though nobody noticed it for centuries.
Karn stood at the centre of the explosion and was unharmed, because he was silver. He dug survivors out of the rubble, about thirty of them, and got them away by sea. He could not find Jhoira.

Urza counted it a fair exchange. Barrin was alive again. Karn looked at the ruins and the dead and thought that nothing could excuse it. Hundreds of people had died so that a few might live, and Karn did not forgive it.
The school went on, afloat. Its survivors continued their studies aboard a great sailing ship, which they named New Tolaria.
The same year saw another arrival out of the past, far away, with no connection to Tolaria at all.

In about 170 AR the merfolk Empress Galina of Vodalia had fled from the lobster-like homarids through a magical portal with many of her people. The portal carried them three thousand years forward. In 3307 AR they came out of it in the waters of a merfolk realm called Etlan Shiis. After the first shock, Galina's army defeated the council that ruled there, and she founded her empire a second time as New Vodalia. She reigned over it for nine hundred years.
Jhoira had survived, in a part of the island where time ran normally. She was alone there for ten years.

She learned the island as nobody else could. She mapped the edges of every region of fast time and slow time, by throwing things across them and watching what happened. She found a pool whose water had been changed by the disaster, and she drank from it. The slow-time water all but stopped her ageing. She would look like a young woman for thousands of years.
She found two other survivors.

One was Teferi. He was inside a bubble of time so slow that he looked like a statue: a boy caught in mid-stride, running, with his clothes on fire. Jhoira could not reach him. She threw a wet blanket across the edge at him. It took five years to arrive and put the flames out.

The other was Kerrick. He and the Phyrexians who had come at his call were trapped in a deep gorge where time ran ten times faster than outside. He could not get out. But for every year that passed on the island, ten passed for him.

In 3317 AR Urza, Barrin and Karn sailed back to Tolaria with a new class of students. Their first steps ashore were a disaster. People walked into the invisible edges of the time regions and died. Then a wild-haired, sun-darkened woman came out of the trees and showed them where it was safe to walk.

Jhoira was furious with Urza for what his experiment had done, and she showed him the worst of it. She took him to the gorge. A hundred years had passed inside it. It was now a fortress, and it was full of negators.

Kerrick had changed his name to something more Phyrexian, K'rrik. He had built vats and was breeding generation after generation of killers. Time had been unkind to his own body. His flesh had died on him and he had replaced it piece by piece with grafts from his own creatures, until he looked like a man stitched together out of eels, with venomous spikes at every joint. Only his face and his blue eyes were still human. One thing held him back. He had very little metal.

Urza began to rebuild, and in 3320 AR he attacked. He bombed the gorge from a great airship. It did heavy damage, and K'rrik lured the ship low enough to destroy it. Urza and Jhoira both lived, but Jhoira was so badly hurt that she fell into a sleep from which nobody could wake her. She lay unconscious for ten years.
Jhoira woke in 3330 AR, the year the rebuilt Academy was finished.

She had the answer ready. Water was less affected by the broken time than living flesh was. By running water from a fast region into a slow one, a passage could be made between the two through which a person could safely pass. She built a machine to do it.

The first use of it was to fetch Teferi. The passage was only a rough prototype, and only the toughest bodies could go through it: Urza's and Karn's. They went into the slow bubble and pulled the boy out.

Twenty-three years had gone by outside, by the chronicle's dates. The encyclopaedia elsewhere says thirty. For Teferi it had been well under a minute. He was still fourteen. Everyone he had known was dead or grown up. The girl he had adored was now a woman who had lived through things he could not imagine. He was miserable for a while and felt out of step with the whole world. Karn and Jhoira helped him through it, the golem he had tormented and the girl who had thought him a pest, and in the years that followed the prankster grew into a serious and very able mage. Time became his special study.

Jhoira's machine did more than rescue one boy. It turned the island's ruin into its greatest asset. A researcher could now step into a fast-time region, do ten years of work, and step out again a year later. Water from the slow regions could add centuries to a human life. Barrin used it, and so did others. For the first time Urza had a way to catch up with an enemy who had a start of five thousand years.
The enemy in the gorge had the same advantage, of course, and had had it for longer.

chapters.title: Jedit Ojanen and the Tyrant of Tirras

blocks.p: While Urza was rebuilding his school on Tolaria, a war was fought on the continent of Jamuraa that had nothing to do with Phyrexia at all. It is one of the old adventure stories of Dominaria, and it finishes a tale that an earlier chapter left open.

That tale was about the tiger warriors. About 2600 AR a planeswalker named Terrent Amese made a people by fusing human and tiger, to guard a place of power in the jungle of Scarwood. He let them believe that he was their god. Their first leader, Ojanen, saw through him and led the tribe towards freedom. Terrent Amese cursed Ojanen's line and loosed a monster called Ur-Drago on the tribe. Ojanen faced it alone while his people fled, and nobody ever learned how the fight ended. The tiger people settled in a desert and came to believe that their kindly god had abandoned them because of Ojanen's sin. They grew timid and suspicious of anything new, and for seven hundred years they kept away from the forest where they were made.

Another earlier chapter mentioned the city of Tirras. It grew up at the foot of the Blue Mountains on soil washed down by the floods of the Thaw, a crowded city shut in by mountains and desert, with one river, the Toloron, leading south.
The story was first told in a comic and then retold in three novels, named Johan, Jedit and Hazezon. It is followed here through the encyclopaedia.

Three places lay along the Toloron. At its source stood Tirras. At its mouth, on the sea coast, stood the free city of Bryce. Halfway down stood Palmyra, a village of pirates, outlaws and misfits. East of the river stretched the Sukurvian Desert, where enormous sand wurms hunted beneath the dunes.

Bryce was governed by Hazezon Tamar, an ageing, white-bearded man in the robes of the desert coast. He carried a scimitar as a badge of office, but his real weapon was his mind. He was a mage, and his speciality was sand.

Palmyra was the home of Adira Strongheart, a pirate captain decades younger than Hazezon, who dressed like a man and wore gold bangles from her hair to her boots. She led a band of adventurers called the Robaran Mercenaries, and kept the best seven of them about her as bodyguards. For all their name, they could be a kindly company, and they went on many errands of mercy.

The two had been married. They wed in 3320 AR. In 3324 AR the mercenaries plundered the ship of a prince from the far continent of Corondor and came away with a fortune. Hazezon sold the goods, grew rich, settled down and became governor of Bryce. Adira had no wish to settle down. She left him, went back to Palmyra, and stayed a pirate.

The ruler of Tirras was a mage named Johan. He was tall, with skin the colour of fire, tattooed in so many stripes that he looked like a tiger himself. Two horns curled down from his brow and a third jutted from his chin. He was a master of the magic of mountains and fire, and of illusion, and he wrapped himself in protective spells so strong that he could fight in the front rank beside his soldiers without fear.

Johan called himself Emperor of the Northern Realms. He had united his own city with the barbarian tribes of the mountains, and he believed, sincerely, that he was good for his people and that all of Jamuraa ought to be ruled by him. His city had to expand or starve, and it could only expand down the river.
In 3334 AR Johan marched south. Hazezon and Adira put aside their quarrel and met him at Palmyra.

They had an unexpected ally. A stranger had walked out of the eastern desert: a creature nobody on the river had ever seen, two metres tall and as heavy as a horse, with the striped face of a tiger, white with age about the muzzle. He wore a harness of bark and carried a knife of bronze. His name was Jaeger Ojanen. Among the tiger warriors he was that rare thing, a wanderer, who had left the oasis of his people to see the world.

The battle was decided by Hazezon. He raised a magical sandstorm that scattered Johan's army. In the confusion Johan and Jaeger came face to face. Then the sand opened beneath them, and a wurm took the old tiger.
Johan had lost his army, and he blamed the tiger man for it.
Johan fled alone across the desert on the back of a fire drake and barely reached an oasis. It was Efrava, the hidden home of Jaeger's tribe.

The tiger warriors had never seen a human being. They had thought that humans were a legend. Johan disguised himself as an ordinary man and looked about for someone he could use. He found Jaeger's son.

Jedit Ojanen was as restless as his father, and he wanted above all to know what had become of him. Johan laid a charm on him. Under its influence Jedit begged the elders to let the stranger stay, with himself as guardian. The elders agreed unwillingly.

Johan toured the oasis from end to end with Jedit at his side. All the while he was quietly binding its land to himself as a source of magic, and mapping it for a future conquest. He meant to send Jedit to kill Hazezon and Adira. The plan turned on him. He was found out, killed two tiger guards and fled west into the desert. Jedit, free of the charm and furious, went after him.

Johan's road led to a fortress in the marshes, the home of Shauku. Shauku was an ancient vampire who kept a library of terrible books and let scholars read them for a price in blood. She lured Johan in with a promise of knowledge about where the tiger men had come from. Her real purpose was to make him her slave.
Johan broke free. Jedit and Adira Strongheart arrived on his trail, and between all of them the castle was destroyed. Johan escaped again and made his way home to Tirras.

He had learned something useful. He now knew of a whole people of tiger warriors living in an oasis that lay exactly between the two halves of Jamuraa. Enslaved, they would be an army nobody could stop, and their home was the perfect base. His conquest of the continent would begin with them.
Jedit had learned something too. He could not find his father, but he found his father's friends. He joined the Robaran Mercenaries and became the comrade of Adira and Hazezon.
Then he did what no tiger warrior had done in seven hundred years. He went into Scarwood.

In the heart of the jungle he found the great temple that his ancestors had built, the Tabernacle at Pendrell Vale. The true history of his people was painted on its walls: the maker who was no god, the slavery, and Ojanen's stand.

The monster was still there. By one account Jedit was carried by magic back to the moment of the old duel itself. Either way it was Jedit Ojanen who fought Ur-Drago in those halls, and killed it, and finished what the first Ojanen began.

He took the truth back to the desert. The tiger tribes had split into four bands over the centuries. Jedit persuaded all four that Terrent Amese had never been a god, that their ancestor had been a hero and not a sinner, and that the forest now belonged to the elves who had lived in it since. He won them a right of safe passage to visit the place of their beginning. For the first time since the exodus, the cat warriors acted as one people.
Johan had learned from the sand wurms. This time he would cross the desert through the air. In Tirras he built a fleet of flying ships.

The Robaran Mercenaries went north to spy on him and were caught. Johan shut Hazezon and Adira in a room with no door and no window. He did not know that Hazezon had mastered the art of stepping from one place to another by magic. The two got out and carried a warning home, and the city-states of the south began building flying ships of their own under Hazezon's direction.
The fleets met over the oasis of Efrava. The humans of the river and all the tribes of the tiger warriors fought side by side against the tyrant.

Johan commanded from his flagship, the Icewind, and for a time his magic carried all before it. He turned one of Hazezon's own spells back on him and struck him down. The surviving mercenaries boarded the Icewind and went straight for the emperor. Johan's spells made him all but invulnerable and terribly strong. He killed Adira Strongheart with his bare hands, tearing the heart out of her chest.
